docs.title: Ajax
docs.text:
Reinforcement-learning agents in JAX, compiled end to end with the environment, including average-reward, expert-guided and world-model agents. A whole training run, environment and every seed included, one compiled program.

Compared with Stable-Baselines3 and its JAX version SBX, Ajax differs in four ways:

  • End to end on the accelerator: the environment and the training loop compile into one JAX program, as in PureJaxRL, Rejax, Stoix and Brax's training agents, with no Python step between them, on a CPU or a GPU.
  • Average-reward agents: ASAC and APO maximise the reward per step, with no discount, for tasks that never end.
  • Expert-guided agents: learn from a controller you already have, or from recorded transitions, by cloning, imitation, residual policies, hand-over, prior data in the replay or offline training. Choosing the pieces names each method and its paper: TD3+BC, Q-filtered cloning, kickstarting, residual RL, JSRL, IBRL, RLPD's prior data, IQL, CQL, Cal-QL, ReBRAC, GAIL, DAgger.
  • World models: DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2, following the code behind their papers' results.

Why Ajax shows each with an example and compares Ajax with SB3, SBX, PureJaxRL, Brax, Stoix and Rejax, including when to use them instead.

Ajax has sixteen agents, from SAC and PPO to DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2. Each implements a published paper, and its page lists where it departs from it. Several seeds train side by side in one program, on a CPU or a GPU. Research features (learning from an expert, exploration rules, diagnostics) are extensions, passed as extensions=(...) rather than added as new arguments to the agents. An agent refuses, when built, an extension it cannot run; Compatibility shows which agent runs which.

git clone https://github.com/YannBerthelot/Ajax.git
cd Ajax
uv sync

from ajax import PPO
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = PPO("CartPole-v1")  # 4 environments x 2048-step rollouts: one update per 8,192 steps
# Evaluate after every update; use_wandb=False keeps the results in memory only.
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=8_192, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[1, 2, 3], n_timesteps=40_960, logging_config=logging)

print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])  # one row per seed, one column per evaluation

docs.text: Kind Agents Off-policy actor-critic SAC, ASAC (average reward), REDQ, TD3 Offline, then online IQL Incremental, no replay AVG Value-based, discrete actions DQN, PQN On-policy PPO, APO (average reward) Supervised, command-conditioned UDRL Imitation of an expert, no reward DAgger Differentiable simulation APG World models DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and its multi-task variant

docs.title: What else is in the box
docs.text:
• Extensions: expert guidance, exploration, critic-target changes, actor and critic pre-training, offline RL, adversarial imitation and diagnostics, each usable with the agents that run the training phases it touches.
  • Training offline: a replay agent trains on a transition dataset before it acts, then fine-tunes online.
  • Expert guidance: learn from an existing controller, which reads the environment's raw observations and answers in its action units.
  • Memory: GRU, LSTM, transformer or Mamba blocks, with R2D2-style sequence replay.
  • PID policy: a PID controller as the actor, whose learned gains deploy as a plain PID.
  • Differentiable simulation: APG through gymnax dynamics, across distributions of physical parameters.
  • World models: DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2, following the paper-era official code.
  • Environments: gymnax, Brax and MuJoCo Playground by id, with wrappers for normalisation, observation noise, reference tracking and more; every continuous agent's [-1, 1] actions are mapped onto the environment's bounds.
  • Logging and checkpoints: evaluations as arrays, W&B or TensorBoard, resuming in another process.
  • Performance: every seed in one program, a persistent compile cache, one per machine and JAX version.
  • Comparing agents: AdaStop, which trains more seeds only while the answer is unclear, and confidence intervals for one agent's metrics.
  • Reproduction: Ajax agents trained beside reference implementations on the same JAX environment, under a written protocol.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: Ajax has sixteen agents, all exported from ajax. Each follows a published paper, and each page says where Ajax departs from it. Every agent takes an environment (TDMPC2MultiTask: a dataset, and environments to evaluate on), its own hyperparameters, episode_length and action_repeat (for Brax and Playground environments) and extensions=(). It trains one or several seeds in a single compiled program with agent.train(seed=[...], n_timesteps=...).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Agent Family Paper Actions Memory Extra extension phases SAC off-policy actor-critic Haarnoja et al. 2018 (arXiv:1801.01290) continuous yes on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss, action ASAC off-policy actor-critic, average reward Adamczyk et al. 2025 (arXiv:2501.09080v2) continuous yes on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss REDQ off-policy actor-critic, critic ensemble Chen et al. 2021 (arXiv:2101.05982) continuous yes on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss TD3 off-policy actor-critic, deterministic policy Fujimoto et al. 2018 (arXiv:1802.09477) continuous yes on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss IQL offline actor-critic, expectile value Kostrikov, Nair and Levine, ICLR 2022 (arXiv:2110.06169) continuous no on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss AVG incremental actor-critic, no replay Vasan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2411.15370) continuous no on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss DQN value-based, replay Mnih et al., Nature 2015 discrete no on_target, critic_loss PQN value-based, parallel environments, no replay Gallici et al. 2024 discrete no on_target, critic_loss PPO on-policy policy gradient Schulman et al. 2017 (arXiv:1707.06347) both yes on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss APO on-policy policy gradient, average reward Ma et al. 2021 (arXiv:2106.03442) both no on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss UDRL command-conditioned supervised learning Schmidhuber 2019 (arXiv:1912.02875) both no actor_loss DAgger imitation by dataset aggregation, no reward Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, AISTATS 2011 (arXiv:1011.0686) both no actor_loss APG gradients through a differentiable simulator Busetto et al. 2024 (arXiv:2411.06482) for APG.contextual_controller continuous yes actor_loss DreamerV3 model-based, learns in imagination Hafner et al. 2023, Nature 2025 (arXiv:2301.04104v2) both built in none TDMPC2 model-based, plans at every step Hansen, Su and Wang, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.16828) continuous no none TDMPC2MultiTask model-based, offline, several tasks the same paper continuous no none
  • Actions: both means discrete and continuous action spaces. Agents that take only one kind check it at construction.
  • Memory: whether the agent accepts memory= (a GRU, LSTM, transformer or Mamba block; see Memory). DreamerV3's world model is recurrent by design.
  • Extension phases: every agent folds pretrain, post_update and eval_metrics; the column lists the others it folds. An extension that needs a phase the agent does not fold is refused at construction. See Extensions.
  • Continuous actions: every continuous agent acts in [-1, 1], squashed by tanh or clipped there, and Ajax maps that range onto the environment's bounds before each step: centre + half_range * action. On gymnax Pendulum, whose torque lies in [-2, 2], the agents reach the whole range. Experts are written in the environment's units; Ajax reads them in the agent's. See Environments.
  • Evaluation: with a logging_config, every agent evaluates its policy every log_frequency steps on num_episode_test episodes and train returns the evaluations. Each evaluation draws fresh random keys (new initial states), and a rerun of the same seed draws the same ones. The model-free agents evaluate their deterministic action (the mean, or the greedy action); DreamerV3 samples, as its reference does, and TD-MPC2 plans in evaluation mode. For SAC, TD3, REDQ, AVG, DQN, PQN and PPO, Eval/mean bias is the critic's estimate minus the discounted return actually obtained, averaged over the evaluated steps.

docs.title: Which agent should I use?
docs.text:
Start from your problem, not from the algorithm.

Discrete actions. PPO is the general choice; it also takes memory and image observations. DQN learns from a replay buffer, so it reuses every sample many times. PQN has no replay: it learns from many environments at once, which suits fast JAX simulators.

Continuous actions, and samples are cheap. If the simulator runs many copies in parallel, PPO learns from large fresh rollouts and needs no replay buffer.

Continuous actions, and every sample counts. Use an off-policy agent with a replay buffer. SAC is the default; TD3 learns a deterministic policy; REDQ trains an ensemble of ten critics with twenty critic updates per step, so it does far more work per sample.

A task that never ends, such as holding a setpoint: discounting only shortens the agent's view. ASAC (off-policy) and APO (on-policy) optimise the average reward per step instead.

Only a dataset, no simulator to explore with (logged runs, a plant's history): IQL trains on it offline (train_offline) and can fine-tune online after; TD3+BC is TD3 with a cloning term (TD3).

Learning one transition at a time, without a replay buffer or target networks: AVG.

The observation hides part of the state (a velocity, a cue seen earlier): give PPO, SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC or APG a memory=. DreamerV3 is recurrent already.

You have an expert controller (a PID, a hand-written policy): SAC has the most expert support, and it alone folds the action phase, which lets the expert act during collection. SAC, TD3, REDQ and APO can clone the expert into the actor before training (the CloningPretrain extension), and SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC and APO accept the ImitationLoss term. See Expert guidance. SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, PPO and APO can also learn a PID controller directly, with the PID policy of Networks. To imitate the expert without a reward, use DAgger.

Your simulator is differentiable (a gymnax environment that exposes its transition gradients) and you want one controller for a family of systems: APG. Its contextual controller reads the tracking history, so one controller can serve the whole family.

You want a model of the environment. DreamerV3 learns inside its world model and handles discrete and continuous actions. TD-MPC2 plans with its model at every step, for continuous control with fixed-length episodes (terminating ones with episodic=True). Both do much more computation per environment step than the model-free agents. To train one model offline on data from several tasks, use TDMPC2MultiTask.

Supervised learning instead of value estimation: UDRL learns which action leads to which return, then asks for more.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: The CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: 4 environments, 8,000 steps, Pendulum or CartPole by agent) last ran at main a8a13c2, with every agent updating within the run. Counting execution alone, without compilation: PPO, APO, DQN, PQN, AVG, UDRL and APG ran at 9,000 to 37,000 steps per second; SAC, TD3 and ASAC at 1,250 to 2,700; REDQ at 47, since it makes 20 updates of 10 critics per step; DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 at about 370 and 290, with smaller models than the papers'. The presets differ by agent, so the figures compare runs of one agent over time better than agents with each other. The benchmarks run on a CPU; Ajax claims no GPU speed-up. The full table is in PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md; see also Performance.

docs.title: APG
docs.text:
Analytic Policy Gradient trains a deterministic controller by differentiating the closed-loop return through the simulator itself. Each update runs the controller for horizon steps on a batch of systems and follows the exact gradient of the summed reward with respect to the controller's parameters, back through every step of the physics. There is no critic, no replay buffer and no exploration noise, so it needs an environment whose transitions carry gradients.

Papers: APG is the general method of training a policy by backpropagation through a differentiable simulator. APG.contextual_controller is the configuration of Busetto, Breschi, Forgione, Piga and Formentin, One controller to rule them all, 2024 (arXiv:2411.06482): a transformer over the tracking history closed by a PID layer, trained across a family of systems.

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text:
Feature APG Discrete actions no Continuous actions yes, tanh-bounded by default (squash=True), mapped onto the environment's bounds Memory (memory=) yes: GRU, LSTM, transformer, Mamba Environments gymnax environments with transition gradients: Pendulum, MountainCarContinuous, PointRobot, Reacher, Swimmer Families of systems yes, system_class= Several seeds in one call yes, train(seed=[...]) Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, actor_loss Resume and checkpoints yes; a split run equals the uninterrupted one (probe, and the resume contract with memory)

Brax and Playground environments are not supported: they take no per-step parameters and have their own gradient path. An environment that cannot expose its gradients raises instead of training on zero gradients.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Train one controller for a family of pendulums whose mass and length vary:

import gymnax
from ajax import APG
from ajax.environments.system_class import UniformPerturbation

_, params = gymnax.make("Pendulum-v1")
systems = UniformPerturbation(params, fields=("m", "l"), scale=0.1)  # +-10 %
agent = APG("Pendulum-v1", n_envs=16, horizon=50, system_class=systems)
state, aux = agent.train(seed=[1, 2], n_timesteps=80_000)
print(aux.matching_loss.shape)     # (seeds, updates): 80,000 / (16 * 50) = 100 updates
print(aux.matching_loss[:, ::20])  # minus the closed-loop return

train returns (state, aux) whatever the logging: aux holds every update's loss, matching_loss (minus the mean closed-loop return), m_rmse, grad_norm (the gradient's global norm, before clipping) and timestep. With a logging_config, every log_frequency steps it also evaluates the controller on num_episode_test systems, drawn afresh at each evaluation, and sends Eval/episodic mean reward and Eval/m_rmse to the logging backend. aux.evaluations then holds what each update logged, NaN on the updates that did not evaluate, with or without a backend.

The in-context controller of Busetto et al., trained in stages on a reference-tracking task (train_curriculum, the paper's Algorithm 2):

# doc: skip (compiles a transformer and trains 700,000 steps; tests/agents/APG/test_APG.py covers the curriculum)
import gymnax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from ajax.agents.APG import APG, CurriculumStage, train_curriculum
from ajax.environments.model_reference import LinearReferenceModel, ModelReferenceWrapper, StepReference
from ajax.environments.system_class import FixedSystem, UniformPerturbation
from ajax.wrappers import InitialStateWrapper

plant, params = gymnax.make("Pendulum-v1")
fixed_start = lambda key, s, p: s.replace(theta=jnp.asarray(0.0), theta_dot=jnp.asarray(0.0))
plant = InitialStateWrapper(plant, fixed_start)  # the paper keeps the initial conditions fixed
task = ModelReferenceWrapper(  # track a reference model's step response
    plant,
    StepReference(horizon=100, min_value=-0.5, max_value=0.5, min_duration=20, max_duration=50),
    LinearReferenceModel.first_order(a=0.9, b=0.1, c=1.0, d=0.0),
    output_fn=lambda obs: jnp.arctan2(obs[1], obs[0]),
)
systems = UniformPerturbation(params, fields=("m", "l"), scale=0.05)
stages = [  # the nominal pendulum first, then the whole family
    CurriculumStage(APG.contextual_controller(task, FixedSystem(params), env_params=params), n_timesteps=200_000),
    CurriculumStage(APG.contextual_controller(task, systems, env_params=params), n_timesteps=500_000),
]
*_, (state, aux) = train_curriculum(stages, seed=0)  # one (state, aux) per stage: keep the last

docs.title: Key hyperparameters
docs.text:
Argument Default What it does n_envs 8 systems drawn and simulated in parallel per update horizon 100 closed-loop steps differentiated through learning_rate 5e-4 AdamW step size weight_decay 0.0 AdamW weight decay (0 is plain Adam) beta_1, beta_2 0.9, 0.999 Adam's moment rates (its epsilon is torch's 1e-8) lr_schedule None "warmup_cosine": linear warmup over warmup_steps updates, then cosine decay to the call's last update; when train keeps the optimiser (reset_optimizer_on_resume=False), to the run's, set by the call that builds it (Checkpoints) warmup_steps, lr_end_fraction 0, 0.1 warmup length, and the final rate as a fraction of learning_rate max_grad_norm 1.0 gradient clipping by global norm (None turns it off) actor_architecture ("128", "relu", "128", "relu") MLP in front of the memory or output; () for a linear embedding memory None memory block (MemoryConfig or a dict) pid None PIDHeadConfig: close the controller with a learnable PID layer squash True bound actions to [-1, 1] with tanh; without it they are clipped there system_class None distribution over the environment's parameters; None trains on env_params only controller_factory None builds a custom controller module (see Controller in ajax.agents.APG.networks) episode_length, action_repeat None, 1 accepted as by every agent; on gymnax environments, the only ones APG takes, the episode length is the environment's and the repeat must be 1

APG.contextual_controller(env, system_class, ...) sets the paper's values: 8 layers, 4 heads, width 128, context 100, one system per update (n_envs=1), horizon 100, betas (0.9, 0.95) with weight_decay=0 (plain Adam), 5,000 warmup updates then cosine decay to a tenth of the rate, no gradient clipping (max_grad_norm=None), and a PID output layer. Its final_norm=False rebuilds a controller saved before the transformer ended with its final LayerNorm (see Memory). Such a controller's parameters also map onto the new network, which computes the same outputs: controller_params_with_final_norm(params, memory) moves the controller's LayerNorm, which played that final norm's part, into the transformer. It maps the parameters only, so a resumed training state must restart its optimizer.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Budget. One update uses n_envs * horizon steps of n_timesteps.
  • Actions. Squashed or clipped, the controller's [-1, 1] action is mapped onto the environment's bounds inside the differentiated rollout, so on gymnax Pendulum (torque in [-2, 2]) the controller reaches the whole range.
  • Deviations from Busetto et al., each backed by runs on the pendulum tracking task (see the APG docstrings): actions are tanh-bounded (the reference leaves them unbounded); gradients are clipped, since BPTT over 100 steps across a family of systems diverged without it; the PID layer starts as the identity (K_P = 1, K_I = K_D = 0) instead of all three gains at 1, which trained markedly worse under the bounded action (fresh-system M-RMSE 0.33 against 0.25). These runs predate the mapping of actions onto the environment's bounds: the pendulum's torque was then capped at 1 of its
  • Not backed by runs: the transformer's LayerNorms, its final one included, keep a bias and an epsilon of 1e-6, where the reference's have no bias and 1e-5 (buswayne/in-context-controller at 7eb094ce17: transformer_onestep.py:33 and :156, train_onestep_lin_CL.py:103). The paper trains each curriculum stage to a loss tolerance; Ajax gives each stage a fixed n_timesteps.
  • Initialisation. A transformer memory starts as the reference's GPT: kernels from N(0, 0.02²), the residual projections at 0.02/√(2 n_layers), zero biases (transformer_onestep.py:162-166, :189-195; MemoryConfig(init="nanogpt")). Other memory kinds keep flax's.
  • Curriculum. train_curriculum resumes each stage from the previous one's parameters and, by default, restarts the optimizer and its schedule at each stage. All stages must share n_envs, the network and the PID layer.
  • Tasks. ajax.environments.model_reference turns a plant into a reference-tracking task: ModelReferenceWrapper, a StepReference signal and a LinearReferenceModel whose response the plant must match. On such a task the loss is the paper's closed-loop matching cost and m_rmse its M-RMSE.
  • Differentiable simulation covers system classes, transition gradients and the reference-tracking wrapper.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Unit tests (tests/agents/APG) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning, including the curriculum. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: it reaches the exact optimum of a small problem whose best action is reachable only through the transition's gradient, and a run split by a checkpoint equals the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: Pendulum tracking, 4 environments, 8,000 steps) APG ran at 34,958 steps per second of execution (5,339 with compilation) at main a8a13c2 (PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

docs.text:
contextual_controller(
    env_id,
    system_class=None,
    n_envs=1,
    horizon=100,
    n_layers=8,
    n_heads=4,
    d_model=128,
    context=100,
    final_norm=True,
    learning_rate=0.0005,
    weight_decay=0.0,
    warmup_steps=5000,
    pid=_DEFAULT_PID,
    beta_2=0.95,
    lr_schedule="warmup_cosine",
    max_grad_norm=None,
    actor_architecture=(),
    **kwargs,
)

The in-context controller of Busetto et al. 2024.

Defaults follow the paper (Table 2: 8 layers, 4 heads, context 100, width 128, b=1 system per iteration, N=100 horizon) and the reference code (AdamW betas (0.9, 0.95), eps 1e-8, 5k-step warmup then cosine decay to lr/10, no gradient clipping). Deviations, each backed by runs on the pendulum tracking test bed: actions are tanh-bounded (Ajax convention; the reference leaves u unbounded), and the PID head starts at the identity rather than the reference's all-ones coefficients (see _DEFAULT_PID). Not reproduced: the reference (buswayne/in-context-controller at 7eb094ce17) sets its scheduled rate on its first parameter group only (train_onestep_lin_CL.py:241), so its LayerNorm weights keep the peak rate, and decays only tensors of two or more dimensions (transformer_onestep_CL.py:72-77; moot at weight_decay=0). Not backed by runs: the LayerNorms, ln_f included, keep a bias and flax's epsilon 1e-6, where the reference's have no bias and epsilon 1e-5 (buswayne/in-context-controller at 7eb094ce17: transformer_onestep.py:33 calls F.layer_norm with 1e-5, :156 builds ln_f = LayerNorm(n_embd, bias=config.bias), and train_onestep_lin_CL.py:103 defaults --bias to False). The transformer starts as the reference's GPT does (APG_MEMORY_INITS). final_norm=False rebuilds the transformer without its final LayerNorm, only to restore a checkpoint saved before it (see :class:~ajax.networks.memory.MemoryConfig); an expand-then-contract shim (CLAUDE.md, refactoring rule 10), it is removed together with MemoryConfig.final_norm. Extra kwargs go to :class:APG.

docs.title: ajax.agents.APG.networks.controller_params_with_final_norm
docs.text:
controller_params_with_final_norm(params, memory)

A Controller's parameters saved before its transformer or mamba memory ended with a final LayerNorm, mapped onto the network built now.

The Controller then applied its own LayerNorm (norm) to the memory's output, before the output layer; it now leaves that to the core's final LayerNorm (ln_f). Both are the same LayerNorm at the same place, so moving norm to memory_cell/core/ln_f keeps the outputs identical. params is the variables dict as saved ({"params": ...}), memory the new network's config. Only the parameters map: an optimizer state saved with them keeps the old tree, so a resumed training state must restart its optimizer.

Expand-then-contract (CLAUDE.md, refactoring rule 10): goes with MemoryConfig.final_norm.

docs.title: APO
docs.text:
Average Policy Optimization is PPO for the average-reward criterion. Instead of discounting future rewards, it learns how much reward the policy earns per step on average and judges each action by how much better than that average it does. This suits continuing tasks, such as holding a setpoint, where there is no natural horizon and a discount factor only shortens the agent's view. The clipped update and the minibatch epochs are PPO's own code.

Paper: Ma et al., Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning with Trust Region Methods, 2021 (arXiv:2106.03442). Ajax follows the authors' official code, xtma/apo, where it is more specific than the paper.

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: Feature APO Discrete actions yes Continuous actions yes, a Gaussian around a tanh-bounded mean, clipped and mapped onto the environment's bounds Memory (memory=) no Environments gymnax, Brax, MuJoCo Playground Image observations no PID policy yes, actor_architecture=PIDPolicy(...) (Networks) Several seeds in one call yes, train(seed=[...]) Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss Resume and checkpoints yes; a split run equals the uninterrupted one (probe and resume contract)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from ajax import APO
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = APO("Pendulum-v1", n_envs=8, n_steps=256, batch_size=64, normalize_observations=True)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=10_240, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[1, 2], n_timesteps=51_200, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])
print(state.average_reward)  # the estimated reward per step, one per seed

This budget shows the calls; it is too short to learn the swing-up.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Each update first moves two running averages towards the rollout's means, at rate alpha: the reward rate rho (the mean reward) and b (the mean predicted value). The first update sets them to the first rollout's means, as the official code does. The advantages are GAE without a discount on the differential reward r - rho. The critic fits the differential value; its target is shifted by nu * b, which pulls the values back towards a zero mean. Without that penalty the values are defined only up to a constant and can drift. Each minibatch then takes one step of both networks down the sum of PPO's clipped surrogate, the value loss and the entropy bonus.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Episode ends. The advantage chain stops at every episode end, and a terminal state's next value is dropped, as in the official code. One difference: the reference drops time-limited steps from the loss because it has only the reset observation there. Ajax keeps the final observation, so a truncated step bootstraps on it and is trained on, as PPO does.
  • Advantage normalisation runs once over the whole rollout, not per minibatch as in Ajax's PPO; the official code's config turns it off (the differences below).
  • Shuffling. Every epoch draws a new split of the rollout into minibatches, as APO's official code does.
  • Hidden layers. The actor and the critic each have two hidden layers of 64 tanh units, as the official code's mean and value networks: xtma/apo's config sets only normalize_observation (apo/experiments/configs/mujoco/apg/mujoco_appo.py:20), so rlpyt's MujocoFfModel builds both with its defaults (rlpyt/models/pg/mujoco_ff_model.py:21-22, :33-49). They start as its torch Linear layers (rlpyt/models/mlp.py:27-31) do: kernel and bias uniform in ±1/sqrt(fan_in) (encoder_kernel_init="torch_linear"; torch 1.5.1, which rlpyt's environment files pin, torch/nn/modules/linear.py:79-84). Not the official code's: the output layers start as Ajax's, the mean layer lecun_uniform (below) and the value layer orthogonal(1.0), both with zero biases, where the official code leaves them at torch's default too. Until October 2026 APO's hidden layers were two of 128 units, starting orthogonal with zero biases; a checkpoint saved then restores into an APO whose actor_architecture and critic_architecture are both ("128", "tanh", "128", "tanh"), and the default network refuses it with that advice.
  • Actor head. A continuous APO's actor is the official code's: xtma/apo at bfcd997 runs rlpyt's MujocoFfAgent (exp.py:17, :38) from the authors' fork, xtma/rlpyt at e28bb20. It is a Gaussian whose mean is tanh of the mean layer (rlpyt/models/pg/mujoco_ff_model.py:23, :40-41), with one learned log-std per action dimension, starting at 0 (std 1) and not clipped (:24, :50, :78; rlpyt/agents/pg/gaussian.py:34-38 sets no bounds, no clip and no squashing). The sample itself is not squashed: the log-probability and the entropy bonus are the Gaussian's, of the raw sample (rlpyt/distributions/gaussian.py:81-97, :108-134, :208). The evaluation acts with the mean, as the official evaluation agent sets the std to 0 (apo/agents/mujoco_eval.py:15). log_std_bounds adds a clip, which the run config records. A PID policy's output takes the same tanh, and its log-std the same clip. A discrete APO ignores the head. Not the official code's: the mean layer starts lecun_uniform (torch's default initialisation there). Until October 2026 APO squashed its samples with tanh and clipped the log-std to [-20, 2]; the parameters are the same, so a checkpoint saved then restores, with the same deterministic action, tanh of the mean layer, and samples as the new head does.
  • Actions in the environment. As for every agent, Ajax clips the sample to [-1, 1] and maps it onto the environment's bounds (Environments). The official code hands the raw sample to the environment (rlpyt/envs/gym.py:66-67); its MuJoCo tasks clamp it to their control range in the simulation, and Gymnasium's charge the control cost on the unclamped action (gymnasium/envs/mujoco/hopper_v4.py:97, :138 in Gymnasium 1.2.0).
  • Optimiser. As in the official code, one Adam steps the whole model (apo/algos/apg/base.py:28) at 3e-4, without a schedule (apo/experiments/configs/mujoco/apg/mujoco_appo.py:5, :16), down the clipped surrogate plus vf_coef (1, appo.py:27) times the value loss minus ent_coef times the entropy (apo/algos/apg/appo.py:145-158), once per minibatch. Its gradient is clipped to global norm 10 over every parameter, actor and critic at once (appo.py:106-112, mujoco_appo.py:8), with torch's formula (torch 1.5.1, torch/nn/utils/clip_grad.py:33-37). Adam acts on each coordinate on its own, so Ajax keeps one Adam state per network, both stepped together on that one gradient: the same optimiser, with a learning rate per network as torch's parameter groups allow. Until October 2026 each network took its own step, clipped to norm 0.5 on its own; a checkpoint saved then restores, its moments and step counts kept.
  • Entropy bonus. As in the official code, the loss subtracts 0.01 (entropy_loss_coeff, mujoco_appo.py:9) times the batch mean of the policy's entropy (appo.py:155-158). A continuous APO's is its Gaussian's, log_std + log sqrt(2 pi e) summed over the action dimensions (rlpyt/distributions/gaussian.py:81-97, :102-103); the log-std does not depend on the state, so the bonus pushes it up and leaves the mean alone. Until October 2026 the weight was 0; ent_coef=0 reproduces runs from then (the parameters are unchanged, so their checkpoints restore).
  • Remaining differences from the official code (xtma/apo at bfcd997, its config apo/experiments/configs/mujoco/apg/mujoco_appo.py, on xtma/rlpyt at e28bb20), each a default the constructor can set:
  • Advantage normalisation: off there (normalize_advantage=False, mujoco_appo.py:15; apo/algos/apg/base.py:90-98 would standardise them), on here (normalize_advantage=True).
  • Rollout shape: 10 environments of 200 steps there (batch_B=10, batch_T=200, mujoco_appo.py:27-28), 2,000 samples in 20 minibatches of 100 (minibatches=20, :12); 4 environments of 2,048 steps here, 8,192 samples in minibatches of 64. Both take 10 epochs (:13).
  • Value-bias coefficient: rm_vbias_coeff=1.0 in the config exp.py runs (mujoco_appo.py:7), while the repository's sweep, run_exp.py, tries 0, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3 and 1.0 (run_exp.py:55) and APPO's own default is 0.1 (apo/algos/apg/appo.py:27); nu=0.1 here. The sweep also sets the discount to 1.0 (run_exp.py:52, the other values commented out), as Ajax's APO has none, where the config alone has 0.99 (mujoco_appo.py:10).
  • Output layers: the mean layer starts lecun_uniform and the value layer orthogonal(1.0), with zero biases, where the official code leaves both at torch's nn.Linear default (see Hidden layers).
  • Episode ends and actions: time-limited steps are trained on, and the sample is clipped to [-1, 1] before the environment (the notes above).
  • n_steps and batch_size must divide one another unless num_minibatches is set; the constructor refuses them otherwise.
  • Expert. Cloning an expert into the actor before training is the CloningPretrain extension, and a cloning term during training the ImitationLoss extension; APO supports both (Expert guidance). With expert_policy set, the rollout stores the expert's actions, from its state when it has one, and the evaluation also reports the expert's return.
  • APO is the on-policy counterpart of ASAC, the average-reward off-policy agent.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: No learning curves are published for APO yet. Unit tests (tests/agents/APO and the contracts every agent shares) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning, such as its differential advantages. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: the reward rate it learns, episode ends, extension phases, and a run split by a checkpoint matching the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: Pendulum, 4 environments, 8,000 steps) APO ran at 16,390 steps per second of execution (4,024 with compilation) at main a8a13c2 (PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

Bases: ActorCritic

Average-Policy Optimization (APO, Ma et al. 2021) for discrete and continuous action spaces. See https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.03442

docs.title: ASAC
docs.text:
Average-Reward Soft Actor-Critic is SAC for the average-reward criterion: it maximises the long-run reward per step instead of a discounted sum, so it has no gamma. Its critics learn a differential soft value on r - theta, where theta tracks the entropy-regularised reward rate. Use it for continuing tasks, where no discount is natural; episodic tasks fit by charging each termination a learned penalty.

Paper. Adamczyk et al., Average-Reward Soft Actor-Critic, 2025 (arXiv:2501.09080v2).

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: ASAC Continuous actions (Box) Yes Discrete actions No Learning Off-policy, replay buffer Vectorised environments (n_envs) Yes Recurrent memory (memory=) Yes, without extensions or expert_policy PID policy (actor_architecture=PIDPolicy(...)) Yes Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from ajax import ASAC
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = ASAC("Pendulum-v1", n_envs=4, learning_starts=1_000)  # no gamma
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=2_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=4_000, logging_config=logging)

print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])  # one row per seed
print(state.theta)  # the reward-rate estimate, one per seed

This budget only shows the call; Pendulum needs more steps to be solved.

With an expert_policy, ASAC stores the expert's actions along each trajectory, from its state when it has one, and takes the CloningPretrain and ImitationLoss extensions (Expert guidance).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Target. r - theta + min(Q'_1, Q'_2)(s', a') - Q'(0, 0) - alpha log pi(a'|s') with a' ~ pi(.|s'). The shift by the target critics' value at the origin, Q'(0, 0), is their reference point: a differential value is defined only up to a constant.
  • Episode ends. The target bootstraps through every end. A termination is charged a penalty instead, subtracted from the terminal transition's reward: an average (at rate tau_theta) of p_0 times the batch's mean reward, terminal rewards counted as zero.
  • Reward rate. After each update theta moves, at rate tau_theta, towards the batch mean of the penalised reward minus alpha log pi(a|s), with fresh actions a ~ pi(.|s).
  • One update. The penalty, then a critic step, an actor step on alpha log pi - min_i Q_i, a temperature step on fresh samples of the updated policy (skipped with fixed_alpha), the theta step and the target update. Each iteration steps every env once, then makes one update.
  • Temperature. As in the authors' published runs, alpha is fixed: 0.2 by default. Those runs use 0.05 for Humanoid and Swimmer; pass alpha_init=0.05 for those. fixed_alpha=False learns it as SAC does.
  • Two critics. ASAC always uses two critics; it has no num_critics.
  • Extensions. ASAC tells its extensions there is no discount: they receive gamma=None.
  • Initialisation. As the authors' code (stable-baselines3's SAC actor and plain torch critics): every layer, the mean and log-std heads included, starts as torch's nn.Linear does, its kernel and bias uniform in ±1/sqrt(fan_in). With memory=, ASAC keeps its previous initialisation until Ni et al.'s is audited.
  • Actions and evaluation. As SAC: a tanh-squashed Gaussian in [-1, 1], mapped onto the environment's bounds; evaluation uses the mean action. The logged evaluation return is the usual episodic sum. ASAC reports no Eval/mean bias.

docs.text: The repository records no learning curves for ASAC yet. Unit tests (tests/agents/ASAC and the contracts every agent shares) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: its differential target, its average-reward bookkeeping (reward scale, episode ends), memory, and a run split by a checkpoint matching the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: Pendulum, 4 envs, 8,000 steps, updates from step 1,000) ASAC ran at 1,254 steps per second of execution (1,032 with compilation) at main a8a13c2 (see PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

docs.title: AVG
docs.text:
Action Value Gradient is an incremental actor-critic: after each environment step it makes one update on that single transition, with no replay buffer and no target network. It stays stable through normalisation instead: the observations are normalised, the networks' penultimate features are L2-normalised, and the TD error is divided by a running estimate of its scale. Use it when the agent must learn from each step as it comes, without storing past experience.

Paper. Vasan et al., Deep Policy Gradient Methods Without Batch Updates, Target Networks, or Replay Buffers, 2024 (arXiv:2411.15370). The update follows its Algorithm 1 and the authors' code (gauthamvasan/avg).

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text:
AVG Continuous actions (Box) Yes Discrete actions No Learning Incremental: one update per step, no replay buffer Vectorised environments (n_envs) Yes Recurrent memory (memory=) No PID policy (actor_architecture=PIDPolicy(...)) Yes Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss

AVG has no memory option: with one-transition updates, backpropagation through time has length 1, so a memory block could not learn anything temporal without eligibility traces or real-time recurrent learning.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from ajax import AVG
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = AVG("Pendulum-v1")  # one env, learning from its first step
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=1_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=2_000, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])  # one row per seed

This budget only shows the call; Pendulum needs more steps to be solved.

Argument Default What it does n_envs 1 parallel environments actor_learning_rate 6.3e-3 Adam step size of the actor critic_learning_rate 8.7e-3 Adam step size of the critic beta_1, beta_2 0, 0.999 Adam's moment decays (AVG uses beta_1 = 0; Adam's epsilon is torch's 1e-8) actor_architecture, critic_architecture ("256", "leaky_relu", "256", "leaky_relu") hidden layers gamma 0.99 discount learning_starts 0 steps of uniform random actions before the first update alpha_init 0.07 the entropy weight, fixed for the whole run num_critics 1 critics; with more, the actor and the target use their minimum reward_scale 1.0 multiplies the rewards in the target max_grad_norm None gradient clipping expose_recent_rollout False keep the last transition on state.last_rollout for extensions expert_policy None an expert whose return the evaluation reports next to the agent's (Eval/expert bias); its actions, from its state when it has one, reach the expert extensions (ImitationLoss, CloningPretrain, IBRL) episode_length, action_repeat None, 1 simulator steps per episode (1,000 when None) and per agent step, on Brax and Playground extensions () research features (see Extensions)

AVG keeps alpha fixed at alpha_init, as the authors' code does, so it has no alpha_learning_rate or target_entropy_per_dim. There is no normalize_observations argument, since AVG always normalises its observations, and no reward normalisation.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• TD-error scale. The critic minimises the squared TD error divided by sqrt(max(var(r) + E[G^2] var(gamma), 1e-4)), where r is the entropy-regularised reward, gamma the per-step discount (zero at a termination) and G the returns of finished episodes, as the authors' TDErrorScaler does (incremental_rl/td_error_scaler.py). The scale is 1 while that variance is at most 0.01 and no episode has finished; on a task without terminations it follows the reward's variance alone. The statistics are updated after every step, warm-up included, and shared by all envs; each finished episode's return counts once, whatever n_envs.
  • Actor gradient. The actor loss is alpha log pi(a|s) - Q(s, a) at the action actually executed, reparameterised from its stored pre-squash sample, so the gradient flows through that action.
  • Update order, a deliberate choice. Algorithm 1 writes the critic update before the actor's; the authors' code builds both losses from the same parameters, then steps the actor and the critic. Ajax follows the code, which produced the paper's results: the actor's loss sees the critic before its step, and the critic's target the actor before its step.
  • Time limits. Only a termination stops the bootstrap, as in the authors' code; a transition cut by a time limit bootstraps on its final observation.
  • Several envs. The paper trains on one environment. With n_envs > 1, each update uses the transitions of all envs from the same step.
  • Initialisation. As in the authors' code, every layer starts orthogonal with gain 1 and a zero bias, the mean and log-std heads included. So the first policy's mean and log-std are unit-scale projections of the normalised features, not a near-zero mean and a constant std.
  • Actions and evaluation. A tanh-squashed Gaussian in [-1, 1], mapped onto the environment's bounds; evaluation uses the mean action.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The repository records no learning curves for AVG yet. A conformance check (tests/conformance/test_avg_original.py) makes one update of Ajax's AVG and of gauthamvasan/avg from the same state and transition, and compares the actor, the critic, their optimisers and the TD-error scaler. Two differences of the authors' code are asserted there: its log_std head is read as a log-variance (a covariance's diagonal), and it hands its tanh action to the environment without mapping it onto the box. Unit tests (tests/agents/AVG and the contracts every agent shares) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: its target, discounting, time limits, observation normalisation, and a run split by a checkpoint matching the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: Pendulum, 4 envs, 8,000 steps) AVG ran at 9,460 steps per second of execution (4,027 with compilation), updates included, at main a8a13c2 (see PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

docs.title: DAgger
docs.text:
DAgger learns to imitate an expert. It needs no reward and no critic. The agent lets the expert act at first, then acts itself. Whoever acts, every state it reaches is labelled with the action the expert would take there, and the policy is fitted to all the labels gathered so far. Copying only the expert's own trajectories (behaviour cloning) never shows the policy the states its own mistakes lead to. DAgger collects exactly those.

Paper: Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning, AISTATS 2011 (arXiv:1011.0686), Algorithm 3.1. The authors released no code. The defaults follow the paper and HumanCompatibleAI/imitation at e5ef188 (src/imitation/algorithms/dagger.py and bc.py).

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: Feature DAgger Discrete actions yes; the expert returns its action index as an integer (n, 1) column Continuous actions yes, tanh-bounded, mapped onto the environment's bounds Stateful experts yes; their state is tracked along each trajectory Memory (memory=) no Environments gymnax, Brax, MuJoCo Playground Several seeds in one call yes, train(seed=[...]) Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, actor_loss

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp

from ajax import DAgger
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig


def pd_expert(obs):
    """A PD controller on Pendulum's raw observation [cos θ, sin θ, θ̇]."""
    theta = jnp.arctan2(obs[..., 1], obs[..., 0])
    return jnp.clip(-(2.0 * theta + 0.5 * obs[..., 2]), -2.0, 2.0)[..., None]


agent = DAgger("Pendulum-v1", expert_policy=pd_expert, n_envs=2)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=1_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[1, 2], n_timesteps=2_000, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])         # the policy's return
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean expert reward"])  # the expert's, same episodes

Evaluations log the policy's return, the expert's on the same episodes (Eval/episodic mean expert reward), their difference (Eval/expert bias), the fitting loss (policy/imitation_loss), the iteration's mixing probability (dagger/beta) and the share of environments the expert drove at the last step (dagger/expert_frac).

docs.text: Argument Default What it does expert_policy required the expert to imitate, as in Expert guidance beta_decay 0.0 the expert acts with probability beta_i = beta_decay ** (i - 1) in iteration i; 0 lets it act in the first iteration only iteration_steps 500 timesteps (over all environments) per iteration n_envs 1 environments stepped in parallel buffer_size 1,000,000 labelled states kept batch_size 32 labelled states per gradient step actor_learning_rate 1e-3 Adam step size (eps 1e-8, torch's) actor_architecture ("32", "tanh", "32", "tanh") hidden layers max_grad_norm None gradient clipping by global norm normalize_observations False running observation normalisation episode_length, action_repeat None, 1 simulator steps per episode and per agent step, on Brax and Playground extensions () research features (see Extensions)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
At each step, each environment executes the expert's action with probability beta_i, and the policy's deterministic action otherwise: per environment and per step, as the reference's collector mixes them. The replay keeps every visited state with the expert's action there, whoever acted. It is the paper's aggregated dataset D. Once the replay holds a batch, each step makes one gradient step on a replay batch. The loss is the squared error between the policy's action and the expert's (both in [-1, 1]), or the cross-entropy of the expert's action for discrete actions.

beta_decay=0 is the paper's parameter-free choice, beta_i = I(i = 1). The paper reports that it "often performs best in practice" (Sec. 3). Any value in (0, 1] gives its exponential schedule. The guarantee needs only that the mean of the beta_i goes to 0.

docs.title: DAgger and ImitationLoss
docs.text: A replay agent (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC) given an expert_policy and ImitationLoss with the same expert stores the expert's action at every state it visits and pulls its actor towards those actions on replay batches. That is DAgger's aggregation with beta_i = I(i = 1), plus the agent's reinforcement-learning loss, its critic and its exploration noise. Use DAgger to imitate without a reward, or as the imitation baseline. Use ImitationLoss to improve on the expert. On PPO, APO and AVG the term reads only the latest rollout or step, so there is no aggregated dataset.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Online fit. The paper refits the policy on D after each iteration (Follow-the-Leader). Ajax takes one gradient step per collection step, an online learner. The paper's analysis holds for any no-regret online learner (Sec. 4).
  • The last policy. The paper returns the best policy of the iterations, chosen on validation. Ajax returns the last one; the evaluations show each.
  • Bounded memory. The replay drops its oldest rows past buffer_size. D keeps them all.
  • Deterministic policy, squared error. The reference's behaviour cloning fits a Gaussian policy by likelihood, with an entropy bonus. Ajax's policy is deterministic, as the paper's is, so it fits by squared error.
  • Rewards are not used. They are recorded, and the evaluations measure them, but the policy learns from the expert's actions alone. The critic built beside the actor is unused.
  • The expert's next action. The replay stores the expert's action at each state only. Its action at the next state (next_a_expert), which only critic modules read, stays zero.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: No learning curves are published for DAgger yet. Unit tests (tests/agents/DAgger) check the beta schedule, the mixing and the labels on every stored row. The probes (tests/probing/test_imitation.py) train it on a four-state chain where one state is reached only by the learner's mistakes. The policy must take the expert's action there, which cloning the expert's own states never teaches. A discrete twin checks the cross-entropy fit.

Bases: ActorCritic

DAgger (Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, AISTATS 2011): imitation of an expert by dataset aggregation, with a supervised loss only.

At iteration i the expert acts with probability beta_i = beta_decay ** (i - 1) at each step, the actor otherwise; every visited state joins the replay with the expert's action there, and the actor fits those actions (:mod:ajax.agents.DAgger.train_DAgger). It needs no reward and has no critic. The expert follows the conventions of the expert guide: it may be stateful; a discrete expert returns its action index as an integer (n, 1) column.

Defaults: the paper's parameter-free beta_i = I(i = 1) (beta_decay=0, its Sec. 3: "often performs best in practice"); the rest is the reference code's, HumanCompatibleAI/imitation@e5ef188: 500-step iterations (rollout_round_min_timesteps) and its behaviour cloning's batch of 32, 32-32 tanh network and torch Adam (learning rate 1e-3, eps 1e-8). Its cloning fits a Gaussian by likelihood with an entropy bonus; this actor is deterministic, as the paper's policy, and fits by squared error (cross-entropy for discrete actions).

docs.title: DQN
docs.text:
Deep Q-Network learns one Q-value per discrete action and acts greedily on them. It regresses the Q-network on temporal-difference targets computed with a separate target network, refreshed every few hundred updates, and samples its training data from a replay buffer. It explores with an epsilon-greedy rule whose epsilon decays linearly during training. Double DQN, the dueling network and the squared loss are options of the same agent.

Papers. Mnih et al., Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning, Nature 2015. Options: van Hasselt et al., Deep Reinforcement Learning with Double Q-learning, 2016 (Double DQN); Wang et al., Dueling Network Architectures for Deep Reinforcement Learning, 2016 (dueling network).

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: DQN Continuous actions (Box) No Discrete actions (Discrete) Yes Learning Off-policy, replay buffer Vectorised environments (n_envs) Yes Recurrent memory (memory=) No Image observations (CNN encoder) Yes, with cnn_image_shape Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from ajax import DQN
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = DQN("CartPole-v1", n_envs=4)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=5_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=10_000, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])  # one row per seed

The variants compose through three arguments:

from ajax import DQN
from ajax.agents.DQN.networks import DuelingQNetwork
from ajax.agents.DQN.train_DQN import compute_double_dqn_td_target, mse_td_loss

agent = DQN(
    "CartPole-v1",
    td_target_fn=compute_double_dqn_td_target,  # Double DQN
    q_network_cls=DuelingQNetwork,               # dueling heads
    td_loss_fn=mse_td_loss,                      # squared error instead of Huber
)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=2_000)

Argument Default What it does n_envs 1 parallel environments learning_rate 2.5e-4 step size of centered RMSProp (see Notes) architecture ("128", "relu", "128", "relu") hidden layers of the Q-network gamma 0.99 discount buffer_size 100_000 replay capacity batch_size 64 replay minibatch learning_starts 1_000 steps of uniform random actions before the first update n_gradient_steps 1 gradient steps per iteration target_update_interval 500 gradient steps between target refreshes tau 1.0 refresh rate: 1.0 copies the weights, below 1 is a Polyak step epsilon_start, epsilon_end 1.0, 0.05 exploration rate at the start and the end of its decay epsilon_decay_frac 0.5 fraction of the run over which epsilon decays reward_scale 1.0 multiplies the rewards in the target max_grad_norm None gradient clipping normalize_observations, normalize_rewards False running normalisation reward_normalization_gamma None with normalize_rewards, divide by the spread of the discounted return td_target_fn None the target; None is vanilla DQN, compute_double_dqn_td_target is Double DQN td_loss_fn None the loss; None is the Huber loss with delta 1, mse_td_loss the squared error q_network_cls None the network; None is QNetwork, DuelingQNetwork the dueling one cnn_image_shape, cnn_extra_obs_dim, cnn_spec None, 0, None convolutional encoder for flat image observations; None builds the reference network (see Notes) episode_length, action_repeat None, 1 simulator steps per episode (1,000 when None) and per agent step, on Brax and Playground extensions () research features (see Extensions)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Target. r + gamma (1 - terminated) max_a' Q'(s', a'); Double DQN picks a' with the online network and values it with the target network.
  • Updates per step. Each iteration steps every env once, then (from learning_starts) takes n_gradient_steps gradient steps. With n_envs=4 that is one gradient step per four environment steps.
  • Target refresh. One mechanism covers both classic schemes: every target_update_interval gradient steps the target moves by tau. The hard copy is tau=1.0; a Polyak average is tau < 1 with interval 1.
  • Exploration. Epsilon decays linearly with the training fraction (the timestep over the run's total), from epsilon_start to epsilon_end over the first epsilon_decay_frac of the run. Before learning_starts every action is uniform. Evaluation is greedy.
  • Time limits. A transition cut by a time limit bootstraps on its final observation; only a termination stops the bootstrap.
  • Loss. The default is the Huber loss with delta 1, whose gradient is the TD error clipped to [-1, 1], as the original DQN clips it. make_huber_td_loss(delta) sets another delta; mse_td_loss is the squared error.
  • Optimiser. The authors' centered RMSProp (Graves 2013): each step is the gradient over sqrt(E[g^2] - E[g]^2 + eps), both averages decaying at 0.95. Their eps is 0.01 on a gradient summed over the batch; on Ajax's mean loss the same step takes eps = 0.01 / batch_size**2.
  • Network. A plain MLP without LayerNorm (Mnih et al.'s network has none) and a linear head. It lives in state.actor_state, so the shared evaluation reads it like any actor. As in the authors' Torch7 code, every layer of the MLP and the head starts as nn.Linear does, kernel and bias uniform in ±1/sqrt(fan_in).
  • Images. With cnn_image_shape and no cnn_spec, DQN builds Mnih et al.'s network (MNIH_CNN: 32, 64 and 64 channels, kernels 8, 4 and 3, strides 4, 2 and 1, no padding, then 512 units) when the image is at least 36 pixels a side, the smallest it fits. Smaller images, such as MinAtar's 10 x 10, get MinAtar's network (MINATAR_CNN: one 3 x 3 convolution of 16 channels, then 128 units). Both start as the MLP does. The authors' first convolution is given a padding argument of 1; Ajax does not pad it, as the paper describes. On 84 x 84 images both read 20 x 20.
  • Extensions. on_target extensions reshape the target; critic_loss extensions add a term to the TD loss, with its gradient.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The repository records no learning curves for DQN yet. Unit tests (tests/agents/DQN and the contracts every agent shares) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: its max bootstrap and action indexing, discounting, time limits, extension phases, and a run split by a checkpoint matching the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: CartPole, 4 envs, 8,000 steps, updates from step 1,000) DQN ran at 16,662 steps per second of execution (6,395 with compilation) at main a8a13c2 (see PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

Deep Q-Network (Mnih et al., 2015) for discrete action spaces.

Value-based, off-policy. A single Q-network is trained by TD against a periodically refreshed target network; the policy is greedy over Q, with epsilon-greedy exploration during collection.

docs.title: ajax.agents.DQN.networks.DuelingQNetwork
docs.text:
Bases: QNetwork

Dueling DQN architecture (Wang et al., 2016).

A shared encoder feeds two heads -- a scalar state-value V(s) and a per-action advantage A(s, a) -- recombined as

Q(s, a) = V(s) + A(s, a) - mean_a' A(s, a')

The mean-subtraction fixes the unidentifiability of the V/A split. Select it via DQN(..., q_network_cls=DuelingQNetwork).

Double DQN target (van Hasselt et al., 2016).

Decouples action selection (online network) from action evaluation (target network), removing the maximisation bias of the vanilla max_a' Q_target target:

a*  = argmax_a' Q_online(s', a')
y   = r + gamma * (1 - d) * Q_target(s', a*)

Drop-in for compute_dqn_td_target; select via DQN(..., td_target_fn=compute_double_dqn_td_target).

docs.text:
make_huber_td_loss(delta=1.0)

Build a Huber TD-loss callable.

Huber loss is quadratic within delta of zero error and linear beyond it: its gradient is the TD error clipped to [-delta, delta], the original DQN's clip (google-deepmind/dqn @9d9b1d1 NeuralQLearner.lua:224-226, clip_delta=1 in run_gpu:31), DQN's default at delta = 1.

docs.title: DreamerV3
docs.text:
DreamerV3 learns a model of the environment and trains its policy inside that model. A recurrent world model learns, from replayed sequences, to predict the next latent state, the reward and whether the episode continues. An actor and a critic then learn mostly from trajectories imagined by the model. All three are trained together, one gradient step per update, with the LaProp optimizer and adaptive gradient clipping.

Paper: Hafner, Pasukonis, Ba and Lillicrap, Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models, arXiv:2301.04104v2, 2023; Nature, 2025 (arXiv:2301.04104v2). Official code: danijar/dreamerv3.

Ajax reproduces the code that produced the paper's numbers (commit 2411f7d) plus one later upstream bug fix (29eb964, the replay context). The world-model design notes give the full specification, and deviations.md lists every version choice and every departure from the reference.

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: Feature DreamerV3 Discrete actions yes Continuous actions yes Memory built in: the world model is recurrent (memory= is not accepted) Environments gymnax, Brax, MuJoCo Playground Observations flat vectors only; the environment must not normalise observations or rewards Several seeds in one call yes, train(seed=[...]) Extension phases pretrain, post_update (after every update), eval_metrics Resume and checkpoints yes; a resumed run continues the schedules and the replay, and equals the uninterrupted run (test)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# doc: skip (compiles and trains for about a minute on a CPU; tests/agents/DreamerV3/test_dreamerv3_agent.py covers this path)
from ajax import DreamerV3
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

# The smallest preset and a low train ratio, for a quick look on a CPU.
agent = DreamerV3("CartPole-v1", model_size="1m", n_envs=4, train_ratio=32,
                  batch_size=4, batch_length=16)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=1_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=2_000, num_episode_test=2,
                                 logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Train/episodic mean reward"])  # the score the paper reports
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])

The paper's DMC-proprio protocol (Table 2): the 12M model, 16 environments, a train ratio of 512, action repeat 2, and 500K environment frames, which is 250K rows at repeat 2:

# doc: skip (the paper's full budget; benchmarks/world_models/paper_protocol.py runs it)
from ajax import DreamerV3

agent = DreamerV3("CheetahRun", model_size="12m", n_envs=16, train_ratio=512,
                  action_repeat=2, episode_length=1000)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=250_000)  # 500K env frames

The other arguments (network depths, bins, unimix, the remaining loss scales, the slow critic and the return normaliser) are listed in the API below.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• What n_timesteps counts. One row per environment per vector step, reset rows included, as the reference's step does. env_frames = rows * action_repeat is logged next to it.
  • The score. The paper reports the returns of the stochastic policy's training episodes, logged as Train/episodic mean reward. The evaluation also samples its actions, since the reference has no deterministic mode, and draws fresh keys at each evaluation (new initial states and action noise); a rerun of the same seed draws the same ones.
  • Actions. Continuous actions are clipped to [-1, 1] and mapped onto the environment's bounds, the reference's ClipAction and NormalizeAction.
  • Memory use. Each replay row stores the observation, the action, the reward, the flags and the posterior latent: about 8.3 KB at 12M on a 24-dimensional observation, so the 250K rows of the DMC protocol take about 2.1 GB per seed, and about 3.2 GB with the training step's working set. agent.replay_bytes_per_seed gives the figure after train. Running several seeds multiplies it.
  • Recompilation. Widths, depths, counts, bins, imag_horizon, batch_size, batch_length, train_ratio and replay_capacity fix the compiled program; changing one recompiles.
  • Main deviations (all in deviations.md): training is synchronous and in float32 (the reference is asynchronous and computes in bfloat16); one decoder head for the flat observation; everything is checkpointed and seeded. The two-hot expectation is computed in an exact form (D22); the reference's form adds noise to early predictions under JIT, which measurably changes the early actor entropy.
  • The DMC tasks run on MuJoCo Playground's MJX ports, whose physics differ from dm_control's (E18), so comparisons with the published curves are approximate.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Recorded on CPU in PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md, with the 1M preset and 20,000 rows, before evaluations drew fresh keys: Pendulum swings up from 12,000 rows on (final evaluation -222, against about -1,200 at the start). On CartPole Ajax was compared with the reference code itself on the same protocol, over three pre-registered rounds; once both used the same two-hot expectation, the training statistics' seed ranges overlapped the reference's in at least 52 of 58 windows, and all five Ajax seeds passed the redefined CartPole check, as did all five of the reference's. The GPU validation against the published DMC curves is specified in VALIDATION.md and has not been run yet. The probes (tests/probing) train DreamerV3 briefly on tiny environments with known answers (discounting, a continuous advantage, and a risky-or-safe choice it can only weigh in imagination), and its own tests (tests/agents/DreamerV3) check that a run split by a checkpoint equals the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: CartPole, 4 environments, 8,000 rows, a smaller model than the paper's) DreamerV3 ran at 367 rows per second of execution (275 with compilation) at main a8a13c2.

()

Every other argument is the :class:~ajax.agents.DreamerV3.state.DreamerV3Config field of the same name and default, documented there.

Static hyperparameters (fixing shapes or the program, so changing them recompiles): every width, depth and count, bins, imag_horizon, batch_size, batch_length, train_ratio, replay_capacity; the scalar loss and optimizer coefficients are Python floats of the frozen configuration as well.

Replay memory. The replay is a ring of C = min(ceil( replay_capacity / n_envs), rows per env of the run) rows per env (capacity in rows: deviation D27), resolved by every :meth:train call (:meth:_resolve_replay: a run split into resumed calls keeps the replay of the uninterrupted run). Each row stores the observation, action, reward, flags and the posterior latent (deter float32 and stoch as uint8 class indices), about 4 (obs_dim + action_dim + deter + 1) + stoch + 3 bytes: 8.3 KB at 12m on a 24-dim observation, so the 250K rows of the DMC protocol take about 2.1 GB per seed (:attr:replay_bytes_per_seed gives the resolved figure). The training step needs a working set on top of it, mostly the imagination; it scales with B T (deter + stoch classes): about 1 GB at 12m (B = 16, T = 64, H = 15), so about 3.2 GB per seed for the DMC protocol in all (XLA's memory analysis of the compiled run). The seed vmap multiplies both.

docs.title: IQL
docs.text:
Implicit Q-Learning learns from a fixed dataset without ever asking its critic about actions the data does not contain, which offline RL's critics overrate. A state value V(s) is fitted as an upper expectile of the critic over the dataset's own actions, which approximates the best of them without a max. The critic then regresses on r + γ V(s'). The actor copies the dataset's actions, each weighted by how much better than V it was (advantage-weighted regression).

Paper: Kostrikov, Nair and Levine, Offline Reinforcement Learning with Implicit Q-Learning, ICLR 2022 (arXiv:2110.06169). The defaults and the update order are the authors' JAX code, ikostrikov/implicit_q_learning at 09d7002 (learner.py, critic.py, actor.py, policy.py, configs/).

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: Feature IQL Continuous actions yes; the actor's mean is tanh-bounded Discrete actions no Offline training yes, train_offline(dataset, n_updates) Online fine-tuning yes, train(initial_state=...) after it, the same update Memory (memory=) no Environments gymnax, Brax, MuJoCo Playground Several seeds in one call yes, train(seed=[...]) Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

from ajax import IQL
from ajax.buffers.dataset import record
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig


def pd_expert(obs):
    theta = jnp.arctan2(obs[..., 1], obs[..., 0])
    return jnp.clip(-(2.0 * theta + 0.5 * obs[..., 2]), -2.0, 2.0)[..., None]


agent = IQL("Pendulum-v1", buffer_size=10_000)
data = record(pd_expert, agent.env_args, jax.random.PRNGKey(0), n_steps=2_000)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=1_000, use_wandb=False)
state, offline = agent.train_offline(data, n_updates=3_000, seed=[0], logging_config=logging)
print(offline["Eval/episodic mean reward"])
state, online = agent.train(seed=[0], n_timesteps=1_000, initial_state=state)

Evaluations log, next to the return, the losses of the value, the actor and the critics (value/value_loss, value/actor_loss, value/critic_loss), the mean advantage q - V(s) on the batch (value/advantage) and the mean advantage weight (value/weight).

docs.title: Key hyperparameters
docs.text: Argument Default What it does expectile 0.7 the expectile V fits (0.5: the mean; towards 1: the best action in the data). The reference uses 0.7 on locomotion, 0.9 on antmaze temperature 3.0 the advantage weights' inverse temperature, min(exp(temperature (q - V)), 100); 10 on antmaze gamma, tau 0.99, 0.005 discount; Polyak rate of the target critics actor_learning_rate, critic_learning_rate, value_learning_rate 3e-4 Adam step sizes (eps 1e-8, optax's) actor_architecture, critic_architecture ("256", "relu", "256", "relu") hidden layers, also the value's batch_size, buffer_size 256, 1,000,000 replay batch; capacity, which must hold the dataset reward_scale 1.0 multiplies the rewards in the critic's target learning_starts 0 online: steps before the first update (the replay holds the dataset already) normalize_observations False running observation normalisation of the actor and the critics extensions () research features (see Extensions)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each update samples one replay batch and runs, in the reference's order:

  1. Value. V(s) regresses on q = min_i Q_target_i(s, a) at the batch's own actions, by the expectile loss |expectile − 1(q < V)| (q − V)².
  2. Actor. It maximises E[w log π(a|s)] with w = min(exp(temperature (q − V(s))), 100), with V the value just updated. The policy is a Gaussian on a tanh mean, with one learned log-std per action dimension, clipped to [−5, 2]. The evaluations act with its mean.
  3. Critics. Two Q critics regress on reward_scale · r + γ (1 − terminated) V(s').
  4. Targets. The target critics move by Polyak averaging at rate tau.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Learning-rate schedule. For offline training the reference decays the actor's learning rate to 0 by a cosine over its updates. For that, pass actor_learning_rate=optax.cosine_decay_schedule(3e-4, n_updates). Fine-tuning runs keep it constant, as here by default.
  • Rewards. The reference scales a locomotion dataset's rewards by 1000 over its range of episode returns, and subtracts 1 from antmaze's. Compute the factor from your dataset and pass it as reward_scale (or shift the dataset's rewards).
  • Critics' loss. Their mean squared error over both critics, half the reference's sum. Adam's step is the same but for its eps, whose weight against the gradient doubles.
  • The value's input. V reads the raw observation. With normalize_observations=True only the actor and the critics normalise theirs.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: No learning curves are published for IQL yet. Unit tests (tests/agents/IQL) check the expectile loss and the reference's defaults. The probe (tests/probing/test_offline.py) trains IQL offline on logged one-step rows: V must reach the expectile of their returns, and the actor the advantage-weighted mean of their actions, with the weights clipped.

Bases: ActorCritic

Implicit Q-Learning (Kostrikov, Nair and Levine, ICLR 2022): offline RL with a state value fitted as an expectile of the critic over the data's actions, and an actor fitted by advantage-weighted regression (:mod:ajax.agents.IQL.train_IQL). Train it on a dataset with train_offline, then fine-tune online with train.

Defaults are the reference code's (ikostrikov/implicit_q_learning @09d7002, configs/mujoco_config.py, learner.py, policy.py): expectile 0.7 and temperature 3 (locomotion; antmaze takes 0.9 and 10); 256-256 ReLU networks, orthogonal(sqrt 2) initialisation; Adam at 3e-4 with optax's eps 1e-8 for the actor, the critics and the value; the actor a Gaussian on a tanh mean with one learned log-std per action dimension, clipped to [-5, 2]; batch 256, gamma 0.99, tau 0.005. The reference decays the actor's offline learning rate to 0 by a cosine over its updates: pass actor_learning_rate=optax.cosine_decay_schedule( 3e-4, n_updates) for that. Its locomotion rewards are scaled by 1000 over the dataset's range of returns: reward_scale.

docs.title: PPO
docs.text:
Proximal Policy Optimization collects a fixed-length rollout from n_envs parallel environments, then takes several passes of minibatch gradient steps on it. A clipped objective keeps each update close to the policy that collected the data, so the same rollout can be reused for n_epochs passes without the policy running away. PPO is the default on-policy agent in Ajax: it handles discrete and continuous actions, memory, image observations and the minibatch layouts of Brax's PPO.

Paper: Schulman, Wolski, Dhariwal, Radford and Klimov, Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms, 2017 (arXiv:1707.06347).

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: Feature PPO Discrete actions yes Continuous actions yes (Gaussian; squash=True for a tanh-bounded one) Memory (memory=) yes: GRU, LSTM, transformer, Mamba (Memory), without extensions Environments gymnax, Brax, MuJoCo Playground Image observations yes, a CNN encoder (cnn_image_shape) PID policy yes, actor_architecture=PIDPolicy(...) (Networks) Several seeds in one call yes, train(seed=[...]) Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss Resume and checkpoints yes; a split run equals the uninterrupted one (probe and resume contract)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from ajax import PPO
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = PPO("CartPole-v1", n_envs=4, n_steps=128, batch_size=32)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=4_096, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[1, 2], n_timesteps=20_480, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])  # one row per seed, one column per evaluation

With memory, the update replays the rollout in contiguous chunks of bptt_length steps, each started from the memory the policy had there:

from ajax import PPO
from ajax.networks.memory import MemoryConfig

agent = PPO("CartPole-v1", n_envs=4, n_steps=128, batch_size=32,
            memory=MemoryConfig(kind="gru", hidden_size=32), bptt_length=32)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=4_096)
