PureJaxRL's recurrent PPO, with memory=) cnn_image_shape, cnn_extra_obs_dim, cnn_spec None, 0, None convolutional encoder for flat image observations episode_length, action_repeat None, 1 simulator steps per episode (1,000 when None) and per agent step, on Brax and Playground expose_recent_rollout False keep the last rollout on the state, for measurement extensions extensions () research features (see Extensions)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• batch_size sets the number of minibatches, not their size. Unless num_minibatches is positive, the rollout of n_steps * n_envs samples splits into max(n_steps, batch_size) // min(n_steps, batch_size) minibatches. With the defaults that is 32 minibatches of 256 samples (batch_size * n_envs). This differs from Stable-Baselines3, where batch_size is the minibatch size.
  • Shuffling. Every epoch draws a new split of the rollout into minibatches, as OpenAI Baselines' and CleanRL's PPO do.
  • Where the advantages are computed. The advantages are computed once on the whole rollout and its n_steps * n_envs samples are shuffled flat into the minibatches, as in the PPO paper's Algorithm 1 and OpenAI Baselines' ppo2. unroll_length switches to Brax's PPO: the rollout is cut into fragments of that length that bootstrap at their ends, each minibatch holds whole fragments, and its advantages are recomputed with the current critic. unroll_length=n_steps keeps each environment's whole rollout as one fragment. PPO refuses at construction a length that does not split the rollout evenly into the minibatches.
  • Actions. A continuous PPO samples an unbounded Gaussian by default; Ajax clips the sample to [-1, 1] and maps that range onto the environment's bounds, so on gymnax Pendulum (torque in [-2, 2]) one unit of the Gaussian is two units of torque. squash=True bounds it with tanh instead. Evaluation uses the mean action.
  • Exploration noise. The Gaussian learns one log standard deviation per action dimension, whatever the observation, starting at 0 (a standard deviation of 1) and never clipped (log_std_bounds=None, which the run config records), as PPO's reference code does: OpenAI Baselines at ea25b9e (ppo2's common/distributions.py:96-106; ppo1's ppo1/mlp_policy.py:36-39, gaussian_fixed_var=True), CleanRL at fe8d8a0 (ppo_continuous_action.py:129) and PureJaxRL at 31756b1 (ppo_continuous_action.py:41). As in theirs, it is updated with the rest of the model, under one gradient clip over both networks (see separate networks). log_std_bounds clips every log standard deviation PPO can learn, so by default none is clipped. log_std_state_independent=False with log_std_init=-1.0 builds the head PPO had before: a log standard deviation computed from the observation, starting at -1; log_std_bounds=(-20.0, 2.0) adds the clip it then had, SAC's. A checkpoint saved with that head restores only into that network, and restoring it into the default one is refused with this advice. A PID policy keeps its own log standard deviation, which starts at log_std_init and is clipped to log_std_bounds.
  • Brax-style options. mean_kernel_init, squash, num_resets_per_eval and num_evals reproduce choices of Brax's PPO. They are off by default, as is encoder_layer_norm (a LayerNorm on the encoder's output).
  • Separate networks. The actor and the critic are separate networks. As ppo2's one optimizer, their gradients are clipped together to one global norm, then each takes an Adam step (Adam is per coordinate, so the two are one Adam over the whole model); the value loss is not clipped. As in Baselines' ppo2, their hidden layers start orthogonal with gain sqrt(2), the policy's output layer with gain 0.01 and the value layer with gain 1. An entropy bonus on a squashed policy is a one-sample estimate of the executed action's entropy, as in Brax.
  • Normalisation. With normalize_observations=True the loss sees the observations normalised with the statistics of the step that collected them, as SB3's VecNormalize and CleanRL do.
  • Extensions. PPO folds the loss and target phases, so instrumentation such as ConditioningMetrics works on it (pass expose_recent_rollout=True so it can read the latest rollout). It has no action phase: extensions that act during collection need SAC. A recurrent PPO refuses extensions. See Extensions.
  • Memory. A recurrent PPO minibatches whole chunks of bptt_length steps of the rollout. Libraries disagree on that length, so by default the number of minibatches chooses it: each environment's whole rollout when n_envs is a multiple of the number of minibatches, as OpenAI Baselines' ppo2, CleanRL and PureJaxRL do, otherwise the fewest equal chunks that split (256 steps with the defaults). PPO refuses at construction chunks that do not split. Memory compares the libraries and says how to set it: to reproduce theirs, choose num_minibatches to divide n_envs. unroll_length is for feedforward policies; recurrent ones use bptt_length.

docs.title: GAIL: imitation by a discriminator
docs.text:
GAIL (Ho and Ermon, Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning, NeurIPS 2016, arXiv:1606.03476) trains a policy to imitate demonstrations without their rewards. A discriminator learns to tell the policy's rollouts from the demonstrations, and the policy is rewarded where it is mistaken for the expert. In Ajax it is PPO with the AdversarialReward extension, which folds the reward phase:

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

from ajax import PPO
from ajax.buffers.dataset import record
from ajax.extensions.adversarial import AdversarialReward


def pd_expert(obs):
    theta = jnp.arctan2(obs[..., 1], obs[..., 0])
    return jnp.clip(-(2.0 * theta + 0.5 * obs[..., 2]), -2.0, 2.0)[..., None]


env_args = PPO("Pendulum-v1").env_args
demonstrations = record(pd_expert, env_args, jax.random.PRNGKey(0), n_steps=1_000)
agent = PPO("Pendulum-v1", extensions=(AdversarialReward(demonstrations),))

After each rollout, the rewards become -log(1 - D(s, a)) from the current discriminator, and the discriminator takes n_updates (2) cross-entropy steps on the rollout's rows and as many demonstration rows. It follows HumanCompatibleAI/imitation at e5ef188 (algorithms/adversarial/gail.py, common.py): its 32-32 ReLU reward network and torch's Adam at 1e-3. PPO replaces the paper's TRPO, as in that code. The evaluations still report the environment's return. The discriminator reads the action the environment runs, clipped to [-1, 1], on the rollout and on the demonstrations, as the reference records the clipped action SB3 steps with. Deviations: it reads (s, a) without the running normalisation of the reference's examples, and trains on the whole rollout, where the reference draws demo_batch_size rows.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The reproduction results set PPO beside Stable-Baselines3's on CartPole and Brax's on inverted_pendulum, with learning curves. Unit tests (tests/agents/PPO and the contracts every agent shares) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning, such as the fresh split of each epoch. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: the exact values of small problems, episode ends, memory, extension phases, and a run split by a checkpoint matching the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: CartPole, 4 environments, 8,000 steps) PPO ran at 17,817 steps per second of execution (4,298 with compilation) at main a8a13c2 (PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

docs.title: PQN
docs.text:
Parallelised Q-Network is Q-learning without a replay buffer and without a target network. It collects short rollouts from many environments at once, as PPO does, and regresses the Q-network on Q(lambda) returns computed from them. A LayerNorm after every hidden layer keeps this stable. It is built for many vectorised environments, which replace the buffer as the source of varied data.

Paper. Gallici et al., Simplifying Deep Temporal Difference Learning, 2024.

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: PQN Continuous actions (Box) No Discrete actions (Discrete) Yes Learning On-policy rollouts, no replay buffer Vectorised environments (n_envs) Yes, and it relies on them Recurrent memory (memory=) No Image observations (CNN encoder) Yes, with cnn_image_shape Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from ajax import PQN
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = PQN("CartPole-v1")  # 8 envs, 128-step rollouts
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=32_768, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=131_072, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])  # one row per seed

docs.text:
Defaults are read from PQN.__init__.

Argument Default What it does n_envs 8 parallel environments learning_rate 2.5e-4 RAdam step size (the authors' optimiser, optax.radam) architecture ("128", "relu", "128", "relu") hidden layers; each Dense is followed by a LayerNorm gamma 0.99 discount q_lambda 0.65 the lambda of the Q(lambda) returns n_steps 128 rollout length per env n_epochs 4 passes over each rollout num_minibatches 4 minibatches per pass epsilon_start, epsilon_end 1.0, 0.05 exploration rate at the start and the end of its decay epsilon_decay_frac 0.5 fraction of the run over which epsilon decays reward_scale 1.0 multiplies the rewards in the target max_grad_norm 10.0 gradient clipping by global norm (the authors'); None turns it off normalize_observations, normalize_rewards False running normalisation reward_normalization_gamma None with normalize_rewards, divide by the spread of the discounted return td_loss_fn None the loss; None is half the squared error (the authors'), make_huber_td_loss(delta) the Huber loss cnn_image_shape, cnn_extra_obs_dim, cnn_spec None, 0, None convolutional encoder for flat image observations; None builds the reference network (see Notes) expose_recent_rollout False keep the last rollout on state.last_rollout for extensions episode_length, action_repeat None, 1 simulator steps per episode (1,000 when None) and per agent step, on Brax and Playground extensions () research features (see Extensions)

A rollout holds n_steps * n_envs rows (1,024 by default), which must divide evenly into num_minibatches; PQN raises otherwise.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Returns. With V(s) = max_a Q(s, a), each step's return is G_t = r_t + gamma ((1 - lambda) V(s_{t+1}) + lambda G_{t+1}), and G_t = r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) at the rollout's last step. A termination zeroes V(s_{t+1}); a time limit bootstraps on V(s_{t+1}) but stops the lambda trace there.
  • One update. The returns are computed once per rollout with the current network, then held fixed for n_epochs passes of num_minibatches gradient steps, the rollout reshuffled each pass.
  • Why several envs. Without a buffer, the data's diversity comes from the parallel envs. The probes run PQN with 8 envs because with one env the value of the action it stops exploring drifts.
  • Exploration. As DQN: epsilon decays linearly with the training fraction; evaluation is greedy.
  • Extensions. on_target extensions reshape the returns before they are held fixed; critic_loss extensions add a term to every minibatch's TD loss.
  • Initialisation. As the authors' code (mttga/purejaxql), which sets no initialiser: every Dense layer, the Q head included, starts with Flax's default lecun_normal kernel and a zero bias.
  • Images. With cnn_image_shape and no cnn_spec, PQN builds the authors' image network: Mnih et al.'s (MNIH_CNN) for images of at least 36 pixels a side, MinAtar's (MINATAR_CNN) for smaller ones, each layer he_normal and followed by a LayerNorm. The image features go straight to the Q head; architecture is not used. Their Atari network also divides pixels by 255; Ajax leaves that scaling to the environment.
  • Shared code. PQN reuses DQN's Q-network wrapper, loss and epsilon-greedy collection, and PPO's minibatch shuffler; its own code is the LayerNorm network, the Q(lambda) returns and the on-policy loop.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The reproduction results set PQN beside its authors' code (purejaxql) on CartPole and Asterix-MinAtar, with learning curves. A conformance check (tests/conformance/test_pqn_purejaxql.py) runs one training iteration of each from the same state with the same random numbers and compares them step by step; the differences it finds are listed in the specifications. Unit tests (tests/agents/PQN and the contracts every agent shares) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: its Q(lambda) returns, discounting, episode ends, extension phases, and a run split by a checkpoint matching the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: CartPole, 4 envs, 8,000 steps) PQN ran at 36,961 steps per second of execution (7,358 with compilation) at main a8a13c2 (see PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

Bases: ActorCritic

Parallelised Q-Network (Gallici et al., 2024) for discrete action spaces.

On-policy value-based RL: vectorised rollouts, Q(lambda) regression targets, no replay buffer and no target network -- training stability instead comes from LayerNorm in the Q-network. The policy is greedy over Q, with epsilon-greedy exploration during collection.

docs.title: REDQ
docs.text:
Randomized Ensembled Double Q-learning is SAC with many critics and many critic updates per environment step. Each critic target takes the minimum over a random subset of the target critics, which keeps over-estimation in check even at a high update-to-data ratio, and the actor maximises the ensemble's mean value. Each environment step costs far more compute than SAC's, in exchange for many more critic updates per step.

Paper. Chen et al., Randomized Ensembled Double Q-Learning, 2021 (arXiv:2101.05982). The update follows its Algorithm 1; where the authors' code (watchernyu/REDQ at 7b5d1bf) is more specific, Ajax follows the code (see Notes).

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: REDQ Continuous actions (Box) Yes Discrete actions No Learning Off-policy, replay buffer Vectorised environments (n_envs) Yes Recurrent memory (memory=) Yes, without extensions or expert_policy PID policy (actor_architecture=PIDPolicy(...)) Yes Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# doc: skip (20 critic steps of 10 critics per update: minutes on a CPU)
from ajax import REDQ
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

# 10 critics, targets from the min over 2 of them, 20 critic steps per update.
agent = REDQ("Pendulum-v1", n_envs=4, learning_starts=1_000)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=2_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=4_000, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])  # one row per seed

An SVGD-style variant, which pushes the critics apart in function space, is the KernelRepulsion extension, an Ajax research feature:

from ajax import REDQ
from ajax.extensions.ensemble import KernelRepulsion

agent = REDQ("Pendulum-v1", extensions=(KernelRepulsion(coef=0.1),))

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• One update. num_critic_updates critic steps, each on a fresh replay minibatch and each followed by a target update; then one actor step and one temperature step on the last minibatch.
  • Following the authors' code. Three choices come from watchernyu/REDQ rather than the paper's Algorithm 1. The actor step reads the critics as they were before the last critic step, since the code computes the actor loss before that step's optimizer update; the saved state keeps the updated critics. The critic loss is the sum over the critics of each one's mean squared error. alpha_init=1.0 matches the code's log_alpha starting at 0; the code then uses alpha=0.2 until its first temperature step, a transient Ajax does not reproduce.
  • Initialisation. As the authors' code: every layer of the actor and the critics, the mean and log-std layers included, starts Xavier-uniform with a zero bias, each critic of the ensemble drawn on its own. With memory=, REDQ keeps its previous initialisation until Ni et al.'s is audited.
  • Target entropy. The default is -1 per action dimension. target_entropy_per_dim="mbpo" takes MBPO's per-task value instead, the authors' default, for the Brax ids hopper (-1), halfcheetah (-3), walker2d (-3), ant (-4) and humanoid (-2); any other environment raises.
  • Update-to-data ratio. Each iteration steps every env once, then makes one update, so the ratio of critic steps to environment steps is num_critic_updates / n_envs: 20 with the defaults.
  • Cost. On the CPU speed benchmark below, REDQ executed 47 steps per second, against SAC's 2,218 on the same preset.
  • Actions and evaluation. As SAC: a tanh-squashed Gaussian in [-1, 1], mapped onto the environment's bounds; evaluation uses the mean action. The critics read actions in the environment's units, as the authors' code's do (act_limit * tanh, core.py:238): on a box other than [-1, 1] Adam then steps their action inputs as the authors' does.
  • Time limits. A transition cut by a time limit bootstraps on its final observation; only a termination stops the bootstrap.
  • Diagnostics. REDQ logs how spread out its ensemble is (ensemble_q_std, mean_pairwise_q_dist), computed without gradient.
  • Shared maths. REDQ imports SAC's maths (ajax.agents.SAC.core) instead of copying it.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The repository records no learning curves for REDQ yet. A conformance check (tests/conformance/test_redq_original.py) runs one training step of Ajax's REDQ and of watchernyu/REDQ from the same state, with the same batches, subsets and noises, and compares every critic, target, the actor, the temperature and their optimisers. It accounts for two differences of the authors' code: its first step reads the temperature 0.2 its constructor leaves behind, and its tanh log-determinant adds 1e-6. Unit tests (tests/agents/REDQ and the contracts every agent shares) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning: the summed critic loss, the random subset, the critics the actor reads and the target entropy. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: its targets, discounting, time limits, memory, extension phases, and a run split by a checkpoint matching the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: Pendulum, 4 envs, 8,000 steps, updates from step 1,000) REDQ ran at 47 steps per second at main a8a13c2 (see PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

docs.title: SAC
docs.text:
Soft Actor-Critic learns a stochastic policy that maximises the reward plus the policy's entropy, so it keeps exploring while it improves. Two critics estimate the soft action value, and the target uses the smaller of the two target critics to curb over-estimation. The entropy weight alpha tunes itself towards a target entropy. SAC learns off-policy from a replay buffer, so it reuses each transition many times.

SAC is also the agent with the most expert-guidance support in Ajax: it is the only one that runs action extensions (an expert acting during collection) and keeps a few expert options of its own (see Expert options).

Papers. Haarnoja et al., Soft Actor-Critic, 2018 (arXiv:1801.01290). The learned temperature with a target entropy follows Haarnoja et al., Soft Actor-Critic Algorithms and Applications, 2018.

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text:
SAC Continuous actions (Box) Yes Discrete actions No Learning Off-policy, replay buffer Vectorised environments (n_envs) Yes Recurrent memory (memory=) Yes, without extensions or expert_policy PID policy (actor_architecture=PIDPolicy(...)) Yes Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss, action

The action phase runs only when the agent has an expert_policy and use_pid_policy is off; SAC raises at construction otherwise. See Extensions for what each phase does.

docs.title: Expert options
docs.text:
These options remain on SAC because they reach the network's input size, the collection or the action pipeline, where extensions do not reach yet. Most concern the expert; the last four are research switches of SAC's own. The expert is written in the environment's units and receives the raw (unnormalised) observations; Ajax reads its actions in the agent's units. See Expert guidance.

Argument Default What it does expert_policy None the expert used in training; None is plain SAC eval_expert_policy None an expert used only for the evaluation's comparison metrics expert_buffer_n_steps 20_000 expert steps per env written to the buffer before training expert_fraction 0.7 during warm-up, the chance a step takes the expert's action instead of a uniform one use_pid_policy False the actor outputs the gains of the expert's PID (needs learnable_fields on the expert; refuses augment_obs_with_expert_action) augment_obs_with_expert_action, augment_obs_with_expert_state False append the expert's action or internal state to the observation use_train_frac False append the training fraction to the observation target_entropy_initial_per_dim, target_entropy_ramp_frac None, 0.5 move the target entropy linearly from this start to target_entropy_per_dim over that fraction of training normalize_obs_running False normalize_observations under its old name: warns, and will be removed (Environments) store_policy_action False store the policy's sampled action in the replay instead of the executed one (an off-policy-correctness ablation)

Cloning the expert into the actor before training is the CloningPretrain extension, at the actor's learning rate; fitting a frozen expert critic on the expert's Monte-Carlo returns is MCPretrain, which only SAC supports. jsrl_curriculum is deprecated: it has no effect and warns, since SAC counts each environment's steps in its episode whenever an extension reads them (JSRLCurriculum). skip_critic_pretrain=True is a no-op kept for a downstream project; False raises.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Actions. The actor is a tanh-squashed Gaussian, so its actions lie in [-1, 1]; Ajax maps them onto the environment's bounds, so on gymnax Pendulum (torque in [-2, 2]) SAC reaches the whole range. The warm-up's uniform actions cover the whole box too. The replay stores the agent's [-1, 1] action. Evaluation uses the mean action.
  • Initialisation. As both reference codes (haarnoja/sac, and rail-berkeley/softlearning for the learned temperature): Glorot-uniform kernels and zero biases in every layer. They draw the mean and the log-std from one output layer; Ajax's two heads each take Glorot's bound for their own width (about 1% wider with 256 inputs). With memory=, SAC keeps its previous initialisation until Ni et al.'s is audited.
  • Standard deviation. The log-std is clipped to [-20, 2] and the standard deviation is its exponential, as in haarnoja/sac and in softlearning at the time of the learned-temperature paper. Later softlearning (its TensorFlow 2 port, 2020) uses softplus(x) + 1e-5 instead; Ajax keeps the paper-era form.
  • Updates per step. Each iteration steps every env once, then makes one update: num_critic_updates critic steps, one actor step, one temperature step and one target update. With n_envs=4 that is one update per four environment steps.
  • Time limits. A transition cut by a time limit still bootstraps on its final observation; only a termination stops the bootstrap.
  • Temperature. The alpha step is never gradient-clipped, as in the reference SAC, even with max_grad_norm set: clipping would turn it into a sign step.
  • Ajax additions, not in the paper. policy_update_start and alpha_update_start hold the actor and alpha back until those timesteps; with the default learning_starts=10_000 they change nothing. The target-entropy ramp and the expert options above are research features.
  • Memory. With memory=, SAC replays sequences in the R2D2 way (Kapturowski et al. 2019): burn_in steps warm the memory up, then sequence_length steps are learned from. It refuses extensions and expert_policy.

docs.title: CQL and Cal-QL: offline
docs.text:
CQL (Kumar, Zhou, Tucker and Levine, Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning, NeurIPS 2020, arXiv:2006.04779) is SAC with a critic term that pushes the critic down on actions away from the data's and up on the data's. Cal-QL (Nakamoto et al., Cal-QL: Calibrated Offline RL Pre-Training for Efficient Online Fine-Tuning, NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2303.05479) floors that push at the data's Monte-Carlo returns, so fine-tuning online does not start from values far too low. In Ajax both are extensions on SAC, trained with the offline mode:

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.extensions.offline import CalQL, ConservativeQ

agent = SAC(
    "Pendulum-v1",
    actor_learning_rate=1e-4,  # the references' policy rate
    policy_update_start=0,  # the offline mode counts updates: start at once
    alpha_update_start=0,
    learning_starts=0,
    expert_buffer_n_steps=0,
    extensions=(ConservativeQ(alpha=5.0),),  # or CalQL(alpha=5.0)
)
# state, evaluations = agent.train_offline(dataset, n_updates=1_000_000)

The term is the authors' importance-sampled CQL(H) (aviralkumar2907/CQL at d67dbe9, cql.py:234-264): for each critic, the logsumexp of its values at 10 uniform actions and 10 of the policy's at s and at s', each less its log-density, minus its value at the data's action, times alpha (5 in the references' gym runs). Cal-QL takes the maximum of each policy action's value and the row's return to go first (nakamotoo/Cal-QL at ac6eafe, JaxCQL/conservative_sac.py:227-240). The return to go is the transition dataset's, at its gamma. Online rows have none, so they are not floored; the reference computes them as episodes end. Both need a policy with a density, so a deterministic one (TD3's) is refused. Deviation: SAC's target keeps its entropy term, which the CQL reference's deterministic_backup drops.

docs.title: TD3
docs.text:
Twin Delayed DDPG learns a deterministic policy and two critics. It fixes DDPG's over-estimation with three changes: the target takes the smaller of two target critics, the target action gets clipped noise (target policy smoothing), and the actor and the targets update only every policy_delay critic steps. It explores by adding Gaussian noise to its actions and learns off-policy from a replay buffer.

Paper. Fujimoto et al., Addressing Function Approximation Error in Actor-Critic Methods, 2018 (arXiv:1802.09477). The update follows its Algorithm 1 as the authors' code (sfujim/TD3) makes it, and the defaults are that code's as updated in 2019 (see Notes).

Yes Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, on_target, critic_loss, actor_loss

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Defaults. The authors updated their code's hyperparameters in 2019 "to improve performance": 256-256 layers, learning rate 3e-4, batch 256 and a 25,000-step warm-up. Ajax uses these. The paper's run used 400-300 layers, 1e-3, batch 100 and 10,000 steps; pass them to reproduce it.
  • Actor. A deterministic MLP ending in tanh. As in the authors' code, every layer of the actor and the critics, the actor's last included, starts as torch's nn.Linear does: kernel and bias uniform in ±1/sqrt(fan_in) (not DDPG's ±3e-3 last layer, which TD3 keeps with memory= until Ni et al.'s initialisation is audited). Actions lie in [-1, 1], and Ajax maps them onto the environment's bounds, so the noise levels are in those [-1, 1] units: on gymnax Pendulum (torque in [-2, 2]) an exploration_noise of 0.1 is a torque noise of standard deviation 0.2.
  • Critics. They read the action in the environment's units, c + h a with the box's centre c and half-range h, as the authors' critics read max_action * tanh; on a [-1, 1] box the map is the identity. Adam's steps on a critic's action inputs depend on those units. Their loss sums the critics' squared errors, as the authors' code does.
  • Behaviour policy. clip(mu(s) + N(0, exploration_noise), -1, 1) after the warm-up; uniform random actions before learning_starts. Evaluation uses mu(s) without noise.
  • Target. r + gamma (1 - terminated) min_i Q'_i(s', a'), with a' = clip(mu'(s') + clip(N(0, target_policy_noise), -c, c), -1, 1) and c = target_noise_clip.
  • Actor loss. -Q_1(s, mu(s)): the first critic only.
  • Updates per step. Each iteration steps every env once, then makes one critic step; every policy_delay-th one also steps the actor and the targets, the first actor step coming with the policy_delay-th update, as in the authors' code.
  • Time limits. A transition cut by a time limit bootstraps on its final observation; only a termination stops the bootstrap.
  • PID policy. With actor_architecture=PIDPolicy(...) the actor is a PID whose output goes through tanh; see Networks.
  • Memory. Sequence replay also burns in the target actor's memory, since TD3's bootstrap action comes from it.

docs.title: TD3+BC: offline
docs.text:
TD3+BC (Fujimoto and Gu, A Minimalist Approach to Offline Reinforcement Learning, NeurIPS 2021, arXiv:2106.06860) is TD3 trained on a fixed dataset with a behaviour-cloning term in the actor's loss. Its reference code is sfujim/TD3_BC at 8791ad7. In Ajax it is TD3, ImitationLoss with the dataset's own actions as the target, and the offline mode:

from ajax import TD3
from ajax.extensions.expert import ImitationLoss

agent = TD3(
    "Pendulum-v1",
    normalize_observations=True,  # the dataset's statistics, as the paper's
    learning_starts=0,
    extensions=(ImitationLoss(None, target="replay", alpha=2.5),),
)
# state, evaluations = agent.train_offline(dataset, n_updates=1_000_000)

The paper's actor loss is -λ mean Q(s, π(s)) + mean((π(s) - a)²), with λ = α / mean|Q(s, π(s))| and α = 2.5 (TD3_BC.py:141-143), the actions compared in the environment's units. With alpha, ImitationLoss makes TD3's actor loss exactly that: it adds (λ - 1) times TD3's own -mean Q and the squared difference of the actions mapped onto the env's box. The other settings are TD3's defaults, which match the reference's. The states are standardised with the dataset's statistics. The reference divides by the standard deviation plus 1e-3, Ajax by sqrt(var + 1e-8); the two differ on a column the dataset holds constant. The offline mode evaluates every log_frequency updates, as the reference does every 5,000. A conformance check (tests/conformance/test_td3bc_sfujim.py) makes one update of each from the same state, batch and noise, on Pendulum and MountainCarContinuous, and compares them.

docs.title: ReBRAC: offline
docs.text:
ReBRAC (Tarasov, Kurenkov, Nikulin and Kolesnikov, Revisiting the Minimalist Approach to Offline Reinforcement Learning, NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.09836) is TD3+BC with design choices of its own. The main ones are a behaviour-cloning penalty in the critic's target as well, LayerNorm in the critic, deeper networks and larger batches. Its reference code is tinkoff-ai/ReBRAC at 694385b. In Ajax it is TD3 with TD3+BC's actor term and TargetBC, the target penalty, trained with the offline mode:

from ajax import TD3
from ajax.extensions.expert import ImitationLoss
from ajax.extensions.offline import TargetBC

hidden = ("256", "relu")
agent = TD3(
    "Pendulum-v1",
    actor_architecture=hidden * 3,
    critic_architecture=("256", "relu", "layernorm") * 3,
    actor_learning_rate=1e-3,
    critic_learning_rate=1e-3,
    batch_size=1024,
    learning_starts=0,
    extensions=(
        ImitationLoss(None, target="replay", alpha=1.0),  # actor_bc_coef 1
        TargetBC(beta=1.0),  # critic_bc_coef 1
    ),
)
# state, evaluations = agent.train_offline(dataset, n_updates=1_000_000)

TargetBC subtracts γ (1 − d) β Σ (ã′ − a′)² from the target, with ã′ the next actions TD3's target scored (its target policy plus clipped noise) and a′ the dataset's next action (rebrac.py:134-144). The replay keeps a′ as each row's episode's next row's action. A row ending its episode, or a collected one, has none, so it keeps its target. The coefficients actor_bc_coef and critic_bc_coef are tuned per dataset in the paper.

Deviations from the reference:

  • TD3's actor follows its first critic, and the cloning term's scale is that critic's mean|Q|. ReBRAC uses the minimum over the critics for both.
  • The cloning term averages the squared error over the action dimensions. ReBRAC sums it, so pass coef equal to the action dimension to match.
  • TD3 keeps its reference's initialisation. ReBRAC's layers start their biases at 0.1 and its heads uniform in ±1e-3 (actor) and ±3e-3 (critic).

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The repository records no learning curves for TD3 yet. A conformance check (tests/conformance/test_td3_sfujim.py) runs one update of Ajax's TD3 and of sfujim/TD3 from the same state, batch and noise, on MountainCarContinuous and Pendulum, and compares the change each makes to every parameter and optimiser moment. Unit tests (tests/agents/TD3 and the contracts every agent shares) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning, such as its smoothed target. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: its target smoothing, discounting, time limits, memory, extension phases, and a run split by a checkpoint matching the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: Pendulum, 4 envs, 8,000 steps, updates from step 1,000) TD3 ran at 2,659 steps per second of execution (1,961 with compilation) at main a8a13c2 (see PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

Bases: ActorCritic

Twin Delayed DDPG (Fujimoto et al., 2018) for continuous action spaces.

Defaults are the authors' code as updated in 2019 (sfujim/TD3 a8d53f7, ade6260; its README: "minor adjustments to hyperparameters ... to improve performance"), not the paper's 400-300, lr 1e-3, batch 100 and 1e4 warm-up: - Actor / critic: 256-256 ReLU, plain MLPs (no normalisation layer) - Adam, lr=3e-4 - tau=0.005, gamma=0.99 - Exploration noise: N(0, 0.1) - Target policy noise: N(0, 0.2), clipped to +/-0.5 - Policy delay: 2 - Replay buffer: 1e6, batch=256, learning_starts=25e3

docs.title: TD-MPC2
docs.text:
TD-MPC2 learns a model of the environment in a latent space and plans with it at every step. Its world model has no decoder: an encoder, latent dynamics, a reward predictor and an ensemble of Q-functions, trained together on short sub-trajectories from replay. To act, a sampling planner (MPPI) tries action sequences in the latent model, guided by a learned policy prior, and executes the first action of the best ones. TDMPC2MultiTask trains one such model offline on the data of several tasks.

Paper: Hansen, Su and Wang, TD-MPC2: Scalable, Robust World Models for Continuous Control, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.16828). Official code: nicklashansen/tdmpc2.

Ajax reproduces the paper-era code (b67b21c, whose agent is identical to 5f6fade). The world-model design notes give the full specification, and deviations.md lists every version choice and every departure from the reference.

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: Feature TDMPC2 TDMPC2MultiTask Discrete actions no no Continuous actions yes yes Memory (memory=) no no Environments gymnax, Brax, MuJoCo Playground trains on a dataset; evaluates on any of them Observations flat vectors, raw (no normalisation) flat vectors of different sizes per task Terminating episodes refused, unless episodic=True no Several seeds in one call yes yes Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics the same Resume and checkpoints yes; a checkpoint restored by a new agent equals the uninterrupted run (test) yes, the same

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# doc: skip (about two minutes on a CPU; tests/agents/TDMPC2/test_TDMPC2.py covers this path)
from ajax import TDMPC2
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

# model_size=1 and a smaller planner than the paper's, for a quick CPU run.
agent = TDMPC2("Pendulum-v1", model_size=1, num_samples=64, num_elites=8,
               num_pi_trajs=4, iterations=2, seed_steps=400)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=600, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_200, num_episode_test=2,
                                 logging_config=logging)
print(agent.gamma)  # 0.975, derived from Pendulum's 200-step episodes
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])

The paper's DMC protocol: action repeat 2 over 1,000 simulator steps (500 agent steps per episode), the 5M model, one environment. The paper's "1M environment steps" are 500,000 agent steps:

# doc: skip (the paper's full budget; benchmarks/world_models/paper_protocol.py runs it)
from ajax import TDMPC2

agent = TDMPC2("CheetahRun", model_size=5, action_repeat=2, episode_length=1000)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=500_000)

docs.title: Key hyperparameters
docs.text:
Every default is the paper's (config.yaml at 5f6fade).

Argument Default What it does model_size 5 preset of 1, 5, 19, 48 or 317 M parameters; fills enc_dim, mlp_dim, latent_dim, num_enc_layers, num_q n_envs 1 environments stepped in lockstep, one update per environment step horizon 3 length of the training sub-trajectories and of the plans batch_size 256 sub-trajectories per update buffer_size 1,000,000 environment steps kept in replay seed_steps None random steps before training; None is max(1000, 5 T) updates_per_step 1.0 updates per environment step after the seed phase learning_rate 3e-4 a float or a schedule; the encoder trains at learning_rate * enc_lr_scale (0.3) gamma None None derives it from the episode length T: (T/5 - 1) / (T/5), clipped to [0.95, 0.995] iterations, num_samples, num_elites 6, 512, 64 MPPI iterations, sampled plans and kept plans num_pi_trajs 24 plans proposed by the policy prior consistency_coef, reward_coef, value_coef 20, 0.1, 0.1 world-model loss weights rho 0.5 per-step decay of the loss weights along the horizon entropy_coef 1e-4 policy prior's entropy weight tau 0.01 target Q update rate episodic False accept terminating tasks (the latest code's episodic mode) action_repeat, episode_length 1, 1000 simulator steps per agent step, and per episode (Brax, Playground)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• What n_timesteps counts. Agent steps (environment steps after action repeat); logs also carry env_frames. With episodic=True it counts rows: environment steps plus one per finished episode.
  • Terminations. The paper-era agent bootstraps through every episode end, so a terminating task would train on wrong targets. Ajax counts terminations and raises a ValueError after train if there were any (deviation T10). episodic=True grafts the latest official code's episodic mode (commit eece801) onto the paper-era agent instead: a termination head and variable-length episodes in replay (T29).
  • Evaluation (with a logging_config): every log_frequency environment steps, num_episode_test episodes of the planner in evaluation mode, on a rebuilt environment, each evaluation from fresh initial states (the same ones when a seed is rerun; T9). The paper uses log_frequency=50_000 with 10 episodes. LoggingConfig's default of 1,000 makes a 500-step-episode run spend about twice as long evaluating as training.
  • Replay memory is sized at each train call for the steps the run will have taken: min(buffer_size, total) (T26), in the episodic mode as well (T29). At full capacity it takes 124 MB per seed on DMC Walker. A run trained in chunks, or restored from a checkpoint by a new agent, replays exactly what the uninterrupted run does.
  • Actions. The planner's actions lie in [-1, 1]; Ajax maps them onto the environment's bounds, as the reference scales its actions.
  • Several environments. n_envs > 1 plans for each environment separately and takes n_envs updates per step (T7); the reference uses one.
  • The DMC tasks run on MuJoCo Playground's MJX ports, whose physics differ from dm_control's (E18), so comparisons with the published curves are approximate.

docs.title: Multi-task: TDMPC2MultiTask
docs.text:
The paper's multi-task models are trained offline, on the pooled replay of single-task agents. TDMPC2MultiTask does the same: a learnable task embedding conditions the model, observations are zero-padded to the largest task's size, the unused action dimensions are masked, and each task keeps the discount of its own episode length. Training does no planning, and n_timesteps counts updates. Build the dataset from single-task runs with export_episodes (one run's replay), concatenate_episodes (several seeds of a task) and pool_tasks; save_dataset and load_dataset store it as an .npz file.

# doc: skip (about five minutes on a CPU; tests/agents/TDMPC2/test_TDMPC2MultiTask.py covers this path)
from ajax import TDMPC2, TDMPC2MultiTask
from ajax.agents.TDMPC2.dataset import export_episodes, pool_tasks
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

small = dict(model_size=1, num_samples=64, num_elites=8, num_pi_trajs=4, iterations=2)
tasks = ["Reacher-misc", "PointRobot-misc"]  # 8 and 6 observations, 2 actions, T = 100

episodes = []
for task in tasks:  # one single-task run per task; its replay is the task's data
    agent = TDMPC2(task, seed_steps=500, **small)
    state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_000)
    episodes.append(export_episodes(agent, state, seed_index=0, name=task))
dataset = pool_tasks(episodes)  # every task's episodes must have the same length

multi = TDMPC2MultiTask(dataset, eval_envs=tasks, batch_size=256, **small)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=500, use_wandb=False)
state, history = multi.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_000, num_episode_test=2,
                             logging_config=logging)
print(history["Eval/Reacher-misc/episodic mean reward"])
print(history["Eval/episodic mean reward"])  # the mean over tasks

It also logs Eval/normalized score, the mean over tasks of return / 10 (the paper's normalisation of DMC returns). multi.evaluate(state, num_episodes=10) runs the same evaluation outside training, on a state train returned, and gives the same keys, one value per seed; without eval_envs there is nothing to evaluate on, and it raises. Defaults are the single-task agent's, except batch_size=1024 and task_dim=96, the paper's (T14). The evaluation follows the offline trainer's protocol (T16). Ajax's datasets are generated by its own single-task runs, not the paper's mt30 and mt80 data, so they validate the mechanisms rather than the paper's numbers (T17).

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Recorded on CPU in PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md, with model_size=1 and every other setting at the paper's default, two seeds: Pendulum reaches -143 and -124 after 6,000 steps (a random policy scores about -1,200), and Playground's CartpoleBalance (action repeat 2) reaches 810 and 854 after 10,000 steps, still improving. The GPU validation against the published curves is specified in VALIDATION.md and has not been run yet. The probes (tests/probing) train TD-MPC2 briefly on tiny environments whose answers need its model (a payoff past its planning horizon; twin tasks for the multi-task agent), and its own tests (tests/agents/TDMPC2) check that a run split by a checkpoint equals the run left whole, for both agents. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: Pendulum, 4 environments, 8,000 steps, a smaller model than the paper's) TD-MPC2 ran at 292 steps per second of execution (245 with compilation) at main a8a13c2.

Bases: ActorCritic

TD-MPC2 for continuous control, single task, online.

Paper DMC protocol: action_repeat=2, episode_length=1000 (simulator steps, so T = 500 agent steps, gamma = 0.99, seed_steps = 2500), model_size=5, n_envs=1; n_timesteps counts agent steps, so the paper's "1M env steps" is n_timesteps=500_000 (logs carry env_frames, tdmpc2_spec 4.22).

Static hyperparameters (they fix shapes or trace-time structure): the architecture (model_size preset of {1, 5, 19, 48, 317} M parameters filling the None widths enc_dim, mlp_dim, latent_dim, num_enc_layers, num_q; an explicit width overrides it; tdmpc2_spec 1.20), simnorm_dim, num_bins, vmax (two-hot bins over [-vmax, vmax] in symlog space; the reference's vmin = -vmax, T24), horizon, batch_size, buffer_size, seed_steps and the planner sizes iterations (+2 when the action dimension is >= 20), num_samples, num_elites, num_pi_trajs. Every other hyperparameter is a static Python float as well, except learning_rate, which accepts a float or a schedule Callable[[int], float] (the world model's encoder runs at learning_rate * enc_lr_scale, 5f6fade:tdmpc2/tdmpc2.py:21-28).

Derived from the episode length T in agent steps (:func:ajax.environments.utils.agent_episode_length: brax / playground episode_length // action_repeat, gymnax the env's max_steps_in_episode): gamma=None is clip((T/denom - 1) / (T/denom), discount_min, discount_max) (tdmpc2_spec 2.20, tdmpc2.py:36-49) and seed_steps=None is max(1000, 5 T) (4.3, envs/__init__.py:81).

Replay (:mod:ajax.agents.TDMPC2.buffer, the b67b21c episode buffer): buffer_size env steps, stored in a ring sized at every :meth:train call for the env steps the run has taken when the call ends, min(buffer_size, total) (the reference's clamp to the run length, which saves memory without changing what is replayed; deviation T26). A resumed run -- the same agent continuing, or a new one restoring a checkpoint into its n_timesteps=0 skeleton (ajax.checkpoint) -- moves the carried episodes into the ring of its own call (:meth:~ajax.agents.TDMPC2.buffer.EpisodeBuffer.adopt), so a run trained in chunks replays exactly what the uninterrupted run does. The last call's capacity and bytes are :attr:replay_capacity and :attr:replay_bytes_per_seed (also in :attr:config, hence the run config of the loggers). Memory per seed: R * n_envs * (T + 1) * (obs_dim + A + 1) * 4 bytes with R = ceil(capacity / (T n_envs)) + 1: 124 MB for DMC walker (obs 24, A 6, T 500) at the full 1,000,000-step capacity; the seed vmap multiplies it.

Evaluation (with a logging_config): every log_frequency env steps, num_episode_test episodes of the planner in eval_mode on a rebuilt env with the training action repeat and episode length, each evaluation from fresh initial states (online_trainer.py:27-48; deviation T9). One evaluation makes num_episode_test * T planner decisions (batched over the episodes; on CPU each costs roughly half a training env step, which plans and updates). The paper protocol is log_frequency = 50_000 with num_episode_test = 10 (tdmpc2_spec 4.21); :class:~ajax.logging.wandb_logging.LoggingConfig's default log_frequency of 1000 makes a T = 500 run spend about twice as long evaluating as training.

Continuous actions only. The env must be fixed-length and non-terminating (all DMC tasks): a termination, off the T-step schedule or on its last step, raises ValueError after :meth:train (deviation T10). Observations and rewards are the env's raw values (no normalisation, as in the reference).

episodic=True takes terminating tasks instead (the latest code's episodic mode, nicklashansen/tdmpc2@eece801; deviation T29): a termination head, 1 - terminated in the targets and the planner, the variable-length replay of ceil(min(buffer_size, total) / n_envs) rows per env (total the rows of the run when the call ends, sized and adopted on a resume as the episode ring is), and n_timesteps counting rows (env steps plus one per finished episode). T is then the time limit, still bootstrapped. A run that never updated because every episode terminated within horizon steps raises ValueError after :meth:train.

Extensions: pretrain, post_update (folded after every update, step = env steps) and eval_metrics (with init_state); the other phases are rejected at construction.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default env_id str | EnvType

env id (gymnax, brax or mujoco_playground) or a prebuilt gymnax env.

required n_envs int

lockstep envs; each stepping tick runs n_envs updates (UTD 1 per env step; deviation T7 for > 1).

1 updates_per_step float

updates per env step after the seed-phase burst, max(1, round(n_envs * updates_per_step)) per stepping tick (static); the default 1 is the reference's UTD, which config.yaml does not expose (deviation T28). The burst stays seed_steps updates. Episodic mode: max(1, round(stepped * updates_per_step)) on a tick that stepped stepped > 0 envs.

1.0 episode_length int

simulator steps per episode on brax / playground (ignored on gymnax, which uses its params' max_steps_in_episode).

1000 action_repeat int

simulator steps per agent step (brax / playground; the paper's DMC protocol uses 2).

1 env_params Optional[EnvParams]

gymnax env params (one system).

None weight_decay float

decoupled weight decay of the world model's and the policy's Adam (OptimizerConfig.weight_decay); Ajax's, not a config.yaml hyperparameter: 0 keeps the reference's plain Adam.

0.0 extensions Sequence[Extension]

composable research features (see :mod:ajax.extensions).

()

Every other argument is the hyperparameter of the same name in nicklashansen/tdmpc2@5f6fade:tdmpc2/config.yaml (lr is learning_rate), with its paper default; see the class docstring for the static ones and the derived defaults.

Multi-task TD-MPC2, trained offline on a pooled dataset (paper era).

The reference's multi-task path is offline only (train.py:52; tdmpc2_spec 3.25, 4.1): the updates of the single-task agent, conditioned on each slice's task (:func:ajax.agents.TDMPC2.multitask.update: a learnable task embedding with max-norm 1, zero-padded observations, prefix action masks, per-task discounts), on batches of slices drawn uniformly over the dataset's pooled episodes, no planning during training. n_timesteps counts updates (the reference's iterations; paper: 10M at batch 1024, spec 4.B). The paper protocol is batch_size=1024 (the default here) and task_dim=96 for every model size (deviation T14).

The dataset (:class:~ajax.agents.TDMPC2.dataset.MultiTaskDataset, e.g. :func:~ajax.agents.TDMPC2.dataset.pool_tasks of single-task runs' exports) fixes the tasks: task i has the dataset's obs_dims[i], action_dims[i] and episode length T_i, whose discount is the reference's heuristic of T_i (discount_denom, discount_min, discount_max; spec 2.20). The model sees the padded observation and action spaces; the planner's iteration rule uses the padded action dim (spec 3.1). The dataset is one array set on the device, shared by every seed: the constructor places it there once (whatever built it: host NumPy arrays are transferred then, not at every chunk) and :meth:train passes it to its jitted, seed-vmapped program as an unbatched argument, so the seeds read the same copy (dataset.nbytes) and the program does not embed it.

Logging (with a logging_config): every log_frequency updates, the last update's quantities (Train/..., timestep = updates done), the extensions' eval_metrics and, with eval_envs, an evaluation: a host loop over the tasks runs num_episode_test episodes of each in its own env (eval_envs[i], built with episode_length simulator steps and action_repeat; its dims and agent-step episode length must be task i's), the planner in eval_mode with t0 on each episode's first step: the offline trainer's protocol (offline_trainer.py:22-39; deviation T16: evaluate.py's exploration noise is not reproduced). Logged per task Eval/<name>/episodic mean reward and length, their mean over tasks Eval/episodic mean reward and the normalised score Eval/normalized score, the mean over tasks of return / 10 (the paper's DMC normalisation, meaningful for DMC returns in [0, 1000]; spec 4.20). The first evaluation follows the first log_frequency updates (the reference's follows its first update). Each evaluation starts its episodes from fresh initial states. The embedding renorm of a look-up at evaluation is not persisted (deviation T15).

Static hyperparameters, as :class:~ajax.agents.TDMPC2.TDMPC2.TDMPC2's: the architecture (model_size preset and explicit widths), task_dim, simnorm_dim, num_bins, vmax, horizon, batch_size and the planner sizes. learning_rate accepts a float or a schedule (the task embedding is trained by the world-model optimizer at learning_rate, the encoder at learning_rate * enc_lr_scale).

Extensions: pretrain, post_update (folded after every update, step = updates done) and eval_metrics (with init_state), the phases of the single-task agent; the others are rejected at construction.

PAPER_TASK_DIM episode_length int

Run n_timesteps more updates for every seed (vmapped).

A fresh run initialises the networks (and folds the extensions' init_state and pretrain); initial_state (a state this agent's train returned, or a checkpoint restored into the n_timesteps=0 skeleton) continues a run; its buffers are donated to the first chunk (as ActorCritic.train donates them). docs.title: UDRL
docs.text:
Upside-Down RL turns reinforcement learning into supervised learning. The policy takes a command next to the observation: a return to obtain and a number of steps to obtain it in. It learns, from its own past experience, which action led to which outcome, then is asked for slightly better outcomes than the best it has seen. There is no critic, no value estimate and no discount by default.

Papers: Schmidhuber, Reinforcement Learning Upside Down: Don't Predict Rewards -- Just Map Them to Actions, 2019 (arXiv:1912.02875). Ajax follows its training procedure; the code cites it as Algorithms 3 to 5. The companion paper by Srivastava, Shyam, Mutz, Jaśkowski and Schmidhuber, Training Agents using Upside-Down Reinforcement Learning, 2019 (arXiv:1912.02877), reports the first experiments.

docs.title: Can I use?
docs.text: Feature UDRL Discrete actions yes Continuous actions yes, tanh-bounded, mapped onto the environment's bounds Memory (memory=) no Environments gymnax, Brax, MuJoCo Playground Image observations yes, a CNN encoder (cnn_image_shape) Several seeds in one call yes, train(seed=[...]) Extension phases pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics, actor_loss Resume and checkpoints yes; a split run equals the uninterrupted one (probe and resume contract)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from ajax import UDRL
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = UDRL("CartPole-v1", n_envs=4)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=10_240, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[1, 2], n_timesteps=51_200, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])   # the policy, commanded as below
print(evaluations["Train/episodic mean reward"])  # returns of the episodes collected
print(state.command_target_return)                # the return the agent now asks for

With a logging_config, every log_frequency steps UDRL evaluates its policy on num_episode_test episodes and train returns, next to the evaluation (Eval/episodic mean reward, Eval/episodic entropy, Eval/mean episodic length, and Eval/commanded return and Eval/commanded horizon, the command each episode starts from), the training metrics of those iterations (Train/episodic mean reward, Train/actor_loss, Train/mean_rtg, Train/mean_horizon, Train/n_completed_episodes).

docs.title: Key hyperparameters
docs.text: Argument Default What it does n_envs 1 environments stepped in parallel n_steps 64 length of the segment collected per iteration buffer_capacity 64 segments kept in the replay n_updates_per_iter 64 gradient steps per iteration batch_size 64 samples per gradient step actor_learning_rate 3e-4 Adam step size actor_architecture ("128", "relu", "128", "relu") hidden layers max_grad_norm None gradient clipping by global norm gamma 1.0 discount of the returns-to-go logged as Train/mean_rtg, a diagnostic only: commands, the top-K statistics and the training targets sum rewards undiscounted, as in the paper command_return_init, command_horizon_init 1.0, 100.0 the first command command_topk 32 best episodes the next command is built from command_return_boost 1.0 multiplies the top episodes' mean return command_target_tau 1.0 smoothing of the command (1: replaced every iteration) command_scale_r, command_scale_h 0.02, 0.01 scaling of the command before the network normalize_observations, normalize_rewards, reward_normalization_gamma False, False, None running normalisation cnn_image_shape None convolutional encoder for flat image observations episode_length, action_repeat None, 1 simulator steps per episode (1,000 when None) and per agent step, on Brax and Playground extensions () research features (see Extensions)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each iteration:

  1. collects n_steps steps per environment with the current policy and commands, decreasing each command as reward is received and steps pass;
  2. stores that segment in a first-in first-out replay of buffer_capacity segments;
  3. sets the next command from the command_topk best episodes in the replay: a return between their mean and their mean plus one standard deviation, and their mean length as the horizon;
  4. takes n_updates_per_iter supervised steps, each maximising the log-likelihood of the action taken. Each sample is a state, the action taken there, and as command what actually followed: the reward summed up to a random later step of the same episode, and that number of steps.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Segments, read as episodes. The replay stores fixed-length segments rather than whole episodes, so arrays keep a fixed shape. The sampler and the top-K statistics read episodes whole across segments, so a training command can span any part of an episode the replay holds, not only one segment.
  • Evaluation. Each evaluated episode starts from the current command (state.command_target_return and its horizon), without the random spread that collection adds, and the command decreases as in collection. The policy acts deterministically.
  • Command scaling. The command enters the network multiplied by command_scale_r and command_scale_h (the paper's LunarLander values), so that it is of order one; the replay keeps it unscaled.
  • The policy's encoder ends with a LayerNorm, as Ajax's earlier networks did.
  • The command is carried in the last two entries of the observation; with cnn_image_shape the image is flattened in front of them.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: No learning curves are published for UDRL yet. Unit tests (tests/agents/UDRL and the contracts every agent shares) check its pieces against exact contracts, without learning. The probes (tests/probing) train it briefly on tiny environments with known answers: that it learns from the commands that actually followed and scales its command alike when acting and when training, its extension phases, and a run split by a checkpoint matching the run left whole. On the CPU speed benchmark (benchmarks/agent_bench.py: Pendulum, 4 environments, 8,000 steps) UDRL ran at 12,575 steps per second of execution (4,441 with compilation) at main a8a13c2; its trials spread from 9,604 to 15,069 (PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md).

docs.title: Buffers
docs.text: Off-policy agents store transitions in a flashbax replay buffer. With memory=, they store per-environment trajectories and replay sequences R2D2-style. The world models keep their own replay (DreamerV3, TD-MPC2).

docs.title: ajax.buffers.dataset
docs.text:
Transition datasets: logged or recorded transitions, kept on disk and added to a replay.

A :class:TransitionDataset holds whole episodes as flat rows in time order, each episode contiguous (the replay agents read single transitions; TD-MPC2's offline datasets, :mod:ajax.agents.TDMPC2.dataset, hold [N, L, ...] episodes for its sequence sampler):

================ ========== =============================================== field shape content ================ ========== =============================================== obs [N, O] f32 the env's own observation (not normalised) action [N, A] f32 the action taken, in agent units ([-1, 1]) reward [N] f32 the env's own reward terminated [N] bool a true terminal (no bootstrap) truncated [N] bool a time limit (bootstrap on next_obs) next_obs [N, O] f32 the next observation, the final one at an end is_expert [N] bool whether the expert chose action a_expert [N, A] f32 the expert's action at obs (NaN: unknown) return_to_go [N] f32 sum_k gamma^k r_{t+k} to the episode's end episode [N] i32 the episode's index ================ ========== ===============================================

return_to_go and episode follow from the others. return_to_go is Cal-QL's Monte-Carlo return (Nakamoto et al. 2023), cut at a time limit.

:func:record rolls an expert out, :func:export reads a run's replay, :func:fill_replay adds a dataset to one. :func:save and :func:load follow TD-MPC2's file conventions: an uncompressed .npz of plain arrays and a JSON meta string, no pickle.

docs.title: ajax.agents.recurrent
docs.text:
Shared machinery for recurrent off-policy updates (R2D2-style).

Every off-policy agent with a Q-critic (SAC, ASAC, REDQ, TD3) trains its memory the same way:

  1. Sample contiguous per-env sequences of length burn_in + sequence_length + 1 from a trajectory buffer.
  2. Warm up ("burn in") the actor / online-critic / target-critic carries from zero over the first burn_in steps with the CURRENT params, under stop_gradient — the carries are constants inside the losses.
  3. Train on the next sequence_length steps with BPTT; the final step is not read (each row stores the observation its target bootstraps on, interaction.bootstrap_obs).

sample_and_burnin_sequences implements steps 1-3 once for all agents; the per-agent losses then consume the returned :class:RecurrentCarries through :func:actor_dist and :func:q_values, which run a network on a feedforward batch or, given carries, on a replayed sequence.

A critic's memory reads each row's observation and the action before it, the one taken; the action a loss asks about joins after the memory, at the critic's head, so a taken or a sampled action is a query on the same carry and never feeds it (Critic.query_dim; the recurrent off-policy critic of Ni et al. 2022, cited from memory, unverified).

docs.title: RecurrentCarries
docs.text:
Per-update recurrent context for replayed sequences (R2D2-style).

All carries are burned in from zero on the sequence prefix with the CURRENT params and treated as constants inside the losses (they are stop-gradiented); only the training segment backpropagates through time. The carries hold for the training segment's first row; its rows (obs, the actions taken, resets their episode starts) are the history a bootstrap runs over (:func:_bootstrap_stream).

Kapturowski et al. 2019 show stored state beats zero-init + burn-in at mitigating recurrent-state staleness. docs.title: ajax.compare
docs.text:
Compare agents with AdaStop: train seeds in rounds until the evidence decides.

AdaStop (Mathieu, Della Vecchia, Shilova, Centa de Medeiros, Kohler, Maillard and Preux, "AdaStop: adaptive statistical testing for sound comparisons of Deep RL agents", TMLR 2024, arXiv:2306.10882) is a permutation-based group sequential test with a step-down procedure. At each of up to K interims, every agent still in an undecided comparison adds n runs. A comparison stops once its two score distributions are shown to differ. The chance of declaring any difference where there is none (the family-wise error) stays at most alpha. A comparison still undecided after K interims is "equal": not shown to differ, which does not prove the agents equal.

docs/guide/comparing-agents.md lists the differences from the paper and from the authors' adastop package. :func:difference and :func:resolution say what a verdict leaves open: the gap's size, and the smallest gap the runs could detect.

:func:estimate measures one agent instead: it trains seeds until a confidence sequence pins down each chosen metric.

docs.title: compare
docs.text:
compare(
    agents,
    n_timesteps,
    eval_every,
    score=final_return,
    *,
    baseline=None,
    num_episode_test=10,
    seed=0,
    **adastop,
)

Train and score agents in AdaStop's interims until it decides.

At each interim, every agent still in an undecided comparison trains n new seeds in one train call, evaluated every eval_every steps; score turns the (seeds, evaluations) returns into one score per seed. At most n * K runs per agent; the paper advises n * K >= 30.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default agents Mapping[str, Callable[[], Any]]

a factory per name, building the agent to train.

required n_timesteps int

each run's training budget.

required eval_every int

steps between evaluations.

required score Callable[[ndarray], ndarray]

:func:final_return, :func:last_third, :func:auc or another map from evaluation curves to per-seed scores.

final_return baseline Optional[str]

compare it with each other agent; every pair when None.

None num_episode_test int

episodes per evaluation.

10 seed int

the permutations' seed and the first run seed. Agents train disjoint seeds, so their runs are independent.

0 **adastop Any

:class:AdaStop's n, K, alpha and B.

{}

docs.title: difference
docs.text:
difference(a, b, confidence=0.95, B=10000, seed=0)

mean(a) - mean(b) and its percentile bootstrap interval: B resamples of each sample, with replacement.

docs.title: resolution
docs.text:
resolution(
    a,
    b,
    n,
    K,
    alpha=0.05,
    power=0.8,
    reps=200,
    B=10000,
    seed=0,
)

The smallest gap between two means that AdaStop, run with n, K and alpha, detects with probability power, for scores spread as a and b: what an "equal" can miss.

A simulation, as the power study of the AdaStop paper (Section 5), from the observed spread rather than a known distribution: each of reps replicates draws n * K scores with replacement from each sample, centred on its mean, and adds the gap to b's. The same draws serve every gap, which a bisection narrows to 1/1000 of the samples' spread; samples without spread give 0. Shifting every score says little about a gap made of a few failing runs among scores at a task's maximum.

docs.title: half_width
docs.text:
half_width(width)

A rule for :func:estimate: the interval is at most 2 * width wide.

docs.title: threshold
docs.text:
threshold(value)

A rule for :func:estimate: the interval lies above or below value, so the mean is decided against it.

docs.title: estimate
docs.text:
estimate(
    agent,
    n_timesteps,
    eval_every,
    metrics,
    *,
    delta=0.05,
    n=8,
    max_seeds=64,
    num_episode_test=10,
    seed=0,
)

Train one agent n seeds per train call until every metric's rule holds or max_seeds have trained.

Each metric's mean gets the hedged betting confidence sequence of Waudby-Smith and Ramdas ("Estimating means of bounded random variables by betting", JRSS-B, Section 4.4): adastop's Bounded_Confseq, from the compare extra. It holds at every seed count at once, so stopping on what the scores show keeps its level. The metrics split delta evenly (a union bound), so all intervals hold together with probability at least 1 - delta. n_timesteps, eval_every and num_episode_test are as in :func:compare.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default agent Callable[[], Any]

builds the agent to train.

required metrics Mapping[str, tuple[Callable, tuple[float, float], Callable]]

per name, (score, (low, high), rule). score maps train's evaluations, each (seeds, evaluations), to one value per seed, which low and high must bound for every possible run, not only those seen. rule is :func:half_width, :func:threshold or another test of (lower, upper).

required delta float

the chance that any interval misses its mean.

0.05 seed int

the first run seed; the runs are seed, seed + 1, ....

0

docs.title: Environments and wrappers
docs.text: Agents take a gymnax, Brax or MuJoCo Playground environment, or its id, and wrap it themselves. Every continuous agent acts in [-1, 1], and agent_action_to_env maps its action onto the environment's bounds; an expert speaks the environment's units, and the agent reads it through ExpertInAgentUnits. See Environments and Differentiable simulation.

docs.title: register_brax_builder
docs.text:
register_brax_builder(env_id, builder)

Register a custom brax env builder for env_id.

Mirrors register_playground_builder for brax-stack envs. The builder takes (n_envs, episode_length) and must return a fully wrapped env whose _ajax_env_id attribute equals env_id. Subsequent calls to _build_brax_env(env_id, ...) delegate to this builder. Used when a safety-experiments-style env wraps a stock brax robot with custom termination/observation-augmentation that must survive eval's rebuild. To support action_repeat > 1 the builder must also accept an action_repeat keyword (passed only when > 1).

docs.title: register_playground_builder
docs.text:

Register a custom playground env builder for env_id.

The builder takes (n_envs, episode_length) and must return a fully wrapped env whose _ajax_env_id attribute equals env_id. Subsequent calls to _build_playground_env(env_id, ...) delegate to this builder. To support action_repeat > 1 the builder must also accept an action_repeat keyword (passed only when > 1).

docs.title: build_env_from_id
docs.text:
build_env_from_id(
    env_id,
    n_envs=1,
    fresh_reset=True,
    *,
    episode_length=1000,
    action_repeat=1,
    differentiable_reset=False,
)

Build a wrapped env from its id (gymnax, mujoco_playground or brax).

fresh_reset only concerns mujoco_playground envs (see _build_playground_env); gymnax and Ajax's brax stack already draw a new initial state for every episode.

action_repeat (default 1) repeats each agent action for that many simulator steps on brax / playground envs (see :func:_build_playground_env); episode_length (a keyword, default 1000) then counts simulator steps. gymnax envs do not support it.

differentiable_reset concerns the auto-resets that compute a fresh reset inside step: brax envs, and playground envs with fresh_reset=True (the default). With differentiable_reset=False (the default) they evaluate the reset only on steps where some env is done, inside a lax.while_loop, because the reset can cost as much as many env steps. Gradients through such an env still flow with respect to the actions, the policy parameters and the env state, and forward mode (jax.jvp) works with respect to anything. Only reverse mode through the reset itself -- jax.grad with respect to something the reset depends on, such as physics parameters of the env -- fails, loudly, at trace time: "Reverse-mode differentiation does not work for lax.while_loop". Pass differentiable_reset=True for that case: the reset is then evaluated on every step and kept only for done envs, which reverse mode can cross, at the cost of a reset per step. Transitions are the same either way, up to float rounding. Gymnax envs (whose auto-reset is always computed) and playground's cached auto-reset ignore the flag, and evaluation (evaluate.setup_environment), which never differentiates, rebuilds the env with the default.

docs.title: AutoResetWrapper
docs.text:
AutoResetWrapper(env, differentiable_reset=False)

Bases: BraxWrapper

Automatically resets Brax envs that are done, sampling a new random seed for initialization at each reset. This seed is propagated through info["rng"]

By default the reset is evaluated only on steps where some env is done, inside a lax.while_loop (see :func:_call_if_any), and skipped on the others. Rollouts stay differentiable with respect to the actions, the policy parameters and the env state, none of which the reset depends on, and forward mode (jax.jvp) works with respect to anything. What reverse mode cannot do is differentiate through the reset itself, with respect to something it depends on (e.g. physics parameters of the env): jax.grad then raises "Reverse-mode differentiation does not work for lax.while_loop" at trace time. differentiable_reset=True evaluates the reset on every step instead and keeps the result only for done envs, which reverse mode can cross, at the cost of a reset per step.

docs.title: BatchRngWrapper
docs.text:
BatchRngWrapper(env, n_envs)

Bases: BraxWrapper

Splits an unbatched PRNG key into n_envs keys on reset.

Playground's BraxAutoResetWrapper.reset (and FreshAutoResetWrapper.reset) assumes rng is already shape (n_envs, 2) so it can jax.vmap(jax.random.split)(rng). Ajax callers pass a single unbatched key, so this adapter bridges the two conventions.

docs.title: FinalObsWrapper
docs.text:
FinalObsWrapper(env)

Bases: BraxWrapper

Stashes state.obs in state.info['final_obs'] on every reset/step.

Place this directly below an auto-reset wrapper in the stack. The auto-reset wrapper overwrites state.obs with the reset observation on done, so without this the pre-reset observation is lost — breaking correct value bootstrapping on truncation (PPO/SAC need V(s_T) at truncation, not V(s_reset)). With this wrapper, downstream code can read state.info['final_obs'] to recover the terminal observation.

Backend-agnostic: duck-typed passthrough that works for both brax State and mujoco_playground State (both expose .obs and .info).

docs.title: FreshAutoResetWrapper
docs.text:
FreshAutoResetWrapper(env, differentiable_reset=False)

Bases: BraxWrapper

Auto-resets a batched mujoco_playground env to a fresh initial state.

Drop-in replacement for playground's BraxAutoResetWrapper in Ajax's playground stack (EpisodeWrapper, VmapWrapper, FinalObsWrapper, this, BatchRngWrapper; see ajax.environments.create). With its default full_reset=False, upstream caches each env's first reset and restarts every later episode from it, so a whole run sees only n_envs initial conditions, whereas dm_control draws a new one per episode. Upstream's full_reset=True does draw new ones, but it (a) evaluates a full reset on every step (on CheetahRun, whose reset runs a 200-step stabilisation, ~180x the cost of a step) and (b) replaces the whole info of done envs with the reset's, which zeroes truncation, episode_done and episode_metrics and overwrites final_obs with the reset observation, breaking the V(s_T) bootstrap at truncation.

On a step where some env is done, this wrapper draws a fresh batched reset (computed only on such steps, see :func:_call_if_any) and gives each done env, from it:

  • data and obs;
  • the info entries produced by the base environment's own reset, i.e. its per-episode state (its rng, task targets, ...).

Everything else describes the transition just taken and passes through: reward, done, metrics, and the bookkeeping that the wrappers below write into info on every step (EpisodeWrapper's steps, truncation and episode_*; FinalObsWrapper's final_obs).

differentiable_reset=True evaluates the reset on every step instead, for reverse-mode gradients through the reset itself; see :class:AutoResetWrapper.

docs.title: TerminatedTruncatedWrapper
docs.text:
TerminatedTruncatedWrapper(env)

Bases: GymnaxWrapper

Split a time-limit-inclusive terminal flag back into terminated/truncated.

Stock gymnax >= 1.0 environments already return the two flags apart, so they do not need this wrapper. It is for third-party environments that subclass gymnax's Environment but whose step_env still reports the pre-1.0 done = terminated | truncated, which gymnax's base step hands back in the terminated slot. Left unwrapped, such an env makes every time-limit truncation look like a natural termination, so PPO/SAC drop the V(s_T) bootstrap and silently underestimate the value of long-running states.

The time limit is the truncated flag gymnax's base step reports: it is computed from the pre-reset state, whereas the returned state has already been auto-reset (time == 0) at the limit.

ObservationNoiseWrapper(env, sigma, scale=1.0)

Bases: GymnaxWrapper

Sensor noise on a gymnax env's observations, obs + sigma * scale * N(0, I), drawn afresh at every reset and step from a key folded off the call's own (the env's own draws are unchanged).

The pre-reset observation an episode end leaves in the info gets the step's draw, so a transition's next observation is the one the agent then sees. scale is a scalar or one value per dimension (e.g. the observations' standard deviations). get_obs stays the state's noiseless observation, which an expert reads (interaction.get_raw_obs).
