docs.title: Other end-to-end JAX libraries
docs.text:
These also compile the environment and the training loop into one JAX program, as their repositories read on 17 October 2026:

  • Brax's training agents: PPO, SAC, APG, ARS, ES and behaviour cloning, which can run DAgger online from a teacher policy. They train across devices and hosts. Ajax's APG adds recurrent memory and Busetto et al.'s contextual controller.
  • Stoix: about 25 algorithms, among them R2D2, MPO and MuZero. Its Anakin architecture runs end to end with a JAX environment, and Sebulba trains on environments not written in JAX. It trains across devices.
  • Rejax: PPO, SAC, DQN and its variants, PQN, IQN and TD3. The whole run is jitted, and it can be vmapped over seeds and over hyperparameters (README).

CleanRL's QDagger also learns from a teacher policy, for DQN.

docs.title: When to use something else
docs.text:
• Your environment is not written in JAX. A Gymnasium environment that steps in Python, an external simulator or a real system cannot run inside Ajax's compiled program (Environments). SB3 and SBX take environments with the Gymnasium interface, and SB3 ships a checker for it (custom envs, README). For such environments at scale, Stoix has its Sebulba architecture (Stoix).
  • You train on several devices. Ajax runs on one device for now; it has no pmap or sharding. Brax's training agents and Stoix train across devices (Brax, Stoix).
  • You want a hyperparameter sweep in one program. Ajax compiles the hyperparameters into the program, so each trial of a sweep compiles anew (Performance). Rejax vmaps over hyperparameters as well as seeds (README).
  • You want a mature, stable library. SB3 describes itself as stable, with development focused on bug fixes and maintenance, and lists documentation, high code coverage and type hints among its features (README). It installs with pip, and the RL Baselines3 Zoo adds tuned hyperparameters, pre-trained agents and training scripts (README). Ajax installs from source (Installation).
  • Your observations are dictionaries. SB3 supports single-level Dict observation spaces (algorithms); Ajax's networks read one flat vector, and it flattens image observations into one (Networks).
  • You want SB3's interface with JAX networks. SBX shares SB3's API and works with the RL Zoo (README). It calls itself a proof of concept (README).
  • You want to read or change one algorithm in one file. PureJaxRL's implementations are single files, not a library meant to be imported (README). Its README reports its own speed comparisons with PyTorch implementations, including on a GPU; Ajax has not measured a GPU speed-up.
  • You need an algorithm Ajax does not have, such as A2C, TRPO, TQC, CrossQ or invalid-action masking: SB3, sb3-contrib or SBX have them (algorithms, contrib, README).

docs.title: Checkpoints and resuming
docs.text: A run can stop and continue: in the same process by passing its state back to train, or in another process through a checkpoint file. Either way the continued run is the run that never stopped. The tests check it state by state for every agent (below).

docs.title: In the same process
docs.text:
train returns the whole agent state. Passing it back as initial_state continues the run from its timestep:

from ajax import SAC

agent = SAC("Pendulum-v1", learning_starts=500)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=1_000)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=1_000, initial_state=state)
print(state.collector_state.timestep)  # [2000 2000]

Pass the same seeds in every call. The call may reuse the memory of the state you pass in, so read or save what you need from it first.

docs.title: Across processes
docs.text:
ajax.checkpoint has three functions:

Function What it does save_checkpoint(state, path) writes the state's arrays and counters to path, atomically (a crash mid-write leaves the previous file intact) restore_into(skeleton, path) loads path into skeleton, a fresh state of the same agent checkpoint_exists(path) whether path holds a checkpoint

A checkpoint stores data only. The optimisers' update rules and the networks' functions are code, not data: they come from the skeleton, which an identically configured agent builds with a 0-step train call given the run's train options (an update rule may depend on them, as APG's learning-rate schedule does, below). The agent may be a new instance in a new process. A run that saves a checkpoint after each chunk of training, and picks up from the last one when restarted:

import os
import tempfile

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.checkpoint import checkpoint_exists, restore_into, save_checkpoint

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "sac_pendulum.pkl")
seeds, chunk, total = [0, 1], 1_000, 2_000

agent = SAC("Pendulum-v1", learning_starts=500)
# The skeleton: init only, with the run's options.
state, _ = agent.train(seed=seeds, n_timesteps=0, total_timesteps=total)
if checkpoint_exists(path):
    state = restore_into(state, path)

while (done := int(state.collector_state.timestep[0])) < total:
    state, _ = agent.train(
        seed=seeds,
        n_timesteps=min(chunk, total - done),
        initial_state=state,
        total_timesteps=total,  # the schedules run over the whole run
    )
    save_checkpoint(state, path)
print(state.collector_state.timestep)  # [2000 2000]

The file is a pickle. Load only checkpoints you trust, since unpickling can run code.

docs.title: What a resume keeps
docs.text:
Everything in the state: the network parameters, the optimisers' moments and step counts, the replay buffer, each environment copy where it stood (in the middle of an episode, if it was), the observation and reward statistics, the memory carries, a stateful expert's state, the random keys, the extensions' states, and the counters. Because the counters come back, the evaluations continue on their cadence, each from the key of its own count: a run split in two logs and evaluates at the same steps, on the same episodes, as the run left whole.

Schedules continue rather than restart. Each call trains from the timestep it was given to that timestep plus n_timesteps, and measures the training fraction, the exploration, the extensions' schedules and the logging against the horizon total_timesteps. Pass the whole run's horizon to every call, as the loop above does, and a split run follows the schedules of one call; without it, each call's horizon is its own end.

docs.title: What the tests guarantee
docs.text:
The resume tests train a run in one call and again in two. Between the two calls they save the state, check that it restores leaf for leaf into a new agent's skeleton, and continue from the restored state on that new agent; then they compare the two end states:

Agents Check SAC, ASAC, REDQ, TD3, AVG, APO, PPO, DQN, PQN, UDRL every array of the final state equal, to a relative 1e-5, with every normalisation the agent takes switched on and every call told the run's horizon (DQN's and PQN's epsilon decays across the split); once more with a GRU memory for SAC, ASAC, REDQ, TD3 and PPO APG the same, with and without memory; with memory, the optimiser kept and a warm-up cosine learning rate DreamerV3, TDMPC2, TDMPC2MultiTask the same, in their own test files

The tolerance is there because two programs compiled apart may round differently. A test fails if an agent is added without a row, or one that takes normalisation or memory without the rows for them. Logging is checked too: for SAC, DQN, PPO and PQN, the two halves log and evaluate at exactly the steps the whole run does.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• The seeds must stand at the same timestep. A state whose seeds disagree on the timestep cannot be resumed and raises an error.
  • On-policy agents add a rollout per call. PPO, APO and PQN train in whole rollouts plus one, so each call ends up to a rollout past its budget. A run split into calls ends where one call does when its last call trains the rest, total_timesteps minus the timestep reached (Continuing a run); otherwise it may end elsewhere.
  • APG restarts its optimiser on a resume by default, which its staged curriculum relies on: its learning-rate schedule then spans each call. Pass reset_optimizer_on_resume=False to train to keep it. The kept optimiser runs the schedule it was built with, by the run's first call or the skeleton: give that call reset_optimizer_on_resume=False and the run's total_timesteps too, and the schedule spans the run.
  • Checkpoints follow the code. A checkpoint restores into the state layout of the Ajax version that loads it. When a layout changes, Ajax keeps a conversion for older checkpoints for a while, then removes it. Today these restore:
    • a replay buffer saved before it stored each row's next observation (next_obs, or the environment's own raw_next_obs): the field is rebuilt from the following row, which is what that replay read then;
    • a replay buffer saved with the raw observations and expert flags in a run without an expert, from before the buffer kept them only for an expert: it keeps them, and the resumed run keeps writing them;
    • a state saved before a field that the new layout leaves empty existed: the field is restored empty. A missing field that holds data is a mismatch and still raises;
    • a Brax environment state saved before the observation normaliser kept the raw observation: it is rebuilt from the saved observation and statistics;
    • UDRL's segment buffer saved with cum_rewards, a running sum of its rewards that nothing read: the field is dropped. A saved field that the new layout lacks and does not list as removed is a mismatch and still raises;
    • a UDRL segment buffer saved with a second copy of the environment's own observations (raw_obs, kept for a run with an expert on 2026-10-17): the copy is dropped, since obs holds them. A UDRL buffer of observations the environment normalised is refused: UDRL now keeps them raw. Until 2026-11-17;
    • a PPO's or an APO's optimiser state saved when that optimiser clipped its network's gradient (max_grad_norm), as PPO's two did before PPO took ppo2's one clip over both networks, and APO's two before APO took its official code's, into an optimiser without the clip: the clip holds no data, so the moments and step counts are kept. Another agent's is refused.

docs.title: Comparing agents
docs.text:
Is one agent better than another, and how many seeds does it take to say so? ajax.compare answers with AdaStop (Mathieu et al., "AdaStop: adaptive statistical testing for sound comparisons of Deep RL agents", TMLR 2024, arXiv:2306.10882). It trains a few seeds of each agent, tests, and trains more only while the answer is unclear.

import ajax
from ajax.compare import compare, last_third

result = compare(
    {"SAC": lambda: ajax.SAC("Pendulum-v1"), "TD3": lambda: ajax.TD3("Pendulum-v1")},
    n_timesteps=20_000,
    eval_every=1_000,
    score=last_third,
)
result.decisions  # {("SAC", "TD3"): "equal"}, say
result.seeds  # the seeds each agent trained
result.plot()  # each agent's scores, the decisions as the title

At each of up to K interims, every agent still in an undecided comparison trains n new seeds in one train call, so all of them run in one compiled program. Every pair of agents is compared, or with baseline="SAC" only SAC against each other agent. AdaStop itself takes scores from anywhere, one interim at a time, for runs recorded elsewhere.

docs.title: What it decides
docs.text:
• "larger" or "smaller": the two agents' scores do not come from the same distribution, and the first agent's mean is larger (or smaller).
  • "equal": no difference was shown after n * K runs each. This does not show that the agents are equal: a small difference can need more runs than that.

The chance of reporting any difference between agents that do not differ (the family-wise error) is at most alpha, whatever the number of comparisons. That holds exactly for two agents. With three or more it rests on the paper's shared permutations, which are an approximation there: over 20,000 simulated comparisons of equal agents at alpha = 0.05, two agents gave 0.044 and three or four gave 0.054 to 0.056.

docs.title: What a verdict leaves open
docs.text:
Two numbers say how much a verdict tells, and belong next to it:

from ajax.compare import difference, resolution

a, b = result.scores["SAC"], result.scores["TD3"]
gap, (low, high) = difference(a, b)  # mean(a) - mean(b), 95% bootstrap interval
smallest = resolution(a, b, n=5, K=5)  # the gap detected 80% of the time

difference estimates the gap between the means. resolution is the smallest gap that AdaStop, with the same n, K and alpha, detects with probability power (0.8 by default) for scores spread like these. It simulates, as the paper's power study does, but resamples the observed scores instead of assuming a distribution. An "equal" rules out gaps much larger than the resolution; it says nothing about smaller ones. On normal scores with 32 runs each (n = 8, K = 4) the resolution is about 0.75 standard deviations.

docs.title: The score
docs.text:
The test compares one number per run, and the choice of that number changes the question:

  • final_return: the last evaluation, or how the run ends.
  • last_third: the mean over the last third of the evaluations, or how steadily it stays there.
  • auc: the mean over all evaluations, or how fast it learns.

They can disagree on the same runs. Choose the score before seeing the results: picking it afterwards voids the error guarantee.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
At most n * K runs per agent: 25 with the defaults n = K = 5. A comparison stops early only on a clear difference; agents that differ little, or not at all, use every run. The paper advises n * K >= 30 for the means to be well estimated. Very few runs cannot reject anything: with n = 2 and K = 2 no outcome is extreme enough at alpha = 0.05. The test itself takes milliseconds; the training is the cost.

The reference comparison reports an AdaStop verdict on its recorded runs.

docs.title: Differences from the paper and the authors' package
docs.text:
The authors' adastop package (0.1.3) compares the observed difference with quantiles of the signed permuted differences, which about doubles the error rate (0.097 at alpha = 0.05 over 1,000 simulations of equal agents). It can also reject on rounding alone, when every permutation gives the same statistic. ajax.compare follows the paper instead, with these choices:

  • Absolute values on both sides of the test, as in the paper's Eqs. 8-9.
  • Statistics equal up to rounding tie.
  • Level that ties leave unspent at an interim carries to the next, as in the authors' package.
  • Permutations are always Monte Carlo (B draws, the identity first); the paper enumerates them when there are fewer than B.
  • No early acceptance (the paper's Appendix F, which gives no error bound for it), as in the package's default.
  • Every agent adds the same n runs per interim, as in the paper.

docs.title: One agent: how sure is a number?
docs.text:
With nothing to compare, the question is how well one agent does: its success rate, say. estimate trains n seeds per train call until each chosen metric is known well enough, or max_seeds have trained:

from ajax.compare import estimate, final_return, half_width, threshold


def final(evals):  # evals: train's evaluations, each (seeds, evaluations)
    return final_return(evals["Eval/episodic mean reward"])


result = estimate(
    lambda: ajax.PPO("CartPole-v1"),
    n_timesteps=100_000,
    eval_every=10_000,
    metrics={  # name: (per-seed score, its true bounds, when to stop)
        "solved": (lambda evals: final(evals) >= 475, (0, 1), threshold(0.8)),
        "final return": (final, (0, 500), half_width(25)),
    },
    n=16,
    max_seeds=128,
)
result.interval  # {"solved": (0.83, 1.0), "final return": (452.1, 500.0)}, say
result.mean, result.met, result.seeds, result.scores

threshold(t) stops once the interval lies above or below t, deciding whether the mean is above t; half_width(w) once it is at most 2 * w wide. The intervals are the hedged betting confidence sequence of Waudby-Smith and Ramdas ("Estimating means of bounded random variables by betting", JRSS-B, Section 4.4), the authors' Bounded_Confseq from the adastop package: install the compare extra (uv sync --extra compare, or depend on ajax-rl[compare]). It comes from adastop's main branch until a release includes it.

  • Valid at every seed count at once: with probability at least 1 - delta the interval holds the true mean after every round, not only after a number of seeds fixed in advance, so stopping once the scores look good enough keeps the guarantee.
  • All metrics together: delta is split evenly between them (a union bound), so each extra metric widens every interval a little.
  • Only within true bounds: (low, high) must bound every score a run could get, not only those seen: (0, 500) for CartPole's return, about (-3254, 0) for Pendulum's. A score outside them is refused.
  • mean is the sample mean; the interval need not be centred on it.

The cost is many seeds. A metric that is 1 on every seed has a 95% lower bound of 0.63 after 16 seeds and 0.92 after 64. On the reference comparison's recorded runs, 16 seeds left PPO on CartPole a success rate (final return of at least 475) of 0.88 within [0.45, 1] and a final return of 468 within [275, 500], and SAC on Pendulum a final return of -146 within [-1359, 0]. So decide against a threshold rather than aim for a width; prefer metrics whose bounds are close to what runs reach, such as success rates or KPI fractions, to returns; and train many seeds per round, which share one compiled program.

docs.title: Differentiable simulation
docs.text:
Reinforcement learning usually treats the environment as a black box: the agent sees rewards, never how they depend on its actions, and estimates that dependence from many trials. When the simulator is written in JAX, the dependence can be computed exactly instead. Run the controller in closed loop, sum the rewards, and jax.grad gives the gradient of that sum with respect to the controller's parameters, back through every step of the physics.

This is the analytic policy gradient. It works well when the dynamics are smooth and the horizon is short to moderate: there is no critic to learn and no noise to average out, so each update is precise. It works poorly through contacts and other discontinuities, and over long horizons, where gradients can explode or vanish.

Ajax supports it at three levels: environments whose transitions keep their gradients, families of systems and tracking tasks to train on, and the APG agent, which includes the in-context controller of Busetto et al., 2024.

docs.title: Differentiable environments
docs.text:
Ajax's collectors cut gradients at every environment step, as reinforcement learning expects. gymnax (from version 1.0) also detaches its transitions by default; a few environments let you switch that back on. with_transition_gradients(env) does so, through any Ajax wrappers around the environment, and raises for an environment that cannot, instead of silently returning zero gradients. Today these are Pendulum, MountainCarContinuous, PointRobot, Reacher and Swimmer.

closed_loop_rollout runs a policy against such an environment for a fixed number of steps with no gradient cut anywhere. The policy is any function (carry, obs, resets) -> (action, carry), where carry is its memory (None for a memoryless one) and resets marks episode starts. Here, plain gradient ascent tunes the two gains of a PD controller over a family of pendulums:

import gymnax
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from ajax.environments.differentiable import closed_loop_rollout, with_transition_gradients
from ajax.environments.system_class import UniformPerturbation

env, params = gymnax.make("Pendulum-v1")
env = with_transition_gradients(env)
systems = UniformPerturbation(params, fields=("m", "l"), scale=0.2)  # mass, length +-20 %


def mean_return(gains, key):
    def pd(carry, obs, resets):
        theta = jnp.arctan2(obs[:, 1], obs[:, 0])
        torque = -(gains[0] * theta + gains[1] * obs[:, 2])
        return jnp.clip(torque, -2.0, 2.0)[:, None], carry

    system_key, rollout_key = jax.random.split(key)
    batch = systems.sample(system_key, 16)  # 16 pendulums, one per parallel env
    rollout, _ = closed_loop_rollout(pd, None, rollout_key, env, batch, horizon=50)
    return rollout.reward.sum(axis=0).mean()  # rollout leaves are (horizon, envs, ...)


gains = jnp.array([1.0, 0.1])
step = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(mean_return))
for i in range(20):
    value, grad = step(gains, jax.random.PRNGKey(i))
    gains = gains + 1e-3 * grad  # ascend the return
print(value, gains)

closed_loop_rollout hands the policy's actions to the environment as they are, so the policy above returns torques in the environment's units; APG maps its controller's [-1, 1] actions onto the bounds itself (below).

This path is gymnax only: Brax and MuJoCo Playground environments take no per-step parameters and have their own gradient machinery. For those, differentiable_reset=True in build_env_from_id lets gradients flow through the automatic reset as well (see Environments).

docs.title: Families of systems
docs.text:
A controller tuned for one plant may fail on its neighbours. A system class is a distribution over an environment's physical parameters, so training can cover a whole family:

  • UniformPerturbation(nominal, fields, scale) draws each listed parameter as p · (1 + U(−scale, scale)), independently, leaving the others nominal; a vector or matrix field is scaled by one factor per system. Busetto et al. build their meta-dataset this way, with scale=0.05. A misspelt field raises when the class is built.
  • FixedSystem(nominal) always returns the nominal system; it is the first stage of a curriculum.
  • Subclass SystemClass and implement sample(rng, n) for anything else.

sample(rng, n) returns parameters with a leading axis of n, one system per parallel environment. Ajax's gymnax reset and step notice that axis and simulate each environment with its own system. APG trains on such parameters (its system_class, or a sample passed as env_params), and DreamerV3 and TDMPC2 take a sample as env_params. The other agents compile env_params into their collection step as a constant, so they take one system for every copy and refuse a sample when built.

docs.title: Tracking tasks: model-reference control
docs.text:
In model-reference control, the controller makes a plant's measured output y follow the output of a reference model driven by a reference signal r: say, a first-order lag towards each new setpoint. Three pieces turn any gymnax environment into such a task:

  • StepReference(horizon, min_value, max_value, min_duration, max_duration) draws piecewise-constant references: steps of random height held for a random number of steps.
  • LinearReferenceModel is the reference model, x' = A x + B r, y_d = C x + D r. LinearReferenceModel.first_order() defaults to the paper's model.
  • ModelReferenceWrapper(env, reference, model, output_fn=...) is the task as the controller sees it: the observation is the tracking error and the previous action, [e, u_prev] (optionally followed by the plant's own observation), and the reward is −‖y_d − y‖². The undiscounted return is minus the matching cost, and sqrt(−return / horizon) is the paper's M-RMSE. The error is computed from the observation the plant returns, so sensor noise on the plant (an ObservationNoiseWrapper under the task) reaches the controller and the reward alike. On the step a plant episode ends, the reward scores the plant's last output before its reset, and the final observation a time limit bootstraps on is in the controller's view too, so any agent can train on the task.

All three are plain jnp, so the task stays differentiable when the plant is. ajax.wrappers.InitialStateWrapper(env, fn) sets each episode's initial state, for tasks that fix it, as the paper does.

docs.title: Training a controller with APG
docs.text:
APG puts these together. Each update samples n_envs systems from the system class, runs the controller on them for horizon steps, and takes one optimiser step on minus the mean return. One update consumes n_envs · horizon of n_timesteps. The controller is deterministic and its actions are bounded with tanh (squash=True), then mapped onto the environment's bounds, as every agent's are (Actions); an unsquashed controller is clipped to [-1, 1] first. The map is differentiable, so gradients flow through it.

A controller made of a small MLP and a learnable PID output layer, trained to track step references across pendulums whose mass and length vary by 30 %:

import gymnax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from ajax import APG
from ajax.agents.APG import PIDHeadConfig
from ajax.environments.model_reference import (
    LinearReferenceModel,
    ModelReferenceWrapper,
    StepReference,
)
from ajax.environments.system_class import UniformPerturbation
from ajax.wrappers import InitialStateWrapper

plant, params = gymnax.make("Pendulum-v1")
params = params.replace(g=0.0)  # no gravity: a pure inertia to steer


def at_rest(key, state, params):  # every episode starts at angle 0, at rest
    return state.replace(theta=jnp.asarray(0.0), theta_dot=jnp.asarray(0.0))


task = ModelReferenceWrapper(
    InitialStateWrapper(plant, at_rest),
    StepReference(horizon=100, min_value=-0.5, max_value=0.5, min_duration=20, max_duration=50),
    LinearReferenceModel.first_order(a=0.9, b=0.1, c=1.0, d=0.0),
    output_fn=lambda obs: jnp.arctan2(obs[1], obs[0]),  # the measured output: the angle
)
systems = UniformPerturbation(params, fields=("m", "l"), scale=0.3)

agent = APG(
    task,
    system_class=systems,
    n_envs=8,
    horizon=100,
    actor_architecture=("64", "relu"),
    pid=PIDHeadConfig(),  # close the controller with a learnable PID layer
)
state, aux = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=8 * 100 * 200)  # 200 updates
print(aux.m_rmse[0, 0], aux.m_rmse[0, -1])  # (seeds, updates): falls from about 1.7 to 0.45

train always returns every update's loss, matching_loss, m_rmse, grad_norm and timestep, with a seed axis first. With a logging_config, it also evaluates on freshly drawn systems every log_frequency steps. The APG page lists every hyperparameter.

Two defaults depart from a plain implementation, both for stability on this test bed: gradients are clipped to a global norm of 1 (max_grad_norm; without it, training across a system class diverged), and actions are tanh-bounded.

docs.title: The in-context controller
docs.text:
Busetto, Breschi, Forgione, Piga and Formentin, One controller to rule them all, 2024 (arXiv:2411.06482), train one controller for a whole class of systems. It never learns which system it faces explicitly; it infers it from the history of tracking errors and inputs it has seen in the current episode, as a transformer reads its context. APG.contextual_controller(task, system_class) builds that configuration:

  • a decoder-only transformer over the episode's history (8 layers, 4 heads, width 128, context 100), with a linear input embedding (actor_architecture=()), closed by a PID output layer;
  • one system per update (n_envs=1) and a horizon of 100;
  • Adam with betas (0.9, 0.95) (AdamW once weight_decay is above its default of 0), a 5,000-update linear warm-up, then cosine decay to a tenth of the learning rate.

Ajax departs from the reference code in three places, each backed by runs on the pendulum tracking test bed: actions are tanh-bounded, gradients are clipped, and the PID layer starts as the identity (gains 1, 0, 0) rather than all ones. Those runs predate the map of actions onto the environment's bounds, when the pendulum's torque was capped at 1 of its 2. A fourth difference is not backed by runs: the transformer's LayerNorms keep a bias and an epsilon of 1e-6, where the reference's have no bias and 1e-5 (buswayne/in-context-controller at 7eb094ce17: transformer_onestep.py:33 and :156, train_onestep_lin_CL.py:103).

The paper trains in stages of growing diversity (its Algorithm 2): one system first, then the class. train_curriculum chains CurriculumStage(agent, n_timesteps) objects through Ajax's resume path, carrying the parameters over and, by default, restarting the optimiser and its schedule at each stage (reset_optimizer=True). The stages must share n_envs, the network and the output head; each may have its own task and system class. The paper trains each stage to a loss tolerance; Ajax gives each a fixed budget.

# doc: skip (compiles an 8-layer transformer and trains 700,000 steps)
import gymnax
from ajax import APG
from ajax.agents.APG import CurriculumStage, train_curriculum
from ajax.environments.system_class import FixedSystem, UniformPerturbation

# `task` as in the APG example above
_, params = gymnax.make("Pendulum-v1")
systems = UniformPerturbation(params, fields=("m", "l"), scale=0.05)
stages = [
    CurriculumStage(APG.contextual_controller(task, FixedSystem(params)), n_timesteps=200_000),
    CurriculumStage(APG.contextual_controller(task, systems), n_timesteps=500_000),
]
results = train_curriculum(stages, seed=0)  # one (state, aux) per stage

docs.title: The PID output layer
docs.text:
PIDOutputHead closes a network with a learnable PID. The network emits a signal z_k, and the layer applies

u_k = K_P z_k + K_I Σ_{j≤k} z_j + K_D (z_k − z_{k−1})

with learnable gains, one triple per action dimension. The integral term helps remove steady-state error on step references, and Busetto et al. report faster training with it. Like a memory block, the layer carries a state (the running sum and the previous signal), reset at episode starts.

PIDHeadConfig sets it up for APG: use_p, use_i, use_d switch each term on (a disabled term has no parameter); kp_init=1, ki_init=0, kd_init=0 start it as the identity; anti_windup stops the integral from growing while the output is beyond that magnitude in the same direction (about 3 suits a tanh bound, where tanh is within 0.5 % of its limit).

Ajax has two PID components, which do different jobs:

PID output layer (pid=PIDHeadConfig()) PID policy (Networks) Acts on the network's own output signal the tracking-error terms in the observation Role the last layer of a larger controller the whole actor Agents APG SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, PPO, APO Deploys as the network plus the layer a plain PID with the learned gains

docs.title: Your own controller
docs.text:
APG(controller_factory=...) trains any Flax module you build, given the agent's context (env_args, network_args, action_dim, pid, squash). The module must follow the Controller contract in ajax/agents/APG/networks.py: a static stateful attribute, initialize_carry(rng, batch_size) when stateful, and a call that returns a deterministic distrax distribution (plus the new carry when stateful). This lets downstream projects train their own architectures with the same trainer.

APG also takes extensions in the actor_loss phase, whose dictionary holds the rollout, the controller's actor_params and the per-system returns, plus the phases every agent runs (pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics). See Extensions.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• APG: hyperparameters, notes and results.
  • Environments: building environments and wrappers.
  • ajax/environments/differentiable.py, system_class.py and model_reference.py: the source, with the paper's equations in the docstrings.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text: Ajax trains on JAX environments: gymnax, Brax and MuJoCo Playground, or any environment with gymnax's interface, such as TargetGym. The environment runs inside the same compiled program as the agent, so it must be written in JAX: a Gymnasium environment that steps in Python cannot be used.

docs.title: Environments by name
docs.text:
Pass an id as the agent's first argument. Ajax looks it up in this order and uses the first match:

  1. gymnax: "Pendulum-v1", "CartPole-v1", "MountainCarContinuous-v0", ...
  2. MuJoCo Playground: "CheetahRun", "CartpoleBalance", ...
  3. Brax: "ant", "halfcheetah", ...

Brax and Playground ids need Ajax's brax or playground extra (Installation). An unknown id raises ValueError, naming the extras that are not installed. The agent builds n_envs copies, which step in parallel.

from ajax import PPO, SAC

agent = SAC("Pendulum-v1")  # gymnax
agent = PPO("CartPole-v1")  # gymnax, discrete actions

gymnax environments with image observations are flattened to one vector, because the networks read flat vectors. A CNN encoder can rebuild the image from it.

docs.title: Brax and Playground
docs.text:
Every agent takes episode_length and action_repeat for an environment built from a Brax or Playground id. episode_length counts simulator steps, 1,000 by default; gymnax environments keep their own time limit, set in their parameters (below). On a CPU, Playground environments run MJX's pure-JAX implementation.

Playground draws a new initial state for every episode (fresh_reset=True), as dm_control does. Runs made before this became the default restarted every episode of copy i from one cached state. To reproduce them, or to change how the environment is built, build it with build_env_from_id and pass it to the agent with the same n_envs:

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.environments.create import build_env_from_id

# Every episode of copy i restarts from the same cached state, as older runs did.
env, _ = build_env_from_id("CartpoleBalance", n_envs=4, episode_length=1_000, fresh_reset=False)
agent = SAC(env, n_envs=4)

build_env_from_id(..., differentiable_reset=True) lets jax.grad flow through the reset itself, for instance to physics parameters, at the cost of computing a reset at every step. Without it, gradients still flow through the actions, the policy and the environment state. See Differentiable simulation.

Evaluation rebuilds a Brax or Playground environment from its id. A prebuilt Brax environment with wrappers of your own would lose them there. Register a builder instead, and every rebuild uses it:

from ajax.environments.create import register_brax_builder, register_playground_builder

A builder takes (n_envs, episode_length), returns the fully wrapped environment and sets its _ajax_env_id attribute to the id. To support action repeat it also accepts an action_repeat keyword.

docs.title: Your own environment
docs.text:
Any gymnax environment works: pass the instance, and its parameters as env_params. Wrappers you add stay on during training and evaluation.

import gymnax

from ajax import SAC

env, params = gymnax.make("Pendulum-v1")
params = params.replace(max_steps_in_episode=100)  # shorter episodes
agent = SAC(env, env_params=params, learning_starts=500)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_000)

SAC("Pendulum-v1", env_params=params) does the same with an id. Brax and Playground ids take no env_params: passing some raises.

docs.title: TargetGym
docs.text:
TargetGym's set-point tasks (aircraft, process control, industrial plants) use gymnax's interface, so an instance goes straight in:

# doc: skip (needs the optional plane group: uv sync --group plane)
from target_gym import Plane3DCircle

from ajax import SAC

agent = SAC(Plane3DCircle(), n_envs=4, learning_starts=1_000)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=20_000)

The Plane3DCircle scenario of benchmarks/perf_bench.py trains on it (Performance); the per-agent benchmark does not. The plane dependency group installs it.

docs.title: Wrappers
docs.text:
Ajax ships gymnax wrappers for common changes to a task:

Wrapper (ajax.wrappers) What it does InitialStateWrapper(env, init_state_fn) replaces the reset state, for every episode (fixed or narrowed initial conditions) ObservationNoiseWrapper(env, sigma, scale=1.0) adds sensor noise to the observations (see below) TerminatedTruncatedWrapper(env) splits an old-style done into terminated and truncated (see time limits) PIDTermsWrapper (ajax.environments.pid_terms) adds a PID's error terms to the observation (see below) 
import gymnax
import jax.numpy as jnp

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.wrappers import InitialStateWrapper, ObservationNoiseWrapper

env, params = gymnax.make("Pendulum-v1")


def hanging_down(key, state, params):
    """Start every episode at rest, hanging down."""
    return state.replace(theta=jnp.asarray(jnp.pi), theta_dot=jnp.asarray(0.0))


env = InitialStateWrapper(env, hanging_down)
env = ObservationNoiseWrapper(env, sigma=0.05)
agent = SAC(env, env_params=params, learning_starts=500)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_000)

For anything else, subclass ajax.wrappers.GymnaxWrapper: it forwards every method to the wrapped environment (self._env), so you override only what you change.

import gymnax

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.wrappers import GymnaxWrapper


class ScaleReward(GymnaxWrapper):
    """Divide every reward by 10."""

    def step(self, key, state, action, params=None):
        obs, state, reward, terminated, truncated, info = self._env.step(
            key, state, action, params
        )
        return obs, state, reward / 10.0, terminated, truncated, info


env, params = gymnax.make("Pendulum-v1")
agent = SAC(ScaleReward(env), env_params=params, learning_starts=500)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_000)

Two more modules turn one environment into a family of tasks: ajax.environments.model_reference (follow a reference model's response) and ajax.environments.system_class (a distribution over physical parameters, one system per copy). Differentiable simulation covers both.

docs.title: Sensor noise
docs.text:
ObservationNoiseWrapper(env, sigma, scale) adds sigma * scale * N(0, 1) to every observation, drawn afresh at every reset and step. scale is one number or one per observation dimension, such as the observations' standard deviations. The final observation of an ended episode gets the same draw as the step, so a stored transition holds the observation the agent saw. The environment's own random draws are unchanged.

The noise sits on the observation only: the state's get_obs stays noiseless, and that is what an expert reads on a gymnax environment. ObservationNoiseWrapperBrax does the same on a Brax or Playground stack built by build_env_from_id; since evaluation rebuilds those from their id, add it inside a registered builder.

docs.title: Normalisation
docs.text:
Two arguments normalise what the agent learns from, with running statistics pooled over the n_envs copies:

  • normalize_observations=True: each observation dimension to mean 0 and variance 1.
  • normalize_rewards=True: divides rewards by a running standard deviation, by default of the single-step reward. With reward_normalization_gamma=0.99 it uses the standard deviation of the discounted return instead, as Stable-Baselines3's VecNormalize and Gymnasium's NormalizeReward do.

The logged returns stay in the environment's units. Evaluation normalises observations with the training statistics, frozen, and never normalises rewards.

The agents learning from the rollout they just collected (PPO, APO and PQN) normalise in the environment. Its statistics live in the environment state: state.collector_state.env_state.normalization_info.obs for gymnax (in info["normalization_info"] for Brax), with mean and var. Every copy holds the same pooled values. To run the policy on a new observation yourself, normalise it as (obs - mean) / sqrt(var + 1e-8) first.

The replay agents (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, DQN, UDRL) learn from rows collected long before, so their replay keeps the environment's own observations and rewards, and a replayed row is normalised with the current statistics, as Stable-Baselines3's replay buffer does under VecNormalize. UDRL's rewards are the exception for now: its segments keep them normalised by the environment. The agent normalises observations itself: the statistics live in state.collector_state.obs_norm_info (mirrored on its networks, which apply them, so get_pi takes raw observations) and cover the dimensions SAC appends to the observation (an expert's action or state), not UDRL's command. A replayed reward is divided by the environment normaliser's current statistics. SAC's normalize_obs_running=True, the switch's old name, warns and will be removed: pass normalize_observations=True. An expert policy always reads the raw observation, in the environment's own units: see Expert guidance.

docs.title: Raw observation columns
docs.text: Some observation entries must keep their units: a PID's gains only mean something on errors in the plant's units. An environment or wrapper declares its first k columns raw with a raw_obs_columns = k attribute. Every normaliser, in the environment or in the agent, then leaves those columns unchanged and normalises the rest. PIDTermsWrapper declares its terms this way.

docs.title: PID error terms
docs.text:
A PID controller acts on the tracking error e = target - current, its integral I and its difference D. PIDTermsWrapper puts (e, I, D) in front of a gymnax environment's observation, so any agent can read them:

# doc: skip (needs the optional plane group: uv sync --group plane)
from target_gym import FirstOrderSystem

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.environments.pid_terms import PIDTermsWrapper

# FirstOrderSystem observes [x, target]: index 0 is controlled, index 1 its set-point.
env = PIDTermsWrapper(FirstOrderSystem(), current_idx=(0,), target_idx=(1,), dt=1.0)
agent = SAC(env, n_envs=4, normalize_observations=True, learning_starts=500)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_000)
stats = state.collector_state.obs_norm_info  # SAC normalises observations itself
print(stats.mean[0, 0], stats.var[0, 0])  # the three terms are pinned at mean 0, variance 1

The observation becomes [e, I, D, raw observation], 3 * n_errors columns longer. dt is the sampling period: the integral sums dt * e and the difference is divided by dt, so gains keep their continuous-time units. integral_limit clamps the integral (anti-windup). The terms restart with every episode, auto-resets included. The PID policy reads them.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Every continuous agent acts in [-1, 1] on each action dimension, whatever the environment's bounds: these are the agent's units. Before each step, Ajax maps the action onto the environment's box [low, high]: it clips the action to [-1, 1], then sends c + h * a, with c = (high + low) / 2 the centre of the box and h = (high - low) / 2 its half-width (CleanRL's action_bias and action_scale). On gymnax's Pendulum, whose torque goes from -2 to 2, an action of 1 applies a torque of 2. A dimension with an infinite bound gets the clipped action as it is, and discrete actions pass through. Brax and Playground actions already lie in [-1, 1], where the map is just the clip. With per-copy parameters from a system class, each copy is mapped onto its own system's bounds.

The map is the same for every agent and everywhere an action reaches the environment: collection, evaluation and expert rollouts. SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, UDRL and APG (by default) squash their actions into [-1, 1] with tanh; PPO samples an unbounded Gaussian unless you pass squash=True, and APO one whose mean is bounded by tanh: their samples are clipped by the map. The replay buffers and rollouts store the action in agent units.

ajax.environments.utils.agent_action_to_env is the map and env_action_to_agent its inverse, which does not clip. An expert policy returns actions in the environment's units, and Ajax reads them through the inverse: see Expert guidance.

docs.title: Action repeat
docs.text: Every agent takes action_repeat: each agent step runs the simulator that many times with the same action and returns the summed reward. It works on Brax and Playground environments built from an id; episode_length then counts simulator steps, so an episode lasts episode_length // action_repeat agent steps. gymnax environments and prebuilt environments support only 1 and raise otherwise. The world models use it for their papers' protocols (see World models).

docs.title: Time limits
docs.text:
An episode can end in two ways. It terminates when the task itself ends: the pole fell, the robot crashed. It is truncated when it hits the time limit, which is not part of the task. Ajax keeps the two apart: after a termination the value of what follows is zero, but after a truncation the agent bootstraps on the value of the last observation, as Stable-Baselines3 and CleanRL do. Treating a time limit as a termination would teach the agent that the world ends there, and underestimate the value of long-running states.

Auto-resetting environments return the next episode's first observation when an episode ends. Ajax recovers the last observation of the ended episode from the step's info (final_observation on gymnax, final_obs on Brax and Playground, where Ajax's wrapper stack records it) and stores it for the bootstrap.

Each backend reports the two flags its own way:

  • gymnax 1.0 returns terminated and truncated apart. Ajax uses them as they are.
  • Older gymnax-style environments return one done that folds in the time limit, which gymnax hands back as terminated: every time limit then looks like the end of the task. Wrap such an environment in TerminatedTruncatedWrapper, which keeps terminated only where the time limit was not reached.
  • Brax and Playground report the time limit in info["truncation"], set by their episode wrapper.

The algorithm pages note the agents that treat episode ends differently, such as the average-reward agents.

docs.title: Expert guidance
docs.text:
Often a controller already exists for the task: a tuned PID, a model predictive controller, a hand-written rule, an earlier policy. Starting reinforcement learning from scratch throws that knowledge away. Expert guidance lets an agent learn from such an expert: copy it at the start, let it act while the agent is still poor, use its values in the critic's target, and then improve on it.

In Ajax, an expert is any function you pass to an agent or to an extension. SAC uses it the most: it fills the replay buffer with the expert's experience and lets the expert extensions shape collection, the critic and the actor. SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG and APO can clone it before training, and those and PPO, APG and UDRL can imitate it through an extra actor-loss term. DAgger imitates it with no reward at all. Recorded transitions, from an expert or any earlier run, can start a replay agent's buffer (PriorData). Choosing the pieces names each method, its paper and the agents that run it.

docs.title: The expert
docs.text:
An expert maps observations to actions. Ajax accepts two forms:

  • Stateless: expert(obs) -> action.
  • Stateful, for a controller with memory such as a PID's integral: an object with init_state(n_envs), which returns the starting state for n_envs environments, and expert(state, obs) -> (action, new_state). TargetGym's PID experts (target_gym.experts.pid.FunctionalExpertPolicy) follow this form.

Four conventions matter:

  1. The expert lives in the environment's units, both ways. It reads the environment's own observation, before any observation normalisation and without the columns an agent appends (the training fraction, the expert's own state). It returns actions in the environment's bounds: on Pendulum, a torque between -2 and 2. Ajax reads that action in the agent's units, [-1, 1] (see Actions), without clipping it, so it can be stored and compared with the agent's own actions; when it is executed, the usual map sends it back to the environment, clipped at its bounds.
  2. Its state is tracked. Wherever Ajax runs a stateful expert itself, it keeps one state per environment copy and starts every episode from init_state: SAC's replay prefill, warm-up and collection, the cloning and Monte-Carlo rollouts, and every agent's evaluation.
  3. It works on batches. Ajax calls it on one observation per environment, and on replay batches. Index the last axis (obs[..., 0]), not the first, and keep the action's last axis ([..., None] for one action).
  4. It is part of the compiled program: a plain function or a frozen dataclass works.

A stateful expert, a PID on Pendulum's angle:

from dataclasses import dataclass

import jax.numpy as jnp

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PIDExpert:
    """A PID on the pole's angle; its state is the error's integral."""

    kp: float = 2.0
    ki: float = 0.1
    kd: float = 0.5
    dt: float = 0.05  # Pendulum's time step

    def init_state(self, n_envs):
        return jnp.zeros((n_envs, 1))

    def __call__(self, integral, obs):
        theta = jnp.arctan2(obs[..., 1:2], obs[..., 0:1])  # raw [cos, sin, velocity]
        integral = integral + self.dt * theta
        torque = -(self.kp * theta + self.ki * integral + self.kd * obs[..., 2:3])
        return jnp.clip(torque, -2.0, 2.0), integral  # newton-metres, as the env takes them


agent = SAC("Pendulum-v1", expert_policy=PIDExpert(), learning_starts=500)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=1_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_000, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean expert reward"])  # the PID's own return

Extensions that call an expert themselves, on the observations of a replay batch (ImitationLoss, IBRL, LCBGatedBootstrap, CriticBlend, PhiRefresh), call it as expert(obs), on raw observations, where no expert state exists. A stateful expert is allowed there in one case only: when it is the agent's own expert_policy (the same object), on an agent that stores that expert's actions (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, APO). The extensions then read the actions the agent stored at collection, computed from the expert's tracked state, instead of calling it. Any other stateful expert is refused when the agent is built.

docs.title: Which agents take an expert
docs.text:
Agent expert_policy= Expert extensions SAC replay prefill, warm-up actions, collection extensions, the expert's evaluation return all TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, APO the expert's evaluation return CloningPretrain, ImitationLoss; IBRL, LCBGatedBootstrap on TD3, REDQ and AVG; ExpertValueMetrics on TD3, REDQ and ASAC DAgger required: the expert acts and labels every visited state; its evaluation return CloningPretrain, ImitationLoss (continuous actions)

The other agents (PPO, DQN, PQN, UDRL, APG and the world models) take no expert: CloningPretrain raises on them when training starts. PPO, APG and UDRL with continuous actions take ImitationLoss with a stateless expert. A discrete policy has no mean action for it, DQN and PQN have no actor, and the world models fold no actor phase.

With an expert, evaluations also log Eval/episodic mean expert reward, the expert's return on the same episodes as the agent's, and Eval/expert bias, the agent's return minus the expert's (positive once the agent does better). SAC takes a separate eval_expert_policy when the expert to compare against is not the one to learn from.

None of this works with memory= yet: recurrent SAC, TD3 and REDQ refuse an expert and extensions.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
SAC on Pendulum with a PD controller that is good near the top and poor elsewhere. Three extensions build on it: MCPretrain fits a critic to the expert's returns, OnlineBC pulls the actor towards the expert early on, and EDGEExploration lets the expert act while the critic rates it higher than the policy.

import jax.numpy as jnp

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.extensions.expert import OnlineBC
from ajax.extensions.exploration import EDGEExploration
from ajax.extensions.pretrain import MCPretrain
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig


def pd_expert(obs):
    """A PD controller on Pendulum's raw observation [cos θ, sin θ, θ̇]."""
    theta = jnp.arctan2(obs[..., 1], obs[..., 0])
    torque = -(2.0 * theta + 0.5 * obs[..., 2])
    return jnp.clip(torque, -2.0, 2.0)[..., None]  # the env's torque range


agent = SAC(
    "Pendulum-v1",
    expert_policy=pd_expert,
    expert_buffer_n_steps=1_000,  # expert steps written to the replay before training
    learning_starts=1_000,
    extensions=(
        # The frozen expert critic, fitted to ~1,000 steps of the expert's returns.
        MCPretrain(pd_expert, n_mc_steps=100, n_mc_episodes=10, n_steps=200),
        OnlineBC(bc_coef=1.0, critic_warmup_frac=0.2),
        EDGEExploration(gate="argmax", decay_frac=0.3),
    ),
)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=1_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=2_000, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])
print(evaluations["Eval/expert bias"])       # agent minus expert
print(evaluations["edge/live_expert_frac"])  # share of envs the expert drove

At this budget the agent has barely started; the example shows the wiring. Give MCPretrain a few hundred thousand expert steps and train for tens of thousands of steps for a real run (its defaults collect about a million).

docs.title: What SAC does with an expert, step by step
Before training
docs.text:
1. Replay prefill. SAC runs the expert for expert_buffer_n_steps steps in each environment (default 20,000) and writes them to the replay buffer, flagged as expert rows. Every row also stores the expert's action at s and s′, which several extensions read later. Set it to 0 to skip.
  2. Cloning, by extension. CloningPretrain(expert, n_steps=...) rolls the expert out for n_steps steps per environment, in the observation layout the agent sees, and trains the actor to reproduce its actions for epochs passes in batches of batch_size, at the actor's learning rate. The actor learns on observations standardised with the dataset's statistics, so the agent's running observation statistics start from them (an agent that kept none gets them), and the actor keeps seeing inputs as it did when cloned. reset_log_std=True restores the cloned actor's exploration noise afterwards, reset_actor_head=True keeps only its hidden layers, and skip_actor=True leaves the actor as it was. Put it first among the pre-training extensions: the critic pre-trained by the others reads the statistics it sets, and SAC refuses it after them. TD3, REDQ and APO take it too.
  3. Critic pre-training, by extension. MCPretrain runs the expert, fits a separate critic, the frozen expert critic φ*, to its Monte-Carlo returns, and records the range of values it predicts. Unlike a Bellman target, a Monte-Carlo return does not lean on an untrained critic, so it is unbiased. BellmanPretrain instead runs ordinary critic updates on the prefilled buffer; it is kept for ablations.

docs.title: Warm-up
docs.text: Until learning_starts, SAC does not use its policy. At each step, with probability expert_fraction (default 0.7), every environment takes the expert's action; otherwise, a uniform random one. With ResidualPolicy, the warm-up is uniform only.

docs.title: Collection
docs.text:
Collection extensions decide, at each step, whether the expert or the policy acts. SAC runs them in two places, which each extension names in its action_slot:

  • Before the warm-up choice ("pre_warmup"): EDGEExploration (a value-based gate) and JSRLCurriculum (the expert starts each episode, for a shrinking number of steps).
  • After it ("post_warmup"): ValueBox, which lets the expert act wherever its value exceeds a threshold that rises over training. The step that enters this region ends the agent's episode in the stored transition and pays the expert's value as a reward, in place of the bootstrap, whatever its sign.

ResidualPolicy changes what the policy's action means: SAC executes clip(a_E + scale · a_π, −1, 1), in agent units, in collection, in the critic's target, in the actor's loss and in evaluation. The policy then learns a correction to the expert (residual RL).

Steps where the expert acted are flagged in the buffer; value/expert_frac_in_buffer logs their share of each training batch. The replay keeps the raw observations and these flags only in a run with an expert (an agent's expert_policy, or one an extension holds); without one nothing reads them.

docs.title: Critic
docs.text: Target extensions change what the critic learns towards. IBRL and LCBGatedBootstrap compare the expert's and the policy's next actions. CriticBlend and MCVarianceCorrection lean on φ*, so they need MCPretrain in the same stack. PhiRefresh refits φ* during training on the rows where the expert acted.

docs.title: Actor
docs.text:
OnlineBC adds a cloning term to the actor's loss, weighted by φ*'s value at each state and fading out over critic_warmup_frac of training. It needs MCPretrain.

ImitationLoss(expert, q_filter=True) adds the unweighted cloning term (see below) only on the rows where the agent's critics rate the expert's action above the policy's mean action, min_k Q_k(s, a_E) > min_k Q_k(s, μ(s)): the Q-filter of Nair et al. (ICRA 2018, Sec. IV-C). Where the agent already does better than the expert, it stops copying it, with no schedule to tune: a PID that is good near the setpoint and poor in transients keeps guiding only where it still helps. Unlike the paper, the rows are replay rows labelled with the expert's action, not a separate demonstration buffer, and coef weights the cloning term in place of the paper's two weights. The filter needs a critic that ranks actions, a Q critic: SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC and AVG have one, PPO and APO a state-value critic, which cannot rank actions. The minimum runs over all the agent's critics, though TD3's actor follows its first and REDQ's the mean of its ensemble. Pair it with the expert prefill, as the paper pairs it with demonstrations. With ResidualPolicy, whose critic reads the executed action rather than the policy's, it is refused.

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
Three SAC options change the networks' input, because they change its size:

  • augment_obs_with_expert_action=True appends the expert's action to the observation, so the policy can condition on the expert's suggestion.
  • augment_obs_with_expert_state=True appends a stateful expert's internal state (a PID's integral, say).
  • use_train_frac=True appends the fraction of training done.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Besides the expert's return and the bias above, ExpertValueMetrics logs the critic's value at the expert's actions (value/q_expert_mean) and its gap to the value of the actions taken (value/q_gap). EDGEExploration logs edge/live_expert_frac, and ImitationLoss(q_filter=True) the share of a replay batch its filter keeps (imitation/q_filter_frac; not on AVG, which keeps no replay).

docs.title: Choosing the pieces
docs.text:
The agents in brackets are those that accept each piece, as Compatibility lists them from the code. "Developed with Ajax" marks a feature with no external reference.

You want to Use Method Start the replay with good experience expert_buffer_n_steps (SAC, on by default); PriorData with a transition dataset (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, DQN) expert prefill; prior data in the replay as RLPD (Ball et al., 2023), without its symmetric sampling, and optional offline updates Train on recorded transitions alone, then fine-tune online agent.train_offline(dataset, n_updates) (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, DQN, IQL) offline training on the agent's own update; IQL (Kostrikov et al., 2022) Keep the actor near the dataset's actions ImitationLoss(None, target="replay", alpha=2.5) (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC) TD3+BC (Fujimoto and Gu, 2021) on TD3 Keep the critic's target near the dataset's actions too TargetBC with TD3+BC's term (TD3) ReBRAC (Tarasov et al., 2023) Keep the critic low on actions the dataset lacks ConservativeQ (SAC, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, IQL), CalQL (SAC, REDQ, IQL) CQL (Kumar et al., 2020), Cal-QL (Nakamoto et al., 2023) Imitate demonstrations, with no reward and no expert AdversarialReward with a transition dataset (PPO, continuous actions) GAIL (Ho and Ermon, 2016) Start the actor as a copy of the expert CloningPretrain (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, APO, DAgger) behaviour cloning Imitate the expert, with no reward the DAgger agent DAgger (Ross, Gordon and Bagnell, 2011); ImitationLoss with a replay agent's own expert is its aggregation plus the RL loss Keep the actor near the expert early on ImitationLoss (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, APO, DAgger; PPO, APG, UDRL with a stateless expert), OnlineBC (SAC) TD3+BC's actor term (Fujimoto and Gu, 2021), kickstarting (Schmitt et al., 2018) with anneal_frac; OnlineBC developed with Ajax Copy the expert only where the critic rates it higher ImitationLoss(q_filter=True) (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG) Q-filtered behaviour cloning (Nair et al., 2018) Let the expert act while the agent is poor JSRLCurriculum, EDGEExploration, ValueBox (SAC) jump-start RL (Uchendu et al., 2023); EDGE and the value box developed with Ajax Learn a correction to the expert ResidualPolicy (SAC) residual RL (Johannink et al., 2019) Give the critic a head start MCPretrain, then CriticBlend, MCVarianceCorrection, PhiRefresh (SAC) developed with Ajax Make the target account for the expert IBRL (SAC, TD3, REDQ, AVG), LCBGatedBootstrap (SAC, TD3, REDQ) IBRL (Hu et al., 2023); the LCB gate developed with Ajax Measure how the critic rates the expert ExpertValueMetrics (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC)

Some pieces need others. The agent refuses wrong combinations when it is built:

Extension Needs Refused EDGEExploration, JSRLCurriculum, ValueBox, ResidualPolicy SAC with an expert_policy and without use_pid_policy when built OnlineBC, CriticBlend, MCVarianceCorrection, ValueBox, PhiRefresh MCPretrain in the stack when built OnlineBC SAC with an expert_policy, whose actions it clones when built IBRL, LCBGatedBootstrap a discounted agent that keeps the raw next observations they read; LCBGatedBootstrap also a critic ensemble when built BellmanPretrain, ExpertValueMetrics an expert_policy and the agent's replay when built ImitationLoss(q_filter=True) a Q critic (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG); without ResidualPolicy when built; with ResidualPolicy, when training starts CloningPretrain SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG or APO; first among the pre-training extensions the agent when built, the order when training starts

The extensions that hold an expert themselves (CloningPretrain, MCPretrain, PhiRefresh, IBRL, LCBGatedBootstrap, CriticBlend, ImitationLoss) take it as their first argument. Pass the same object you give the agent. The target extensions, PhiRefresh and ImitationLoss then read the actions the agent stored at collection rather than calling the expert again. CloningPretrain must have it when SAC's observations carry the expert's action or state, and MCPretrain when they carry its state; they are refused otherwise.

docs.title: Imitation for TD3, REDQ, ASAC and APO
docs.text:
These agents take ImitationLoss, the behaviour-cloning term of TD3+BC (Fujimoto and Gu, 2021) with a fixed expert as the target: coef · mean((μ(s) − a_E(s))²) / 4, where μ(s) is the actor's mean action and a_E(s) the expert's, both in agent units. Dividing by 4 maps the squared distance of two actions in [-1, 1] to [0, 1]. Unlike OnlineBC, it is unweighted and needs no expert critic. Give the agent the same expert as its expert_policy to use a stateful one: the term then reads the actions the agent stored along each trajectory. With anneal_frac=f, the term's weight falls linearly from 1 to 0 at the fraction f of training, as in kickstarting (Schmitt et al., 2018), so the agent ends on its own objective; kickstarting uses a cross-entropy to a stochastic teacher and tunes the schedule, where here the expert is deterministic and the schedule linear. Its Q-filter (q_filter=True, see Actor) runs on TD3, REDQ and ASAC too; APO's critic rates states, not actions, so it refuses the filter. These agents can also start from a clone of the expert:

import jax.numpy as jnp

from ajax import TD3
from ajax.extensions.expert import ImitationLoss
from ajax.extensions.pretrain import CloningPretrain


def pd_expert(obs):
    theta = jnp.arctan2(obs[..., 1], obs[..., 0])
    return jnp.clip(-(2.0 * theta + 0.5 * obs[..., 2]), -2.0, 2.0)[..., None]


agent = TD3(
    "Pendulum-v1",
    expert_policy=pd_expert,  # logs the expert's own return at evaluations
    learning_starts=500,
    extensions=(
        CloningPretrain(pd_expert, n_steps=1_000, epochs=2),
        ImitationLoss(pd_expert, coef=1.0),
    ),
)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=2_000)

docs.title: Learning a PID's gains: SAC's gain mode
docs.text:
With a stateful PID expert that exposes learnable_fields, anchor_gains and step_with_gains (TargetGym's FunctionalExpertPolicy after register_learnable_gains), SAC(use_pid_policy=True) learns to schedule the expert's gains instead of acting directly. The actor outputs one number a in [-1, 1] per learnable gain; the gain applied is anchor · 10^a, between a tenth and ten times the expert's own. The PID computes the action. SAC refuses this mode, when it is built, with the collection extensions (their action phase never runs in it), ResidualPolicy and augment_obs_with_expert_action (the expert's action does not exist before the actor has chosen the gains).

It is different from the PID policy, in which the actor itself is a PID whose gains are learned, for any continuous-action agent.

docs.title: Limits and caveats
docs.text:
• No memory. Recurrent SAC, TD3, REDQ and ASAC refuse an expert and extensions.
  • SAC is the hub. Most expert extensions read quantities only SAC's update provides; the catalogue gives each one's scope.
  • Stateless queries. An extension that calls its expert on replayed observations needs a stateless expert, unless it is the agent's own on an agent that stores its actions (see The expert).
  • Budgets add up. The prefill, cloning and MCPretrain collections run before the first training step and are not counted in n_timesteps.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Extensions: the phases and the full catalogue.
  • SAC: every SAC option.
  • Networks and the PID policy.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
An extension adds a research feature to an agent's training without changing the agent: an extra term in a loss, a change to the TD target, another way to pick actions while collecting, an expert to learn from, a pre-training step, or measurements logged at each evaluation. Ajax ships twenty-four of them, listed in the catalogue below.

Why extensions instead of agent options? An agent's constructor takes its paper's hyperparameters plus extensions=(). The exceptions are expert_policy (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, APO), whose return each evaluation logs, and a few SAC options (its expert's prefill and warm-up mix, the observation augmentations, the PID gain mode, use_train_frac, store_policy_action), kept because they change the network's input, the collection or the action pipeline, which extensions do not reach yet (SAC). A feature written into an agent grows that agent's file and ties it to one experiment; SAC once had about a hundred constructor keywords that way. Kept apart, a feature works with every agent that runs the parts of training it touches, and each agent's code stays readable next to its paper.

docs.title: Using extensions
docs.text:
Pass a tuple (or list) of extension objects as extensions=. Each object holds its own settings:

from ajax import PPO
from ajax.extensions.instrumentation import BiasVorePenalty, ConditioningMetrics
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = PPO(
    "CartPole-v1",
    expose_recent_rollout=True,  # keep the latest rollout for ConditioningMetrics
    extensions=(
        BiasVorePenalty(alpha=0.3),  # an extra critic-loss term
        ConditioningMetrics(),  # measurements at each evaluation
    ),
)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=8_192, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[1, 2], n_timesteps=16_384, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Cond/critic_srank"])  # one row per seed, one column per evaluation

A few rules follow from how Ajax compiles training:

  • Extensions are fixed for a run. They are compiled into the training program, so changing a setting means a new agent and a new compilation. Two extensions with equal settings compare and hash equal, as static arguments must. A second agent built the same way traces the same program again, and the compile cache loads it instead of compiling it, unless the run logs.
  • What changes during training lives in the agent's state, in state.ext_state (one entry per extension). It is saved in checkpoints and carried over when you resume a run.
  • One-shot work runs once. An extension's initial state and its pretrain step run on a fresh run only, not when a run resumes from initial_state=.
  • Measurements need evaluations. Extensions that add metrics run when the agent evaluates, which needs a logging_config. Their keys then appear in the returned evaluations next to Eval/episodic mean reward (see Logging).
  • Order matters only where it can. Target changes apply one after the other, in list order. Loss terms add up, so their order does not matter. For collection actions, the last extension that proposes one wins.

An empty tuple costs nothing: the agent's program is the same as without the argument.

docs.title: The phases
docs.text:
An extension overrides one or more phases, the points of the training loop where it may act. Every other phase keeps a default that changes nothing.

Phase When it runs What it may do Across a stack init_state once, on a fresh run build the extension's state one state per extension pretrain once, before training, on a fresh run change the agent's state (clone the actor, pre-train a critic) in list order reward after each rollout, before the agent's targets replace the rollout's rewards, and update the extension's own state in list order, each sees the previous result on_target at each critic update change the TD or value target, and log metrics in list order, each sees the previous result critic_loss at each critic update add a term to the critic loss, and log metrics summed actor_loss at each actor update add a term to the actor loss, and log metrics summed action at each collection step replace the action the agent would take the last proposal wins eval_action at evaluation replace the evaluation action no agent runs it yet transform_action at each collection step, in the losses and at evaluation make the executed action a function of the policy's and the expert's the first one acts post_update after each update change the agent's state (schedules, refreshes) in list order eval_metrics at each evaluation add metrics to the log merged

The agent hands its stack (an ExtensionStack) to its training step, which makes one call per phase: fold_init (every initial state, then every pretrain), fold_on_target, fold_critic_loss, fold_actor_loss, fold_post_update and fold_eval_metrics. Each call gets a random key of its own, on which the agent draws nothing else (init_state and eval_metrics split it, one sub-key per extension). On an empty stack a fold returns its input untouched and draws nothing. The action and transform_action phases are the exceptions: SAC's action pipeline calls them directly (see below).

docs.title: Which agent runs which phase
docs.text:
Every agent runs pretrain, post_update and eval_metrics, which belong to the shared training loop. The others depend on what the agent's update has: a target, a critic, an actor, a collection step it lets an extension change.

Agent on_target critic_loss actor_loss action, transform_action SAC yes yes yes yes, with an expert_policy TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, IQL yes yes yes no PPO, APO yes (value targets) yes yes no DQN, PQN yes yes (the Q-network's loss) no no UDRL, DAgger, APG no no yes no DreamerV3, TDMPC2, TDMPC2MultiTask no no no no

docs.title: What an agent has, and what an extension needs
docs.text:
Each agent says what its algorithm has, in capabilities:

Capability Meaning Agents actor a policy network trained by gradient all but DQN, PQN q_critic a learned action value Q(s, a) SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, DQN, PQN, TDMPC2, IQL v_critic a learned state value V(s) PPO, APO, DreamerV3, IQL discounted it maximises a discounted return all but ASAC, APO, UDRL, DAgger, APG replay its updates sample stored past transitions SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, DQN, UDRL, DAgger, DreamerV3, TDMPC2, IQL off_policy its update stays correct on actions its policy did not choose all but PPO, APO, APG critic_ensemble two critics or more SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, TDMPC2, IQL; AVG with num_critics of 2 or more obs_networks its policy and value networks read the observation, not a world model's latent state (memory needs it) all but DreamerV3, TDMPC2

A run adds what its configuration gives: critic (a Q or V critic), continuous_actions or discrete_actions (the environment), agent_expert (the agent has an expert_policy), and phi_star when an extension of the stack fits it (MCPretrain).

An extension needs what its phases imply (on_target and critic_loss a critic, actor_loss an actor, action an off-policy update, since the executed action is then not the policy's, transform_action continuous actions) and what it declares in requires. An extension needing nothing runs on every agent. When the agent is built, an extension needing something its run lacks is refused with MissingCapability, which names it:

import jax.numpy as jnp

from ajax import DQN
from ajax.extensions.expert import ImitationLoss


def expert(obs):
    return jnp.zeros(obs.shape[:-1] + (1,))


try:
    DQN("CartPole-v1", extensions=(ImitationLoss(expert),))
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)  # DQN cannot run ImitationLoss ('imitation_loss'), which needs actor (...), continuous_actions (...).

When the run has everything but the agent's code does not pass it on yet (it does not fold the phase, bind the extension's context, put a batch key in the phase's batch or store a replay field), the refusal is NotWired, which says what is missing.

Compatibility shows, for every agent and module, which runs, which the algorithm cannot run, and which is not wired yet.

Two more limits:

  • action and transform_action are SAC's alone, and only with an expert_policy and without use_pid_policy. SAC's collection step offers two places for an extension to act, before and after its warm-up choice, and an extension says which one in its action_slot ("pre_warmup" or "post_warmup"). Expert guidance explains them.
  • Memory and extensions do not mix yet. With memory=, PPO, SAC, TD3, REDQ and ASAC raise when training starts if you also pass extensions. APG takes both.

docs.title: What a phase hands an extension
docs.text:
on_target, critic_loss and actor_loss hand the extension a batch dictionary of the quantities at that point of the update. The keys an agent always passes are listed, per phase, in ajax.extensions.base.PHASE_BATCH_KEYS:

Phase Every agent folding it Some agents add on_target observations, next_observations, rewards, gamma actions, dones, reward_scale (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, DQN, PQN); raw_next_observations, next_a_expert (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG; None where nothing stores them); terminated, truncated (PQN, PPO, APO); gae, values (PPO, APO) critic_loss observations, targets critic_params, critic_state (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, PPO, APO); actions (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, DQN, PQN); q_state (DQN, PQN) actor_loss actor_params, actor_state, observations raw_observations, pi_mean (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, PPO, APO, APG, UDRL, DAgger; pi_mean None for a discrete policy; UDRL only with extensions); a_expert (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, APO, DAgger; None without an expert_policy); critic_state (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG); actions (UDRL); rollout, returns (APG)

gamma is None for an average-reward agent. dones marks where the target cut the bootstrap. targets is the target, held constant. The critic (critic_params, or DQN's and PQN's q_state) and the actor (actor_params) are the parameters being differentiated. pi_mean is the actor's mean action. raw_observations are the environment's own observations, before any normalisation; a replay agent keeps them only in a run with an expert, and passes None otherwise, except UDRL, whose segments hold them anyway. An agent may add keys of its own: read its fold call.

An extension never falls back to adding nothing, so a misplaced extension cannot look like a result. One declaring the keys it reads (batch_keys) is refused when the agent is built if the batch lacks them: ImitationLoss on PPO, whose actor batch has no pi_mean. One reading a key it does not declare raises when the program is built.

docs.title: What an extension declares
docs.text:
Besides its phases, an extension states what it needs as class attributes, which the agent reads when it is built:

Attribute What it says buffer_fields replay fields beyond the agent's own that the extension reads. Today only raw_next_obs, the environment's own next observation; SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC and AVG store it when an extension declares it, and the other agents refuse such an extension. expert_fields the fields holding an expert. The agent converts each one to agent units, and a run whose extensions hold an expert keeps the replay fields only experts read. experts() the experts the extension calls itself, without a state, on the observations it is given. reads_agent_expert_actions the extension reads the expert's actions the agent stored at collection when its expert is the agent's own expert_policy (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG and APO store them). requires the capabilities it needs beyond those its phases imply (needs() returns them all; an extension whose needs depend on its options overrides it). provides the capabilities it gives the rest of its stack: MCPretrain provides phi_star. context the agent-context keys it cannot work without (bind_to_agent); an agent's extension_context lists those it binds. pretrain_context the ExtensionContext fields its pretrain reads (update, buffer: PriorData); an agent's pretrain_context lists those its loop fills. batch_keys per phase, the batch keys it reads beyond those every agent folding the phase passes (reads() returns them). reads_step_in_episode the extension reads each copy's step within its episode, which the agent then counts. action_slot where in SAC's action pipeline its action runs.

φ* is a separate critic fitted to an expert's returns before training. MCPretrain fits it (it provides phi_star); OnlineBC, CriticBlend, MCVarianceCorrection, ValueBox and PhiRefresh read it (they require phi_star). Without MCPretrain in the stack they would add nothing for the whole run, or fail when the program is built, so the agent refuses them. EDGEExploration scores with φ* when it exists and with the agent's own critic otherwise, so it needs no MCPretrain.

docs.title: What is checked, and when
docs.text:
When the agent is built, its stack is refused (ValueError, naming each offending extension) if an extension:

  • needs a capability the run lacks (MissingCapability): φ* without an MCPretrain in the stack, the agent's expert_policy on an agent without one, a Q critic on PPO;
  • implements a phase the agent does not run, needs context the agent does not bind, reads a batch key the phase's batch lacks or a replay field the agent does not store (buffer_fields) (NotWired);
  • calls a stateful expert without its state. An extension calls its expert on the observations it is given, where no expert state exists.
