A stateful expert is allowed only when it is the agent's own expert_policy, on an agent that stores its actions from the expert's tracked state, and the extension reads those actions;
  • (SAC) acts in collection without an action_slot, or acts in collection or makes the policy residual in a run without an expert_policy or with use_pid_policy.

When training starts, CloningPretrain raises when placed after another pre-training extension, and PriorData on a replay whose rows it cannot fill.

docs.title: Catalogue
docs.text:
The checks above are necessary but not always sufficient: the last column says where each extension does its job, and Compatibility, generated from the code, where the agent accepts it. "SAC with an expert" means SAC(..., expert_policy=...).

Learning from an expert (ajax.extensions.expert)

Extension What it does Phases Works with OnlineBC Pulls the actor's mean action towards the expert's, weighted by φ*'s value at each state, fading to zero over the first critic_warmup_frac of training. Logs online_bc/term and its weight online_bc/weight. actor_loss SAC with an expert and MCPretrain ImitationLoss Adds coef · mean((μ(s) − a_E(s))²) / 4, the behaviour-cloning term of TD3+BC, towards a fixed expert it holds. When that expert is the agent's expert_policy, it reads the actions the agent stored, so the expert may be stateful. With anneal_frac, its weight falls linearly to 0 at that fraction of training (kickstarting). With q_filter=True a row counts only where the critic rates the expert's action above the policy's (Q-filtered BC), and evaluations log the share of a replay batch it keeps (imitation/q_filter_frac; not on AVG, which keeps no replay). With target="replay" it clones the replayed rows' own actions, so logged data needs no expert, and with alpha the actor loss becomes TD3+BC's: λ times the agent's own loss plus coef · mean((μ(s) − a)²) with no / 4, λ = alpha / mean|Q_1(s, μ(s))|, the actions compared in the environment's units (see TD3+BC). Logs imitation/term and the squared distance before the filter and the schedule, imitation/mse. actor_loss, eval_metrics SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, APO, DAgger, and PPO, APG and UDRL with a stateless expert (they take none); a discrete policy has no mean action and raises (no cross-entropy form yet). q_filter=True: SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC and AVG, without ResidualPolicy; refused where the critic rates states, not actions (PPO, APO), or there is none (APG, UDRL) ResidualPolicy Executes clip(a_E + scale · a_π, −1, 1): the policy learns a correction on top of the expert. transform_action SAC with an expert, without use_pid_policy JSRLCurriculum The expert acts for the first H_t steps of each episode, the policy afterwards; H_t shrinks from episode_length to 0 over decay_frac of training. Logs jsrl/horizon and jsrl/expert_frac. action, eval_metrics SAC with an expert ExpertValueMetrics Logs the critic's value at the expert's actions (value/q_expert_mean), its gap to the value of the actions taken (value/q_gap) and, with MCPretrain, its gap to φ* (value/phi_star_q_gap_ood), on one replay batch per evaluation. eval_metrics SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC with an expert

Exploration (ajax.extensions.exploration)

Extension What it does Phases Works with EDGEExploration Lets the expert act in place of the policy, step by step, as a gate (gate=) decides. "fixed": with probability fixed_prob; "argmax": whenever the critic rates the expert's action higher; "boltzmann": with a probability that grows with that gap. These three fade out over decay_frac of training. "lcb", "argmax_lcb" and "thompson" also weigh the critics' disagreement. Logs edge/live_expert_frac and its gate's schedule (edge/decay or edge/beta). action, eval_metrics SAC with an expert

Changing the critic's target (ajax.extensions.target_mods)

Extension What it does Phases Works with IBRL Adds γ(1 − d) · max(Q(s′, a_E) − Q(s′, a′), 0) to the target, so the values match acting with whichever of expert and policy looks better. Logs ibrl/bonus and ibrl/expert_wins. on_target SAC, TD3, REDQ, AVG; refused on an average-reward target (ASAC, APO), which has no discount for the bonus LCBGatedBootstrap Blends the policy's and the expert's next-action values in the target, weighted by a sigmoid of their pessimistic (lower-confidence-bound) scores. Logs its pessimism lcb_bootstrap/beta and its mean gate lcb_bootstrap/p_expert. on_target, eval_metrics SAC, TD3, REDQ, which have critic ensembles; refused on an average-reward target (ASAC, APO) CriticBlend Blends the target with a one-step target on φ*, (1 − α) y + α y_E, with α falling from 1 to 0 over critic_warmup_frac. Logs α as critic_blend/expert_weight, and critic_blend/target_gap. on_target, eval_metrics SAC with MCPretrain MCVarianceCorrection Where the critics disagree by more than threshold (variance), uses φ*'s value as the target. Logs mc_variance/replaced_frac. on_target SAC with MCPretrain ValueBox Lets the expert act where its value under φ* exceeds a threshold that rises from the lowest to the highest expert value over training. Logs value_box/threshold, value_box/in_box_frac and value_box/expert_frac. action, eval_metrics SAC with an expert and MCPretrain

Pre-training (ajax.extensions.pretrain)

Extension What it does Phases Works with CloningPretrain Rolls the expert out for n_steps steps per copy and trains the actor to reproduce its actions (epochs passes in batches of batch_size, at the actor's learning rate); the agent's observation statistics start from the dataset's. Logs the mean loss of its first and last epoch, cloning/first_loss and cloning/last_loss. pretrain, eval_metrics SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, APO, DAgger (other agents refuse it when built) MCPretrain Rolls the expert out, fits φ* to its Monte-Carlo returns, records its value range, and by default nudges the agent's own critic towards it. Logs the range, mc_pretrain/v_min and mc_pretrain/v_max, and the fit: its first and last loss, mc_pretrain/first_loss and mc_pretrain/last_loss, and φ*'s mean value at the expert's actions, mc_pretrain/q_expert_mean. pretrain, eval_metrics SAC (other agents refuse it when built) BellmanPretrain Runs n_steps ordinary critic updates on the replay buffer, which holds the expert's prefill, before training. Its values bootstrap from an untrained critic; kept for ablations. Logs the critic loss of its first and last update, bellman_pretrain/first_loss and bellman_pretrain/last_loss. pretrain, eval_metrics SAC with an expert PhiRefresh Every interval steps, refits φ* for steps updates on the replay rows where the expert acted. post_update SAC with an expert and MCPretrain PriorData Adds a transition dataset (ajax.buffers.dataset) to the replay, where it stays, and to the observation and reward statistics, then runs offline_updates of the agent's own update on it before acting. Pair it with learning_starts=0. pretrain SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, DQN (other agents refuse it when built)

Offline RL (ajax.extensions.offline)

Extension What it does Phases Works with ConservativeQ CQL(H)'s critic term: alpha times, for each critic, the logsumexp of its values at n_actions uniform actions and as many of the policy's at s and s' (each less its log-density), minus its value at the data's action. Logs cql/term and cql/gap. critic_loss SAC, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, IQL: a Q critic and a policy with a density, refused on a deterministic one (TD3); see SAC CalQL ConservativeQ with the policy actions' values floored at the row's return to go (Cal-QL), from a transition dataset (return_to_go; collected rows have none). Also logs calql/bound_frac, the share it raised. critic_loss SAC, REDQ, IQL (the replays that keep the return to go); refused on an average-reward critic (ASAC), without a replay (AVG) or on a deterministic policy (TD3) TargetBC ReBRAC's critic penalty: the target less γ (1 − d) β Σ (ã′ − a′)², ã′ the next actions the target scored and a′ the dataset's next action (next_action; a row without one keeps its target). Logs target_bc/penalty and target_bc/known_frac. on_target TD3, whose on_target batch holds its target's next actions (see ReBRAC)

Adversarial imitation (ajax.extensions.adversarial)

Extension What it does Phases Works with AdversarialReward GAIL: a discriminator, trained after each rollout to tell its rows from a transition dataset of demonstrations, replaces the rollout's rewards with -log(1 - D(s, a)); the environment's own reward is not used. It reads the action the environment runs, clipped to [-1, 1]. Logs gail/reward, gail/disc_loss, gail/expert_acc and gail/policy_acc. reward PPO with continuous actions (see PPO)

Critic ensembles (ajax.extensions.ensemble)

Extension What it does Phases Works with KernelRepulsion Adds coef times the mean similarity (an RBF kernel) between the critics' predictions, which pushes the critics of an ensemble apart. Logs kernel_repulsion/term, kernel_repulsion/kernel and kernel_repulsion/bandwidth. critic_loss SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC with two or more critics; other agents, AVG's single critic included, refuse it when built

Measuring the critic (ajax.extensions.instrumentation)

Extension What it does Phases Works with ConditioningMetrics Logs the critic's effective rank (Cond/critic_srank), its fraction of dormant units, its feature and weight norms. It finds the critic from the agent's networks: an ensemble critic, or a Q-network. eval_metrics replay agents given buffer= (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, DQN); PPO, APO and PQN run with expose_recent_rollout=True (AVG too, but its rollout is one step per copy) BiasVoreDecomposition Splits the critic's squared one-step error into squared bias and variance (EVarEst/bias_sq, EVarEst/var_resid, EVarEst/mse, EVarEst/abs_bias), against a one-step target on its current parameters, or your own value_target_fn. eval_metrics as ConditioningMetrics BiasVorePenalty Adds ((1 − 2α)/α) · Var(residual) to the critic loss; alpha=0.5 adds nothing. Logs bias_vore/penalty and bias_vore/residual_var. critic_loss every agent with a critic_loss phase: SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, PPO, APO, DQN, PQN

Sources: TD3+BC is Fujimoto and Gu, 2021; CQL is Kumar et al., 2020, Cal-QL Nakamoto et al., 2023, and ReBRAC Tarasov et al., 2023; GAIL is Ho and Ermon, 2016; Q-filtered BC is Nair et al., ICRA 2018; residual RL is Johannink et al., 2019; JSRL is Uchendu et al., 2023; the kernel's bandwidth follows the median heuristic of SVGD (Liu and Wang, 2016); effective rank is Kumar et al., 2021, and dormant units Sokar et al., 2023, and IBRL is Hu et al., Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning, 2023 (all cited in the code). EDGE, the LCB gates and the bias-variance (EVarEst) measurements are research features developed with Ajax, with no external reference in the code.

docs.title: Measuring a replay agent's critic
docs.text:
ConditioningMetrics and BiasVoreDecomposition need states the agent has visited. An on-policy agent keeps its latest rollout when built with expose_recent_rollout=True, as in the example at the top of this page. A replay agent keeps them in its replay buffer, and the extension must be given the buffer object. The extension is built before the agent, so take the buffer from an agent built with the same settings (n_envs, buffer_size, batch_size):

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.extensions.instrumentation import BiasVoreDecomposition, ConditioningMetrics
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

buffer = SAC("Pendulum-v1", learning_starts=500).buffer  # same settings as below
agent = SAC(
    "Pendulum-v1",
    learning_starts=500,
    extensions=(ConditioningMetrics(buffer=buffer), BiasVoreDecomposition(buffer=buffer)),
)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=1_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=2_000, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Cond/critic_dormant_frac"], evaluations["EVarEst/bias_sq"])

When the batch they need is not available yet (an evaluation before the first rollout, say), these extensions log nothing rather than wrong numbers.

docs.title: Extensions that need the agent's context
docs.text: Some extensions need objects only the agent builds: its environment, network settings, optimisers, replay buffer or discount. They receive them through bind_to_agent, which an agent calls on its whole stack when it builds its training program; each extension picks the arguments it needs and returns a filled-in copy. Each agent lists the keys it binds in its extension_context. SAC binds everything its extensions read, which is why MCPretrain, BellmanPretrain and PhiRefresh work with SAC only. TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG and APO bind their environment, actor optimiser and expert_policy, which is what CloningPretrain needs; TD3, REDQ and ASAC also bind their replay buffer, which ExpertValueMetrics reads. DreamerV3 binds its own context. The other agents bind nothing. You never call bind_to_agent yourself.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text: An extension is a frozen dataclass subclassing Extension that overrides the phases it needs and declares what it reads. Writing an extension walks through the contract, the dictionary each phase receives on each agent, and a complete example. If a feature seems to need a new keyword on an agent, that is the sign it should be an extension instead.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Expert guidance: how the expert extensions fit together with SAC's expert options, with an example.
  • Extensions API: every extension's settings.
  • ajax/extensions/: the source, one module per family.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: A LoggingConfig turns on evaluation and logging. Every log_frequency steps the agent is evaluated and its metrics are recorded: in memory always, and in Weights & Biases or TensorBoard when you ask for them.

docs.title: LoggingConfig
docs.text:
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

logging = LoggingConfig(
    config={"experiment": "baseline"},  # extra fields stored with the run
    log_frequency=5_000,  # evaluate and log every 5,000 environment steps
    use_wandb=False,  # True by default
    use_tensorboard=False,
)
Field Default Meaning config (required) a dictionary stored with each run, with the agent's run configuration added (below) log_frequency 1000 environment steps between evaluations use_wandb True log to Weights & Biases use_tensorboard False write TensorBoard event files project_name, group_name None the W&B project and group run_name None the W&B run name's prefix: each run is named <run_name>_<run id> folder None where TensorBoard runs go: <folder>/tensorboard/<run id>/ (the working directory when None) sweep False for hyperparameter sweeps: SAC evaluates only in the last 20% of training, and the logging worker sends nothing to W&B

With both backends off, train still evaluates and returns the evaluations in memory: the quickest way to get learning curves.

docs.title: The run configuration
docs.text: Each run stores config merged with the agent's agent.config: every argument of the agent's constructor, by name, with the value it was given or its default (TDMPC2MultiTask leaves out its dataset and evaluation environments), and algo_name, the agent's name. train merges them into a copy, so one LoggingConfig can serve several agents' runs. DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 add the values they resolve from those arguments (their discount, replay size and so on). W&B stores the result as the run's configuration; TensorBoard stores it as text and, in each run directory, as config.json with the seed and the run_id added, so a run can be reproduced and paired with others by seed. Values that are not JSON (an environment object, a function) are written as their text.

docs.title: What is logged
docs.text:
Each evaluation records:

Name Meaning timestep environment steps so far Eval/episodic mean reward mean return of the num_episode_test test episodes, with the deterministic policy Eval/mean episodic length mean length of those episodes Eval/episodic entropy the policy's mean entropy along them Eval/mean bias the critic's error on those episodes (below) Eval/mean average reward APO's long-run reward per step; NaN for the others Eval/episodic mean expert reward, Eval/expert bias with an expert policy: the expert's return on the same episodes, and the agent's minus it; NaN without Train/episodic mean reward mean return of the training episodes that ended recently <group>/<metric> the agent's training metrics, such as value/critic_loss or policy/policy_loss

Extensions add their own, such as ConditioningMetrics's Cond/critic_srank. UDRL logs timestep, its training metrics (Train/episodic mean reward, Train/actor_loss, Train/mean_rtg, Train/mean_horizon, Train/n_completed_episodes), its evaluation's return, entropy and length, the command the evaluation starts from (below), and its extensions' metrics. The world models log their own sets: see their pages.

Each evaluation runs on episodes of its own: their initial states and noise are drawn afresh from the evaluation count (Training). Returns are in the environment's units even when the agent normalises rewards. A metric that is NaN (an agent that has not started updating yet, an expert metric without an expert) is dropped from W&B and TensorBoard, but kept as NaN in the returned evaluations.

docs.title: Training diagnostics
docs.text:
Beside its losses, each agent logs a few measures of how its updates go. Like the other training metrics, they are the last update's values; PPO, APO and PQN average theirs over the update's epochs and minibatches.

Name Agents Meaning policy/approx_kl PPO, APO the mean of (r - 1) - log r, r the ratio of the new policy's probability of each action to the old one's: an estimate of how far an update moved the policy, as CleanRL and Stable-Baselines3 log it policy/policy_std PPO, APO the mean standard deviation of the policy's Gaussian, before any squashing (SAC logs the same); NaN for a discrete policy value/explained_variance PPO, APO 1 - Var[target - V] / Var[target] over the minibatch: 1 for a critic that predicts its targets, 0 for one no better than their mean; NaN when the targets do not vary policy/grad_norm, value/grad_norm PPO, APO the global norm of each network's gradient, before clipping. PPO clips the two networks' gradients together (max_grad_norm): the clip acts when the norm of both, sqrt(policy² + value²), exceeds it value/value_bias, value/average_reward APO the value bias b and the reward rate rho the update used policy/epsilon DQN, PQN the exploration rate of the epsilon-greedy schedule at the current timestep value/abs_td_error DQN, PQN the mean of abs(Q(s, a) - target) over the batch value/grad_norm DQN, PQN the global norm of the Q-network's gradient, before clipping policy/grad_norm, value/grad_norm SAC, TD3 the global norm of the actor's and the critics' gradients, before clipping. TD3 logs 0 for the actor on the updates its policy_delay skips value/q_gap TD3 the mean over the batch of the critics' spread, the largest value minus the smallest (abs(Q1(s, a) - Q2(s, a)) for the default twin critics): how far they disagree value/target_noise_clip_frac TD3 the share of the target policy's noise samples that the clip to ±target_noise_clip changed Train/grad_norm APG the global norm of the controller's gradient, before clipping (max_grad_norm) Eval/commanded return, Eval/commanded horizon UDRL the return and horizon each evaluation episode is commanded with at its start, to set beside the return and length it achieves; in normalised units when rewards are normalised

docs.title: Extension metrics
docs.text:
The expert-guided extensions log their schedules and how often the expert acts, and the pretraining extensions what their fit computed, read from the agent state at each evaluation:

Name Extension Meaning edge/live_expert_frac EDGEExploration the share of envs the expert drove on the last collection step edge/decay, edge/beta EDGEExploration the gate's schedule: the decay ("fixed", "argmax", "boltzmann") or the LCB pessimism ("lcb", "argmax_lcb"); the "thompson" gate has none jsrl/horizon, jsrl/expert_frac JSRLCurriculum the guide horizon H_t, and the share of envs the expert drove on the last collection step lcb_bootstrap/beta LCBGatedBootstrap the LCB pessimism β critic_blend/expert_weight CriticBlend the weight α of the expert's target in the blend value_box/threshold ValueBox the expert value above which the expert acts value_box/in_box_frac, value_box/expert_frac ValueBox the shares of envs inside the box and driven by the expert on the last collection step mc_pretrain/v_min, mc_pretrain/v_max MCPretrain the expert's value range, which ValueBox's threshold runs between mc_pretrain/first_loss, mc_pretrain/last_loss MCPretrain the squared error of φ*'s fit to the Monte-Carlo returns, at its first and its last step mc_pretrain/q_expert_mean MCPretrain the mean of φ*'s value at the expert's actions after the fit, over the rollout's states cloning/first_loss, cloning/last_loss CloningPretrain the mean cloning loss of its first and its last epoch (NaN with skip_actor) bellman_pretrain/first_loss, bellman_pretrain/last_loss BellmanPretrain the critic loss of its first and its last update

A pretraining result is the same at every evaluation. It is NaN in a run resumed from a checkpoint saved before the results were kept.

Others log what they compute in the agent's update, its targets or its losses (Writing an extension). Like the agent's training metrics, they are the last update's values, or the mean over the update's epochs and minibatches (PPO, APO, PQN; UDRL's over its updates):

Name Extension Meaning ibrl/bonus IBRL the mean bonus the target gains ibrl/expert_wins IBRL the share of the batch where the expert's next action has the higher value lcb_bootstrap/p_expert LCBGatedBootstrap the mean weight of the expert's next action in the target critic_blend/target_gap CriticBlend the mean of the expert's target minus the Bellman target mc_variance/replaced_frac MCVarianceCorrection the share of targets replaced by φ*'s value kernel_repulsion/term, kernel_repulsion/kernel, kernel_repulsion/bandwidth KernelRepulsion the term added to the critic loss, the critics' mean kernel and its bandwidth bias_vore/penalty, bias_vore/residual_var BiasVorePenalty the term added to the critic loss and the variance of the critic's residual it scales imitation/term, imitation/mse ImitationLoss the term added to the actor loss, and the mean squared distance between the policy's mean action and the expert's, before the Q-filter and the schedule online_bc/term, online_bc/weight OnlineBC the term added to the actor loss and its schedule's weight

docs.title: The value bias
docs.text:
Eval/mean bias measures how far the critic's value estimates are from the returns the policy actually obtains. At each step of each evaluation episode it takes the critic's estimate at the observation and the action taken, subtracts the discounted return realised from that step to the episode's end, and averages over the steps. Positive means the critic overestimates. It is computed in the critic's own units: rewards normalised as in training and multiplied by the agent's reward_scale. An episode cut by the time limit realises no return past it, so even an exact critic shows a positive bias over its last steps.

SAC, TD3, REDQ and AVG report it with their action-value critic, DQN and PQN with their Q-network, PPO with its state-value critic. ASAC and APO, which learn average-reward values rather than discounted ones, report NaN, as does a critic with memory.

docs.title: In memory
docs.text:
train returns the evaluations as a dictionary of arrays, one row per seed and one column per evaluation:

from ajax import PPO
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = PPO("CartPole-v1", n_envs=8, n_steps=128)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=4_096, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=16_384, logging_config=logging)

print(sorted(evaluations))  # every logged name
print(evaluations["timestep"][0])  # [ 4096  8192 12288 16384]
print(evaluations["value/critic_loss"].shape)  # (2, 4)
print(agent.config["algo_name"], agent.config["n_steps"])  # PPO 128

A call that evaluates fewer times than its maximum pads the remaining columns with -1 (timestep) and NaN (the rest). Pass an n_timesteps that is a whole number of the agent's iterations (n_envs steps for the replay agents, n_envs × n_steps for PPO, APO, PQN and UDRL, n_envs × horizon for APG): the iterations stop at a multiple of one, so otherwise an evaluation due at the end of the run does not happen, and train warns.

docs.title: Weights & Biases and TensorBoard
docs.text:
Set use_wandb=True (log in once with wandb login) or use_tensorboard=True. Each seed is its own run, with its own id; after train, agent.run_ids lists them, and train(..., on_ids_ready=callback) hands them to callback before training starts.

Guard your script's entry point

The logging worker is a separate Python process started with spawn, which imports your script again. A script that trains at the top level then tries to train a second time inside the worker, and the run hangs. Put the training under if __name__ == "__main__":, as below.

import json
import tempfile

from ajax import PPO
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig, load_scalars_from_tfevents


def main():
    folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    logging = LoggingConfig(
        config={"experiment": "cartpole-demo"},
        log_frequency=4_096,
        use_wandb=False,
        use_tensorboard=True,
        folder=folder,
    )
    agent = PPO("CartPole-v1", n_envs=8, n_steps=128)
    agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=8_192, logging_config=logging)

    run = f"{folder}/tensorboard/{agent.run_ids[0]}"
    # TensorBoard writes spaces in names as underscores.
    scalars = load_scalars_from_tfevents(run)
    print(scalars["Eval/episodic_mean_reward"])  # [(step, value), ...]
    with open(f"{run}/config.json") as f:
        print(json.load(f)["seed"])  # 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

load_scalars_from_tfevents reads the scalars back without TensorFlow.

docs.title: The logging worker
docs.text:
Training runs inside one compiled program, which must not wait on a network or a disk. At each evaluation, the program hands the metrics to Python through a jax.debug.callback, which puts them on a queue; a separate worker process takes them off and writes them. The worker:

  • runs on the CPU, so it never reserves GPU memory;
  • writes TensorBoard events as they arrive;
  • buffers W&B steps and sends them ten at a time, in one W&B session per batch, because opening a W&B run is slow and W&B allows only one active run per process. W&B charts therefore update in steps of ten evaluations;
  • is drained and stopped when train returns, so every metric is written before train hands back the state.

The worker starts only when a backend is on. The callback has one cost: JAX never stores a program that contains one in its persistent compile cache, so a run with a LoggingConfig compiles again in every new process. See Performance.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
When the current observation is not enough to act well (a velocity the sensors do not show, a cue seen earlier in the episode), the agent must remember. The memory argument adds a memory block to the agent's networks, between the hidden layers and the output heads. Ajax carries the memory from step to step, resets it when an episode ends, and replays it correctly in training.

from ajax import PPO
from ajax.networks.memory import MemoryConfig

agent = PPO(
    "CartPole-v1",
    n_envs=8,
    n_steps=128,
    memory=MemoryConfig(kind="gru", hidden_size=32),
    bptt_length=32,  # learn on 32-step pieces of each copy's rollout
)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=4_096)

docs.title: Which agents
docs.text: Agent Memory PPO memory=, trained on rollouts SAC, ASAC, REDQ, TD3 memory=, trained on replayed sequences APG memory=, trained through the simulator DreamerV3 built in: its world model is recurrent AVG, DQN, PQN, APO, UDRL, TDMPC2 none; memory= raises an error

docs.title: The kinds
docs.text:
MemoryConfig (or the same settings as a dictionary) chooses the block:

kind What it is Cost "gru" a gated recurrent unit steps through a sequence one at a time; keeps one vector per copy "lstm" a long short-term memory cell as the GRU "transformer" causal self-attention over the episode's last window steps trains on a whole sequence in parallel; keeps the last window - 1 inputs per copy "mamba" a selective state-space block, as in Mamba trains in parallel with an associative scan; keeps a small state per copy 
from ajax.networks.memory import MemoryConfig

gru = MemoryConfig(kind="gru", hidden_size=64, num_layers=1)
attention = MemoryConfig(kind="transformer", hidden_size=64, window=32, num_heads=4)
ssm = MemoryConfig(kind="mamba", hidden_size=64, d_state=16, d_conv=4, expand=2)
lstm = {"kind": "lstm", "hidden_size": 64}  # a dictionary works too
Setting Default Used by hidden_size 64 every kind; a multiple of num_heads for the transformer num_layers 1 every kind gradient_checkpoint False every kind: recompute activations in the backward pass, trading time for memory on long sequences window, num_heads 32, 4 transformer: a step attends to itself and the window - 1 steps before it in the same episode d_state, d_conv, expand 16, 4, 2 mamba: state size, causal-convolution width, inner-width multiplier final_norm True transformer, mamba: end with a LayerNorm, as GPT-2 and Mamba do; False only restores a checkpoint saved before it, and goes once none remains (an APG controller's parameters also map exactly onto the new network with controller_params_with_final_norm, which maps the parameters only, so a resumed training state must restart its optimizer) init None every kind: the block's initialisation. None and "flax" are flax's defaults; "stacked_orthogonal" (GRU, LSTM) starts each gate as torch's orthogonal init of the stacked gates leaves it, as Ni et al. do; "gpt2" (transformer) draws every kernel from N(0, 0.02²), and "nanogpt" also scales the residual projections by 1/√(2 num_layers); "mamba" draws the step sizes log-uniformly in [0.001, 0.1], as Mamba does

Acting and training run the same code, a sequence of one step being the acting case, so what the agent learns is what it executes. Each kind is tested for that equivalence.

Memory has a price, on the CPU especially. One measurement in PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md (recurrent SAC on Pendulum, 4 copies, 2,048 steps, CPU) took about 16 s with a GRU or a transformer and about 95 s with Mamba.

docs.title: On-policy: PPO
docs.text: PPO collects a rollout of n_steps per copy (n_envs copies) with the memory running, cuts each copy's rollout into pieces of bptt_length steps and shuffles whole pieces, never single steps, into its minibatches. A piece starts from the memory the policy had at its first step while collecting (recomputed once before the update), never from zero in the middle of an episode. Gradients flow through a piece but not back past its start: bptt_length is how far back backpropagation through time reaches. Where a time limit cut an episode, the value it bootstraps on is the critic's on the episode's final observation, read with the memory that episode built, as sb3-contrib's RecurrentPPO does.

docs.title: The libraries disagree on the length
docs.text:
No PPO paper gives one length for every task, and the reference codes fall into two camps:

Code or paper Piece length A minibatch holds OpenAI Baselines' ppo2 at ea25b9e (baselines/ppo2/ppo2.py:167-180) each copy's whole rollout the whole rollouts of a subset of the copies; it asserts nenvs % nminibatches == 0 CleanRL's ppo_atari_lstm.py at fe8d8a0 (:296-313) the whole rollout (128 steps by default) as Baselines, with the same assertion PureJaxRL's ppo_rnn.py at 31756b1 (:258-291) the whole rollout (128 steps by default) as Baselines; it reshapes the copies into minibatches, which fails when they do not divide RLlib (ray at 00a3adb, rllib/core/rl_module/default_model_config.py:188) max_seq_len=20: episodes cut into 20-step chunks, zero-padded and masked whole chunks Sample Factory at 3d48f55 (sample_factory/algo/learning/learner.py:498-516) recurrence, by default the rollout length (32 steps) whole chunks, shuffled Pleines et al., 2022 (arXiv:2205.11104) tuned per task by grid search; their code (MarcoMeter/recurrent-ppo-truncated-bptt at a1e87a8) uses 8 steps or whole episodes whole chunks, zero-padded and masked

The first three share the copies between minibatches, as Huang et al.'s 37 Implementation Details of PPO (2022) describes; the last three cut fixed-length chunks. sb3-contrib's RecurrentPPO (at 075bd5b) has no length setting: it cuts at episode starts, copy changes and minibatch edges. Morad et al., 2024 (arXiv:2402.09900), argue that fixed-length chunks estimate the full gradient poorly, so a dependency longer than a chunk is unlikely to be learned, and found whole episodes more sample-efficient (with Q-learning, not PPO). All of them, and Ajax, agree on the rest: a piece stays in one minibatch, the memory resets when an episode ends, and a piece starts from the memory the policy had while collecting.

docs.title: What Ajax does by default
docs.text:
With bptt_length=None (the default) the number of minibatches chooses the length: the longest pieces that cut every rollout into equal parts and split exactly into the minibatches.

  • When n_envs is a multiple of the number of minibatches, a piece is a copy's whole rollout and a minibatch holds the rollouts of n_envs // num_minibatches copies: the scheme of Baselines, CleanRL and PureJaxRL.
  • Otherwise each rollout is cut into num_minibatches // gcd(n_envs, num_minibatches) equal pieces. When that count does not divide n_steps no length splits, and PPO refuses the settings at construction.

No published length fits every task, so Ajax keeps the reference codes' whole rollouts whenever the settings allow them, cuts the rollouts only as much as the requested minibatches need, and always trains on the number of minibatches it was asked for. That number is num_minibatches when positive, otherwise max(n_steps, batch_size) // min(n_steps, batch_size) (see PPO).

Settings Minibatches Default bptt_length A minibatch holds PPO's defaults: n_envs=4, n_steps=2048, batch_size=64 2048 // 64 = 32 256: 32 // gcd(4, 32) = 8 pieces per rollout one 256-step piece PureJaxRL's defaults: n_envs=4, n_steps=128, num_minibatches=4 4 128, the whole rollout one copy's rollout CleanRL's defaults: n_envs=8, n_steps=128, num_minibatches=4 4 128, the whole rollout two copies' rollouts n_envs=1, n_steps=32, num_minibatches=2 2 16, half the rollout one half n_envs=4, n_steps=100, num_minibatches=32 32 refused: 8 pieces do not divide 100

docs.title: Setting it
docs.text:
• To reproduce Baselines, CleanRL or PureJaxRL, leave bptt_length=None and set num_minibatches to a divisor of n_envs, as in the second and third rows. PPO's defaults do not (4 copies, 32 minibatches): they learn on 256-step pieces, with 32 × 10 epochs = 320 gradient steps per update, as the feedforward PPO takes.
  • An explicit bptt_length can only shorten the pieces. It must divide the default length (256 with PPO's defaults); PPO refuses any other value. For longer pieces, ask for fewer minibatches.
  • The pieces must cover the memory horizon the task needs. No gradient crosses the start of a piece, so the memory learns to keep a cue only from pieces holding both the step that shows it and the step that needs it. For a cue needed k steps later, 2k-step pieces hold both for only about half the places the cue can fall: make them several times longer than k. The memory still crosses pieces: this limits what the policy learns to keep, not what it uses once learned.
  • Shorter pieces trade that reach for cost. An update takes n_epochs × the number of minibatches gradient steps, whatever bptt_length. Shorter pieces give a GRU or an LSTM, which steps through a piece one step at a time, shorter loops, and with few copies they are what allows more minibatches (one copy needs k pieces for k minibatches). Pieces shorter than the rollout cost one more actor pass per update, for their start memories.

docs.title: Off-policy: sequence replay
docs.text:
The replay agents (SAC, ASAC, REDQ, TD3) store whole trajectories and learn from contiguous sequences, as R2D2 does (Kapturowski et al., 2019):

from ajax import SAC

agent = SAC(
    "Pendulum-v1",
    memory={"kind": "lstm", "hidden_size": 32},
    burn_in=4,  # steps that warm the memory up, without gradients
    sequence_length=8,  # steps learned from after the burn-in
    stored_state=True,  # start from the memory the actor had when it acted
    learning_starts=200,
    batch_size=32,
)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=400)

Each sampled sequence has burn_in + sequence_length + 1 steps. The memory starts from zero, runs through the first burn_in steps with the current networks and no gradient, and the losses then train on the next sequence_length steps. The burn-in lets the memory reach a realistic state before the steps that are learned from. With stored_state=True the buffer also stores the actor's memory at every step, and the actor starts the learned steps from the memory it had when it acted; the critics, which do not run while acting, are still burned in from zero. Kapturowski et al. found stored state better than a zero start with burn-in at keeping the replayed memory close to the one the policy had. The defaults are burn_in=8, sequence_length=16, stored_state=False. The agent refuses at construction a learning_starts that would not leave each copy one whole sequence before the first update (learning_starts // n_envs must exceed burn_in + sequence_length + 1), and stored_state=True without memory=.

A recurrent critic's memory reads each step's observation and the action taken before it. The action the loss asks about joins after the memory, at the critic's head, so asking about another action does not change what the critic remembers (the recurrent off-policy critic of Ni et al., 2022).

With memory, SAC, TD3 and REDQ accept no expert policy and no extensions (behaviour cloning included, which is the CloningPretrain extension), and ASAC and PPO no extensions, yet: they raise an error when training starts rather than run untested combinations. APG takes memory and extensions together.

docs.title: Evaluation and deployment
docs.text: Evaluation runs its own copies of the environment, so each evaluation episode starts the memory from zero, as a deployed policy would. A PID policy takes no memory: its integral and difference already carry the past (see Networks).

docs.title: Networks and the PID policy
docs.text: An agent's networks are set by its constructor: the hidden layers as a tuple of strings, initialisers by name, optional normalisation and an image encoder. The actor can also be a PID controller whose gains the agent learns.

docs.title: Hidden layers
docs.text:
An architecture is a tuple read left to right. A number adds a dense layer of that width; a name adds an activation:

from ajax import PPO

agent = PPO(
    "CartPole-v1",
    n_envs=8,
    n_steps=128,
    actor_architecture=("64", "tanh", "64", "tanh"),
    critic_architecture=("256", "relu", "256", "relu"),
    encoder_kernel_init="orthogonal(np.sqrt(2))",  # the hidden layers' kernels
    critic_bias_init="0.0",  # a number gives a constant initialiser
    encoder_layer_norm=True,  # a LayerNorm after the hidden layers
)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=2_048)

The activations are relu, tanh, leaky_relu, swish, silu and mish; a callable works too. "layernorm" adds a LayerNorm where it stands, so ("256", "layernorm", "relu", "256", "layernorm", "relu") is RLPD's critic (Ball et al., 2023). The agent adds its output heads after the hidden layers: the policy's mean and standard deviation, the value, the Q-values. DQN and PQN take a single architecture for their Q-network.

Each agent's default follows its paper or reference implementation:

Default Agents ("256", "relu", "256", "relu") SAC, ASAC, REDQ, TD3 ("256", "leaky_relu", "256", "leaky_relu") AVG ("128", "tanh", "128", "tanh") PPO ("64", "tanh", "64", "tanh") APO ("128", "relu", "128", "relu") DQN, PQN, UDRL, APG (its controller)

DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 build their own networks to their papers' specifications: see World models.

docs.title: Initialisers
docs.text:
Kernels start from an orthogonal initialiser with gain 1 and biases from zero, except the policy's output layer (the mean, or the logits for discrete actions), whose kernel starts from orthogonal(0.01): a near-zero first mean, or a near-uniform first policy (TD3's deterministic actor starts its last layer uniform in ±3e-3, as DDPG does), and APO's hidden layers, which start as its reference code's ("torch_linear", below). Initialisers are named by string:

  • "orthogonal(0.01)", "lecun_uniform", or any other factory in flax.linen.initializers, with its argument in brackets (np, jnp and math may appear in it, as in "orthogonal(np.sqrt(2))");
  • "zeros", and "trunc_normal_fan_in(1.0)" (DreamerV3's initialiser);
  • a number such as "0.0" or "-1.0", for a constant.

PPO and APO take three of them: encoder_kernel_init for the hidden layers' kernels, actor_bias_init for the policy head's bias and critic_bias_init for the value head's. PPO also takes mean_kernel_init (below). encoder_kernel_init="torch_linear" starts each hidden layer as torch's nn.Linear does: its kernel and its bias both uniform in ±1/sqrt(fan_in), the fan-in being the layer's input width.

docs.title: Layer normalisation
docs.text:
The hidden layers form an encoder that the output heads read. encoder_layer_norm=True adds a LayerNorm on its output. It is off by default, because the SAC, TD3, PPO and DQN papers use plain MLPs. PPO takes it as an argument. SAC, ASAC, REDQ, APO and DQN, and TD3's critics (not its actor), read it from the network configuration, which you can set before training:

from ajax import SAC

agent = SAC("Pendulum-v1", learning_starts=500)
agent.network_args = agent.network_args.replace(encoder_layer_norm=True)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_000)

UDRL turns it on for its policy and APG's controller always keeps a LayerNorm on its encoder, as Ajax's earlier networks did. PQN puts one after every hidden layer, as its paper does, whatever the setting. AVG normalises its penultimate features instead, as its paper does, which overrides the setting.

docs.title: The policy head
docs.text:
PPO exposes the policy head's options. By default its Gaussian learns one log standard deviation per action dimension, whatever the observation, starting at 0 (a standard deviation of 1) and never clipped (log_std_bounds=None), as PPO's reference code does: OpenAI Baselines at ea25b9e (ppo2's common/distributions.py:96-106; ppo1's ppo1/mlp_policy.py:36-39, with gaussian_fixed_var=True), CleanRL at fe8d8a0 (ppo_continuous_action.py:129) and PureJaxRL at 31756b1 (ppo_continuous_action.py:41). log_std_state_independent=False with log_std_init=-1.0 builds the head PPO had before, SAC's: a log standard deviation computed from the observation, which log_std_bounds=(-20.0, 2.0) clips as SAC's is. APO sets its reference code's head (xtma/apo, built on the authors' rlpyt fork): one learned log standard deviation per dimension, starting at 0 and unclipped by default (log_std_bounds=None), around a mean passed through tanh (tanh_mean), with an unsquashed sample; its mean layer is lecun_uniform. The other agents clip theirs, a PID policy's included, to (-20.0, 2.0).

Argument Default (PPO) Effect log_std_state_independent True one learned log standard deviation per action dimension; False computes it from the observation log_std_init 0.0 the initial log standard deviation log_std_bounds None the (low, high) clip of the log standard deviation, whichever head (or PID policy) learns it, low < high (the agent, its network config and the actor refuse others); None leaves it unclipped mean_kernel_init None: orthogonal(0.01), a near-zero first mean the initialiser of the mean's output layer squash False tanh on the sampled action, with the matching log-probability correction (Squashing)

docs.title: Squashing
docs.text:
SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG and UDRL's continuous policy, and PPO's with squash=True, act through tanh, which keeps actions in [-1, 1]. The squashing is one wrapper, not an option of each head: Squashed(actor) wraps any actor, and its policy is squash(pi) of the actor's: Squash(pi) for a distribution, tanh of the action for TD3's deterministic one. Squashed shares the actor's parameters, so they are saved and read under the same names as the actor's alone.

Squash (in ajax.networks.distributions) takes any distrax distribution, its latent, pi.distribution. Sampling and log-probabilities are exact. log_prob(action) inverts tanh, which float32 cannot do once the action rounds to ±1; log_prob_from_raw(raw) reads the pre-tanh sample instead, as a squashed PPO does when it recomputes a log-probability. Two quantities have no closed form: mean() is tanh of the latent's mean, the action the agent evaluates with, not the mean of the squashed action; entropy(seed) is a one-sample estimate, the latent's entropy plus the tanh log-det-Jacobian at a sample, as brax estimates it. The functions latent, sample_with_raw, log_prob_from_raw and entropy read any policy, squashed or not, so code that uses them works with both.

docs.title: Image observations
docs.text:
PPO, DQN, PQN and UDRL can read images through a convolutional encoder. Ajax flattens image observations, so give the image's shape (height, width, channels) as cnn_image_shape; the encoder reshapes the flat vector back. cnn_extra_obs_dim counts extra scalar entries after the image, which join the image features after the convolutions. cnn_spec sets the convolutions:

from ajax import PQN
from ajax.networks.networks import CNNSpec

# MinAtar observations are 10 x 10 images with 4 channels.
agent = PQN(
    "Breakout-MinAtar",
    cnn_image_shape=(10, 10, 4),
    cnn_spec=CNNSpec(channels=(16, 32), kernel_sizes=(3, 3), strides=(1, 1), feature_dim=128),
)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=2_048)

DQN and PQN default to their reference codes' networks (see their pages); PPO and UDRL to CNNSpec(). CNNSpec() with no arguments is this encoder: two ReLU convolutions of 16 and 32 channels (kernels 4 and 3, stride 2, "SAME" padding), then a 128-wide dense layer, all at flax's default initialisation. The image is read in height, width, channels order. padding takes flax's padding ("VALID" for none), layer_norm=True puts a LayerNorm after every layer, before its ReLU, and kernel_init names the initialiser of every layer, as the network's other *_kernel_init settings do.

docs.title: The PID policy
docs.text:
Many control tasks are run by PID controllers, which engineers can read, tune and certify. The PID policy makes the actor such a controller: its action is

u = Kp e + Ki I + Kd D

where e, I and D are the tracking error, its integral and its difference, which PIDTermsWrapper puts first in the observation. The agent learns the gains. Pass a PIDPolicy as the actor_architecture of any continuous-action agent: SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, AVG, PPO or APO.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from flax import struct
from gymnax.environments import environment, spaces

from ajax import SAC
from ajax.environments.pid_terms import PIDTermsWrapper
from ajax.modules.pid_actor import PIDPolicy, pid_gains


@struct.dataclass
class State(environment.EnvState):
    x: jax.Array  # the controlled value
    r: jax.Array  # its set-point


@struct.dataclass
class Params(environment.EnvParams):
    max_steps_in_episode: int = 10


class Setpoint(environment.Environment):
    """An integrator, x <- x + 4u, that must reach a random set-point r."""

    @property
    def default_params(self):
        return Params()

    def reset_env(self, key, params):
        r = jax.random.uniform(key, minval=-1.0, maxval=1.0)
        state = State(time=0, x=jnp.float32(0.0), r=r)
        return self.get_obs(state), state

    def step_env(self, key, state, action, params):
        x = state.x + 4.0 * jnp.clip(action[0], -1.0, 1.0)
        state = state.replace(x=x, time=state.time + 1)
        return self.get_obs(state), state, -((state.r - x) ** 2), jnp.array(False), {}

    def get_obs(self, state, params=None, key=None):
        return jnp.stack([state.x, state.r])

    def observation_space(self, params):
        return spaces.Box(-jnp.inf, jnp.inf, (2,))

    def action_space(self, params):
        return spaces.Box(-1.0, 1.0, (1,))


# The observation becomes [e, I, D, x, r], with e = r - x.
env = PIDTermsWrapper(Setpoint(), current_idx=(0,), target_idx=(1,), dt=1.0)
agent = SAC(
    env,
    env_params=Params(),
    n_envs=4,
    actor_architecture=PIDPolicy(n_errors=1, gains="fixed"),
    critic_architecture=("64", "relu", "64", "relu"),
    actor_learning_rate=3e-3,
    critic_learning_rate=1e-3,
    gamma=0.9,
    learning_starts=500,
)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=4_000, num_episode_test=4)
gains = pid_gains(state.actor_state.params)  # {"kp", "ki", "kd"}, one value per seed
print({name: value.squeeze() for name, value in gains.items()})

The best controller here is Kp = 1/4, Ki = Kd = 0, which reaches the set-point in one step; the repository's tests check that SAC and PPO find it with longer training.

PIDPolicy has two kinds of gains:

  • gains="fixed" makes the gains the actor's only parameters: a linear map with no bias and no hidden layer. The trained policy deploys as a plain PID with the gains pid_gains reads off it, in the agent's units (below) (Lawrence et al., 2022, tune PID gains with reinforcement learning the same way).
  • gains="observation" predicts the gains from the observation with an MLP of architecture, as gain scheduling does. Read them for given observations with PIDActor(policy, action_dim).apply(params, obs, method="gains"), an array of shape (..., 3, action_dim, n_errors); the parameters of a squashed PID actor are the same.

n_errors is the number of errors the wrapper tracks; with several, each action dimension gets its own gain on each error. The gains start at zero: the untrained controller commands the centre of the action box, which is no action on a symmetric box. The stochastic agents explore with a learned standard deviation that does not depend on the observation, clipped as the agent's other heads are (log_std_bounds: none in PPO and APO by default, [-20, 2] in the others).

Each agent's own output rule applies to u. SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC and AVG squash it with tanh and APO takes tanh(u) as its mean, so the deployed controller is a saturated PID; APO samples unsquashed around tanh(u), PPO around u (unless squash=True), and their samples are clipped to [-1, 1]. Like every action, u is in the agent's units and is then mapped onto the environment's bounds (Actions): the deployed controller is c + h · sat(u), with c the centre of the action box, h its half-width and sat the agent's tanh or clip. The learned gains are therefore normalised: a PID written in the environment's units has gains h · K (for small signals, where tanh is close to linear) and the offset c. Observation normalisation leaves the error terms raw, so the gains act on errors in the environment's units, while the gain network of gains="observation" reads the rest of the observation normalised.

A PID policy needs a continuous action space and takes no memory: its memory is the integral and the difference in the observation.

Two other PID features are separate from this one. APG's in-context controller ends with a learnable PID layer on its network's output: see APG. SAC's use_pid_policy lets SAC tune the gains of an expert controller: see Expert guidance.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: A run's time splits into two parts: compiling the program, and running it. For short runs and hyperparameter sweeps the first often dominates; for long runs, the second. This page says what Ajax does about each and how to get the most out of a machine. The numbers come from PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md, where every measurement is described in full. They belong to the machine they were measured on: use them for orders of magnitude, not as promises. They are CPU measurements unless a line says otherwise.

docs.title: The compile cache
docs.text:
train compiles the whole run, environment included, into one program. That takes seconds to tens of seconds, and a fresh Python process would pay it every time. So import ajax points JAX's persistent compile cache at ~/.cache/ajax/jax_compile_cache: a later process that compiles the same program loads it from disk instead.

On the report's Plane3DCircle SAC scenario, run on a GPU, a second launch of the same script took 3.35 s instead of 16.26 s, compile and warm-up fell from 21.5 s to 4.9 s, and peak GPU memory fell from 302 MB to 15 MB, because the compiler's scratch memory is never allocated.

What to know about it:

  • It serves relaunches, not new trials. A rerun of the same script, or a repeated or resumed trial, loads its program from the cache. A new trial of a hyperparameter sweep is a different program: its hyperparameters are compiled in as constants, so it compiles from scratch. The budget, the agent's settings and the shapes are all part of the program.
  • A logged run is not cached. JAX never stores a program that contains a host callback, and the logging worker is fed by one. A run with a LoggingConfig compiles in every new process.
  • One subdirectory per machine and version. Entries are kept per CPU model, architecture, and Python, JAX and jaxlib versions, so environments with different versions, or machines sharing a home directory, do not load each other's programs.
  • Nothing trims it on its own. Clear the directory yourself if it grows too large, or call ajax._compile_cache.prune(root, max_bytes), which deletes the least recently used files until the rest fit (the repository's CI does this once per job).
  • AJAX_JAX_COMPILE_CACHE_DIR moves the cache; AJAX_NO_COMPILE_CACHE=1 turns it off.

docs.title: Seeds share one program
docs.text:
train runs all seeds as one vmapped program, so the fixed cost of compiling and launching is paid once for all of them; running seeds in separate calls pays it again for each. Until the device is busy, extra seeds add little time. An early GPU measurement of SAC, from May 2026 on an older version of Ajax, with small replay buffers and short runs (benchmarks/seed_scaling.jsonl, benchmarks/seed_scaling_p3d.jsonl):

Seeds Pendulum, wall time Plane3DCircle, wall time 1 9.81 s 15.77 s 4 10.51 s 17.46 s 16 10.43 s 18.75 s 32 11.08 s 19.12 s 100 18.37 s

Thirty-two seeds gave 28 times the throughput of one on Pendulum, and a hundred seeds 86 times on Plane3DCircle. Each seed of a replay agent keeps its own buffer, so memory grows with the number of seeds.

The scaling depends on the workload. In the report's scan of real hyperparameter sweeps (wide networks, critic ensembles), going from 20 to 50 seeds made the time per seed and step worse for several method and environment pairs, by up to 81%. Measure your own configuration before settling on a seed count.

docs.title: Parallel environments
docs.text: n_envs copies of the environment step together inside each seed, as one vectorised operation. Unlike seeds, they change the algorithm: an off-policy agent makes one update per iteration, so more copies at a fixed budget mean fewer updates (Training). Pick n_envs for the learning you want, then use seeds to fill the device.

docs.title: CPU or GPU
docs.text:
Small networks on gymnax tasks train well on a CPU: every agent-speed number below is a CPU number, and Ajax makes no claim about its speed on a GPU. A GPU has more room for parallel work: many seeds, many environment copies, wide networks, or a physics simulator such as Brax or Playground. The logging worker always runs on the CPU, so it never takes GPU memory. On a CPU, Playground uses MJX's pure-JAX implementation.

To keep a run on the CPU of a machine with a GPU, set JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu (and CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" to hide the GPU entirely). The repository's tests and benchmarks run this way, so they never compete with an experiment on the GPU.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Evaluation runs num_episode_test whole episodes every log_frequency steps, on top of training: evaluate as often as your curves need, not more. Without a LoggingConfig the evaluation is not compiled at all, and the program can be cached.

docs.title: Agent speeds
docs.text:
benchmarks/agent_bench.py times every agent on a fixed task (CartPole for DQN, PQN, PPO and DreamerV3, a Pendulum tracking task for APG, Pendulum for the others), 4 environment copies, 8,000 steps, one seed, 3 trials, the compile cache off, on a Mac's CPU. Every agent updates within the run: SAC, TD3, REDQ and ASAC start at step 1,000 instead of their default 10,000. Medians of the three trials, from the baseline recorded on 2026-10-12:

Agent Steps per second, execution Steps per second, whole run Compile and warm-up (s) PQN 36,961 7,358 1.0 APG 34,958 5,339 1.6 PPO 17,817 4,298 2.0 DQN 16,662 6,395 0.9 APO 16,390 4,024 2.0 UDRL 12,575 4,441 1.4 AVG 9,460 4,027 1.5 TD3 2,659 1,961 1.4 SAC 2,218 1,635 3.8 ASAC 1,254 1,032 1.6 DreamerV3 367 275 12.9 TDMPC2 292 245 7.3 REDQ 47 47 1.7

"Execution" leaves out the time JAX spends tracing, lowering and compiling the program; "whole run" includes it, because every trial builds a fresh agent, whose program is traced again. REDQ is slow by design: from step 1,000 it makes 20 updates of 10 critics per environment step. UDRL's trials spread the most. DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 run at reduced presets (DreamerV3's smallest size, "1m"; a TD-MPC2 narrowed to 64-unit layers and a smaller planner); at its paper's defaults TD-MPC2 would take minutes per bench run on a CPU, since it updates its model and plans at every environment step. Speeds on your machine will differ; the ratios between agents are the useful part. Developer performance explains how to run the benchmark and the 10% no-regression rule every change follows.

docs.title: Other measured costs
docs.text:
• The action map. Mapping every continuous action onto the environment's bounds (Actions) cost nothing measurable: SAC +0.1%, TD3 +2.8% and PPO +1.0% steps per second, within noise.
  • Playground fresh resets. Drawing a new initial state per episode (the default) costs a reset per episode. On CheetahRun, whose reset runs a 200-step stabilisation, SAC's iterations took about 2% longer, and compile plus first run grew from 36 s to 59 s per cold process.
  • Brax resets. Ajax's Brax wrapper computes a reset only on steps where some copy's episode ended. differentiable_reset=True computes one every step, which cost about 7-13% of a step's time in the report's measurement.
  • Memory blocks in the replay agents: see Memory.

docs.title: Training an agent
docs.text: Every agent trains the same way: build it with an environment and its hyperparameters, then call train. This page covers the arguments every agent shares, what train does with them and what it gives back.

docs.title: Building an agent
docs.text:
An agent's constructor takes the environment first, then its paper's hyperparameters, then extensions=():

from ajax import SAC

agent = SAC(
    "Pendulum-v1",  # an environment id, or a prebuilt environment
    n_envs=4,  # parallel copies of the environment
    actor_architecture=("256", "relu", "256", "relu"),
    critic_architecture=("256", "relu", "256", "relu"),
    gamma=0.99,
    learning_starts=1_000,
)

The defaults follow each paper or its reference implementation; the algorithm pages list them and every deviation. Most agents accept the arguments below; DQN and PQN take one learning_rate and one architecture for their Q-network instead of an actor and a critic.

Argument What it sets Page n_envs parallel environment copies per seed below actor_learning_rate, critic_learning_rate a number, or a schedule of the optimiser step below actor_architecture, critic_architecture hidden layers, or a PID policy for the actor Networks env_params gymnax environment parameters Environments episode_length, action_repeat episode length and repeat of a Brax or Playground id Environments normalize_observations, normalize_rewards running normalisation Environments max_grad_norm global-norm gradient clipping (None: off); twin and ensemble critics are each clipped on their own weight_decay decoupled (AdamW) weight decay of the network optimisers, multiplied by the learning rate: each step multiplies the parameters by 1 - lr * weight_decay (0: plain Adam) memory a recurrent memory block Memory extensions research features: experts, exploration, diagnostics Extensions

An agent refuses what it cannot do when you build it, not halfway through a run: memory on an agent without memory support, SAC on a discrete action space, action_repeat on a gymnax environment, an extension that needs a step the agent's loop never runs or data its replay does not keep (the extension checks list them all).

Each agent also records its run configuration in agent.config: every constructor argument by name (TDMPC2MultiTask leaves out its dataset and evaluation environments), plus algo_name. The loggers store it with each run (Logging).

docs.title: train
docs.text:
from ajax import SAC

agent = SAC("Pendulum-v1", learning_starts=1_000)
state, out = agent.train(
    seed=[1, 2, 3],  # one run per seed, all in one program
    n_timesteps=2_000,  # environment steps this call trains for
    num_episode_test=10,  # test episodes per evaluation
    logging_config=None,  # None: no evaluation, and out is None
    initial_state=None,  # or a state to continue from
    total_timesteps=None,  # the run's horizon; None: this call's end
)

docs.title: The budget
docs.text:
n_timesteps counts environment steps summed over the n_envs copies. An off-policy agent collects one step in each copy per iteration, so 100,000 steps with n_envs=4 are 25,000 iterations. An on-policy agent (PPO, APO, PQN) collects a rollout of n_steps per copy per iteration and trains in whole rollouts: it runs n_timesteps // (n_envs * n_steps) + 1 of them, so it can stop a little past the budget.

The off-policy agents act uniformly at random and do not update until learning_starts steps are collected: 10,000 by default for SAC, TD3, REDQ and ASAC, 1,000 for DQN, 0 for AVG. A short test run must lower it, or the agent never trains.

docs.title: Seeds
docs.text:
seed is one integer or a list. Each seed starts from jax.random.PRNGKey(seed), and train runs all of them at once with jax.vmap: one compilation, one program, every seed in step. More seeds cost little extra time until the device is full (Performance has the measurements), so run the seeds you need in one call rather than one call per seed.

Every array in the returned state has the seed axis first. Seed i's part is jax.tree.map(lambda x: x[i], state).

The same seed on the same machine and library versions gives the same run. Two programs compiled apart, or on different hardware, may round differently, so do not expect identical numbers across machines.

docs.title: Parallel environments
docs.text:
n_envs copies of the environment step together inside each seed. They collect more data per iteration, and each copy starts its own episodes. For an off-policy agent each iteration still makes one update (or the number its own settings ask for), so at a fixed budget more copies mean fewer updates. The defaults differ by agent:

n_envs default Agents 1 SAC, ASAC, REDQ, TD3, IQL, AVG, DQN, UDRL, DAgger, TDMPC2 4 PPO, APO 8 PQN, APG 16 DreamerV3

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
With a logging_config, the agent is evaluated every log_frequency steps on num_episode_test episodes, run in parallel in a separate copy of the environment. The policy acts deterministically: the mean action of a continuous policy, the most likely one of a discrete policy.

Each evaluation draws fresh initial states and noise. Its key is folded from the number of evaluations made so far, out of an evaluation key split apart from the training key when the run starts. So two evaluations of a seed see different episodes, the same seed always sees the same ones, and evaluating repeats none of the random draws the training makes. Every agent follows this, the world models included.

UDRL evaluates through the same code, with the command (desired return and horizon) it would collect with; DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 act through their own latent policy or planner. Their pages say what they log.

docs.title: What train returns
docs.text:
train returns (state, out).

  • Without a logging_config, out is None. The evaluation is not even compiled into the program.
  • With one, out holds the evaluations: a dictionary from each logged name to an array of shape (seeds, evaluations). out["timestep"] says when each evaluation ran. A call that evaluates fewer times than its maximum pads the rest with -1 (the timestep) and NaN (everything else).
  • APG returns its per-update metrics instead. See APG.

The logged names are listed in Logging.

state is the agent's whole state: actor_state and critic_state (the networks, their optimisers and parameters), collector_state (the environments, the replay buffer, the step counter timestep), the random keys (rng for training, eval_rng for evaluation), the evaluation count n_logs, and each extension's state.

docs.title: Continuing a run
docs.text:
Pass a returned state back as initial_state to train further:

from ajax import PPO

agent = PPO("CartPole-v1", n_envs=8, n_steps=128)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=8_192)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=8_192, initial_state=state)
print(state.collector_state.timestep)  # [18432 18432]

The second call continues from the first call's timestep. Its schedules (the extensions', the training fraction, the exploration, the logging's end) continue where they stopped instead of restarting, and run to the horizon total_timesteps. By default that is the call's own end, the timestep reached plus n_timesteps, so a schedule set as a fraction of training, such as DQN's epsilon decay, has already finished at the end of a first call. To split a run and keep the schedules of one call, pass the whole run's horizon to every call. A call whose n_timesteps would take it past the horizon is refused, so the last call trains the rest. An on-policy call trains in whole rollouts plus one and ends up to a rollout past its budget (the last call past the horizon, as one call does), so take the rest from the timestep reached:

total = 16_384
state, _ = agent.train(seed=[0, 1], n_timesteps=8_192, total_timesteps=total)
reached = int(state.collector_state.timestep[0])  # 9216: one rollout past
state, _ = agent.train(
    seed=[0, 1],
    n_timesteps=total - reached,
    initial_state=state,
    total_timesteps=total,
)
print(state.collector_state.timestep)  # [17408 17408], as one call of 16_384

To resume in another process, save the state first: Checkpoints and resuming.

The call may reuse the memory of the state you pass in. Read or save anything you need from it before the call.

docs.title: Training offline
docs.text:
A replay agent (SAC, TD3, REDQ, ASAC, DQN, IQL) can train on a transition dataset alone, with no environment step. train_offline(dataset, n_updates) puts the dataset's rows in the replay and in the normalisers, then runs the agent's own update n_updates times. With a logging_config it evaluates every log_frequency updates and logs the updates done as the timestep. The state it returns is back at timestep 0, so train(initial_state=state, ...) then fine-tunes it online, its replay keeping the dataset's rows:

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

from ajax import TD3
from ajax.buffers.dataset import record
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig


def pd_expert(obs):
    theta = jnp.arctan2(obs[..., 1], obs[..., 0])
    return jnp.clip(-(2.0 * theta + 0.5 * obs[..., 2]), -2.0, 2.0)[..., None]


agent = TD3("Pendulum-v1", learning_starts=0)  # online: update from the first step
data = record(pd_expert, agent.env_args, jax.random.PRNGKey(0), n_steps=1_000)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=500, use_wandb=False)
state, offline = agent.train_offline(data, n_updates=1_000, seed=[0], logging_config=logging)
print(offline["timestep"])  # [[ 500 1000]]: updates done
state, online = agent.train(seed=[0], n_timesteps=1_000, initial_state=state)

train_offline runs the agent's own update, with its extensions' terms: TD3+BC is TD3 with a cloning term, and IQL an agent of its own. PriorData(dataset, offline_updates=N) runs the same updates inside the pre-training of an ordinary train call, without evaluations.

docs.title: Learning-rate schedules
docs.text:
A learning rate can be a function of the optimiser step, such as an optax schedule:

import optax

from ajax import PPO

# Decays linearly to zero over the first 1,000 optimiser steps.
schedule = optax.linear_schedule(init_value=3e-4, end_value=0.0, transition_steps=1_000)
agent = PPO(
    "CartPole-v1",
    n_envs=8,
    n_steps=128,
    actor_learning_rate=schedule,
    critic_learning_rate=schedule,
)
state, _ = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=8_192)

The step counts gradient updates, not environment steps: here 9 rollouts of 10 epochs of 2 minibatches, 180 steps. ajax.schedule.warmup_cosine_schedule builds the linear warm-up then cosine decay used by APG's in-context controller.

docs.title: The shared training loop
docs.text:
Most agents run on one loop, TrainLoop in agents/loop.py. An agent brings only its algorithm: how to build a fresh state and how to make one update. The loop does everything else, the same way for every agent:

fresh run:  build the agent's state, then each extension's state
            and its one-shot pre-training (if any)
resumed:    take the state passed as initial_state
repeat:     collect one step per environment (off-policy)
              or one rollout (on-policy)
            once learning_starts steps are collected:
              update, then let the extensions act after the update
            every log_frequency steps: evaluate and log

The world models (DreamerV3, TD-MPC2) act through their own planner or latent policy and decide how many updates to make per step, but they plug those pieces into the same loop, in the same order. UDRL runs its own iteration (a segment, its replay of segments, its command statistics, its updates) inside the loop's train function. APG and the offline TDMPC2MultiTask, whose iterations differ more, reuse the loop's pieces (the fresh state, the extensions' folds, the evaluation) rather than the loop itself.

Why one loop: collection, the learning_starts gate, the extensions, evaluation, logging and resuming then behave identically across agents and are fixed in one place. A bug fixed there is fixed for every agent, and an extension written for one agent works on the others.

The whole loop is one jax.lax.scan inside one jax.jit, vmapped over the seeds. Python runs once, to build the program; after that the CPU or GPU runs the entire training without returning to Python, except to hand the logs to the logging worker. Architecture describes the loop for contributors.

docs.title: World models
docs.text:
Most agents in Ajax are model-free: they learn values and a policy directly from the experience they collect. A world model agent first learns a model of the environment, a network that predicts what happens next and what reward follows, and then uses that model to decide how to act. Learning the model reuses every transition many times, so these agents tend to need fewer environment steps; the price is more computation per step.

Ajax has two world-model agents, each reproducing its paper's official code:

  • DreamerV3 (Hafner, Pasukonis, Ba and Lillicrap, Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models, 2023; Nature, 2025) learns its policy inside the model, by imagination.
  • TD-MPC2 (Hansen, Su and Wang, TD-MPC2: Scalable, Robust World Models for Continuous Control, ICLR 2024) plans with the model at every step.

docs.title: DreamerV3 in plain words
docs.text:
DreamerV3's world model is recurrent: it compresses everything seen so far in the episode into a latent state, part deterministic memory, part a set of discrete random variables. From that state it learns to reconstruct the observation, predict the reward and predict whether the episode continues. It trains on sequences replayed from a buffer.

The actor learns only from imagined experience. Starting from states the model has encoded, the model imagines 15 steps ahead under the current actor; the critic learns the value of those imagined trajectories (plus a smaller term on the replayed ones), and the actor learns to make them better. The model, the actor and the critic take one joint gradient step per update.

A few choices make one set of hyperparameters work across very different tasks: rewards and values are predicted on a log-like (symlog) scale over fixed bins, returns are normalised by their spread, and the optimiser clips gradients relative to the size of the weights. Because the model carries memory, DreamerV3 handles partially observed tasks without a memory= option.

docs.title: TD-MPC2 in plain words
docs.text:
TD-MPC2's world model has no decoder: it never reconstructs observations. An encoder maps the observation to a latent state, and the model learns to predict the next latent state, the reward and the value (an ensemble of Q-functions) in that latent space. The model is trained to be consistent over a short horizon of replayed steps (3 by default).

To act, it plans. At every step, a sampling planner (MPPI) tries hundreds of short action sequences in the latent model, scores each by its predicted rewards plus the value at the end, and refines the best ones over a few iterations; a learned policy proposes some of the candidates. The first action of the best plans is executed. Planning makes each step slower, but the agent corrects its course at every step.

TDMPC2MultiTask trains one such model offline on the data of several tasks, with a learned task embedding; it does not plan while training.

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text:
DreamerV3 TD-MPC2 Actions discrete and continuous continuous only Episodes that end early (terminations) yes, a model head predicts them refused by default; episodic=True accepts them Partial observability built in: the model is recurrent no memory Who acts the actor, learned in imagination: one network pass per step the planner: 512 candidate sequences, 6 refinements per step by default, some proposed by a learned policy Several tasks in one model no TDMPC2MultiTask, offline Model sizes model_size="1m" to "400m" (default "12m") model_size=1, 5, 19, 48, 317 (millions of parameters; default 5) n_timesteps counts rows: one per environment per step, reset rows included agent steps (rows, one more per finished episode, with episodic=True) Default n_envs 16 1

In short:

  • Discrete actions or hidden state: DreamerV3.
  • Continuous control with fixed-length episodes (the DeepMind Control tasks, for example): TD-MPC2, whose paper-era code is written for exactly that. With terminations, it needs episodic=True, grafted from its later code.
  • One model for many tasks: TDMPC2MultiTask.
  • A cheap baseline or a quick experiment: neither. Both are slow on a CPU (see below); start with a model-free agent such as SAC or PPO.

Both take flat observation vectors only, and want the environment's raw observations and rewards: do not normalise them, the agents do their own scaling as their papers do. Both run gymnax, Brax and MuJoCo Playground environments, and act in [-1, 1] mapped onto the environment's bounds, as their papers and every Ajax agent do (Actions). Both take action_repeat and episode_length for their papers' DeepMind Control protocol (action_repeat=2, episode_length=1000 simulator steps). Both evaluate on fresh episodes at each evaluation, as every agent does (Training). Both take extensions in the phases every agent runs (pretrain, post_update, eval_metrics) and no others.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The smallest presets on Pendulum, as a first look. On a laptop CPU, the DreamerV3 run below took about five minutes and the TD-MPC2 run about two (compilation included):

# doc: skip (about five minutes on a CPU)
from ajax import DreamerV3
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = DreamerV3("Pendulum-v1", model_size="1m", n_envs=4)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=1_000, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=2_000, logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Train/episodic mean reward"])  # the score the paper reports

# doc: skip (about two minutes on a CPU)
from ajax import TDMPC2
from ajax.logging.wandb_logging import LoggingConfig

agent = TDMPC2("Pendulum-v1", model_size=1)  # the first 1,000 steps are random (seed_steps)
logging = LoggingConfig(config={}, log_frequency=600, use_wandb=False)
state, evaluations = agent.train(seed=0, n_timesteps=1_200, num_episode_test=2,
                                 logging_config=logging)
print(evaluations["Eval/episodic mean reward"])

The algorithm pages give faster configurations, the paper protocols, every hyperparameter, and the multi-task pipeline (single-task runs, then export_episodes and pool_tasks, then TDMPC2MultiTask).

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Both agents are much heavier than the model-free ones. In the CPU learning checks recorded in PERFORMANCE_REPORT.md, on a busy shared machine, TD-MPC2 at model_size=1 took 45 minutes for 6,000 Pendulum steps over two seeds, and DreamerV3 at "1m" 68 minutes for 20,000 Pendulum rows. Plan on a GPU for anything beyond a check.

Memory grows with the replay. DreamerV3 stores about 8 KB per row at "12m" on a 24-dimensional observation: the paper's DeepMind Control protocol (250,000 rows) needs about 2 GB of replay per seed, and about 3 GB with the training step's working set. TD-MPC2's whole-episode replay is smaller: about 124 MB per seed for a million steps of DMC Walker. It holds at most the run's steps (min(buffer_size, steps), as the reference clamps it), so a short run allocates less. Seeds trained together multiply these figures. Each agent reports its own figure for a configuration as replay_bytes_per_seed, which the loggers also record with the run's configuration.

docs.title: Fidelity
docs.text:
Each agent follows the code that produced its paper's numbers, not the latest version of the official repository: DreamerV3 danijar/dreamerv3 at 2411f7d plus one later bug fix (29eb964), TD-MPC2 nicklashansen/tdmpc2 at b67b21c. Where the paper and that code disagree, Ajax follows the code; paper typos are treated as typos. Asynchronous or unseeded parts of the reference infrastructure are made synchronous and seeded, so a run is reproducible from its seed. Every place where Ajax departs from the reference is listed, with its impact, in the deviations register.

How far this has been checked:

  • Component by component. Tests compare Ajax's pieces with literal transcriptions of the reference functions, and with fixtures recorded by running the pinned reference code itself.
